tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.
Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.
While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.
Leo used to swimming before school every morning.
By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.**

Present perfect "has finished" signals a past action with a link to now, but "last Tuesday" is a finished calendar anchor that closes the time frame. In exam English, an explicit finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2019) almost never pairs with present perfect. Repair to past simple: "Maya finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday."

**Trap:** Learners often keep present perfect because the work is "done," forgetting that a named finished day kills that tense.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Maya finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday."

**B) Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.**

Present perfect "has met" with "since April" correctly shows a Saturday habit that began in the past and still continues. The starting point is named, but the period remains open into the present, so present perfect — not past simple — is the right tense. Frequency ("every Saturday") sits comfortably inside that open span.

Keep this: present perfect correctly marks the open span from April to now.

**C) While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.**

Past continuous "was rehearsing" paints the longer background scene; past simple "went out" marks the sudden blackout that cut across it. That continuous-plus-simple pairing is the standard past storytelling pattern for an interrupt. "While" cues the in-progress action, and "suddenly" cues the short past-simple event.

**Tip:** Longer background action → continuous; shorter interrupt → simple past.

That pairing is sound — continuous background plus simple interrupt.

**D) Leo used to swimming before school every morning.**

Past habit needs "used to" + base verb, so "used to swimming" is broken. Repair to "Leo used to swim before school every morning." Do not confuse this with "be used to + -ing," which means familiarity, not past habit — different structure, different meaning.

**Trap:** The -ing form after "used to" feels natural if you mix it up with "be used to doing."

That form fails here — rewrite as "Leo used to swim before school every morning."

**E) By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.**

The cue "by + future time" signals completion before that deadline, which needs future perfect, not plain "will plant." Repair to "By next Friday, the volunteers will have planted fifty saplings." Plain will only talks about a future intention, not that the planting will already be done by Friday.

**Trap:** "Will plant by Friday" looks acceptable in casual speech but fails the exam completion-before-deadline test.

Reject the plain will; the clean version is "By next Friday, the volunteers will have planted fifty saplings."
tasks.solution_overview:
These five lines warm up classic tense traps: finished time versus present perfect with "since," a continuous background interrupted by a sudden event, the form of "used to," and future perfect with "by."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Match each verb to its time cue before you decide. Calendar anchors such as "last Tuesday" usually kill present perfect; "since" keeps a habit alive into the present; "while" often sets a continuous scene for a short past-simple interrupt; "used to" needs a base verb; and "by + future time" often wants future perfect, not plain will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the highlighted verb against the time expression in the same sentence. If they clash, mark false and name the repair; if they fit the standard pairing, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.
I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.
We visited the science museum in March.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.**

The departure happened before the trolley arrived, so plain past "already left" under-marks the sequence. When two past events stack, mark the earlier one with had + past participle. Repair to past perfect: "The guests had already left when the dessert trolley arrived."

**Trap:** "Already" with past simple looks fine until you notice a second past event that came later.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "The guests had already left when the dessert trolley arrived."

**B) They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.**

Past perfect "had already left" correctly shows that leaving preceded the trolley's arrival. "Already" sits naturally with past perfect in sequenced past narratives and makes the earlier completion clear. This is the repaired version of the A-line trap.

Accept the line: past perfect correctly marks the earlier past action.

**C) Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.**

Stative "know" resists continuous form, so "is knowing" is wrong in careful exam English. Mental-state verbs (know, believe, own) rarely take -ing when they report a state rather than a temporary action. Repair to "Nina knows every lyric in the musical."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Nina knows every lyric in the musical."

**D) I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.**

"Am used to cycling" correctly means accustomed to that rainy-park routine. After "be used to," a gerund is the expected pattern for a recurring activity you find familiar. This is not the same structure as "used to + base verb" for past habit.

**Tip:** "Am/is/are used to + -ing" is familiarity — not past habit.

That works — "be used to + -ing" correctly marks rainy-park familiarity.

**E) We visited the science museum in March.**

Past simple "visited" with "in March" correctly places a finished outing in a closed time frame. Once the month is named as finished, past simple is the safe default — there is no open link to now that would call for present perfect.

This is sound: closed past time correctly takes past simple.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set contrasts past simple with past perfect in a sequenced narrative, tests a stative continuous trap, and separates "be used to" familiarity from ordinary past simple with a closed time frame.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When two past events stack, the earlier one often needs past perfect. Stative verbs such as "know" resist continuous forms. "Be used to + -ing" means accustomed to, which is different from "used to + V1" for past habit. A finished outing with "in March" is safe past simple territory.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask which action happened first, whether the verb is stative, and whether the time frame is still open. Match the verb form to that timeline before you tick true or false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.
By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.
She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.
This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.
We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.**

"Yesterday evening" is finished time, so present perfect "has changed" clashes with the time adverb. Present perfect hates explicit finished-time adverbs in exam answers. Repair to past simple: "The coach changed the starting line-up yesterday evening."

**Trap:** The change still "matters" now, but a finished-time adverb still blocks present perfect.

That tense clashes with finished time — rewrite as "The coach changed the starting line-up yesterday evening."

**B) By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.**

Completion before a future ferry arrival needs future perfect in the main clause. Plain "will pack" only talks about a future intention, not completion before that docking. Repair to "By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will have packed our bags."

**Trap:** Keeping present "docks" in the time clause fools some writers into keeping plain will in the main clause too.

Mark it wrong and prefer "…we will have packed our bags."

**C) She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.**

"In 2016" closes the period, so present perfect "has been" is wrong for that finished role. A named past year usually blocks present perfect because the time frame no longer touches now. Repair to past simple: "She was a library volunteer here in 2016."

Reject present perfect with a closed year; use "She was a library volunteer here in 2016."

**D) This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.**

"Belong" is stative, so "is belonging" is wrong. Possession and membership verbs stay in simple forms in formal exam prose. Repair to "This scarf belongs to my grandmother."

That continuous fails on a stative — prefer "This scarf belongs to my grandmother."

**E) We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.**

"Used to camp" correctly reports a discontinued past habit by the lake. The later flood explains why the habit no longer holds, which is exactly what "used to" signals. The base verb after "used to" is the right form for past habit.

Keep this: "used to + base verb" correctly marks a discontinued lake habit.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one sentence survives this card. Hunt finished-time clashes with present perfect, demand future perfect after "by the time," reject a closed year with present perfect, and refuse stative continuous — the lone survivor is clean past habit with "used to."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Yesterday evening" and "in 2016" are finished time and block present perfect. "By the time + future" usually wants will have + past participle. "Belong" is stative and stays simple. "Used to + base verb" correctly reports a discontinued past habit.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline every time cue first. If present perfect or continuous fights that cue, mark false; only keep the line that pairs form and meaning cleanly.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.
While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.
By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.
Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.
Omar is owning three vintage cameras.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.**

Present perfect "has displayed" with "since the renovation" correctly links an ongoing practice to its start point. The renovation is a starting boundary that still shapes what the gallery does now, so the open span belongs in present perfect.

Accept the line: "since" keeps present perfect alive for an ongoing gallery practice.

**B) While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.**

Past continuous "were gardening" sets the neighbours' background activity; past simple "slipped" marks the fox's short interrupt through the fence. That is the standard past pairing for an action in progress when something else struck.

That pairing works — continuous gardening background plus a simple fox interrupt.

**C) By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.**

Future perfect "will have learned" places completion of the twelve pieces before year-end. The deadline "by" tells you the learning will already be done at that point, which is exactly future perfect's job.

Keep this: "by" correctly takes future perfect for prior completion.

**D) Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.**

"Used to play" correctly describes a past outdoor habit that has changed on this street. Frequency through dusk fits the "used to + V1" pattern for discontinued habits. Nothing in the form clashes with the meaning.

This is sound: past habit is correctly marked with "used to + base verb."

**E) Omar is owning three vintage cameras.**

Stative "own" should be simple "owns," not continuous. Ownership verbs almost never take continuous in exam English because they report a state, not a temporary activity. Repair to "Omar owns three vintage cameras."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Omar owns three vintage cameras."
tasks.solution_overview:
Four sentences are clean; only the stative continuous fails. Confirm "since" with present perfect, background continuous plus interrupt, future perfect with "by," and past habit before you hunt the ownership trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Since" keeps present perfect alive for an ongoing gallery practice. "While" sets a continuous background for a short past-simple interrupt. "By year-end" invites future perfect. "Used to play" is a textbook past habit. "Own" is stative and should not take continuous.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the four standard pairings first; then ask whether the remaining verb is stative. If it is, reject -ing.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week's briefing.
Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.
The club has published three newsletters this semester.
By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.
When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week's briefing.**

Past simple "explained" correctly anchors a finished talk to "last week's briefing." The briefing is a closed past event, so past simple is the natural choice. There is no open present link that would invite present perfect.

Keep this: explicit past time correctly takes past simple.

**B) Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.**

"Are used to training" correctly means runners are accustomed to that early-winter routine. The gerund after "be used to" is exactly the familiarity pattern you want here. Do not confuse it with "used to + base verb" for past habit.

**Tip:** "Be used to + -ing" = familiarity, not past habit.

That familiarity pattern is sound — "be used to + -ing" fits the early-winter routine.

**C) The club has published three newsletters this semester.**

Present perfect "has published" fits an unfinished period ("this semester") with present relevance. The semester is still open, so the three newsletters stay in present perfect rather than past simple.

Accept the line: an unfinished semester correctly keeps present perfect.

**D) By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.**

Future perfect "will have prepared" correctly places preparation before Friday noon. The clock deadline with "by" is a classic future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that moment.

This works: deadline "by" correctly takes will have + past participle.

**E) When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.**

Past perfect "had already finished" shows the quiz ended before the teacher walked in. The earlier past action needs had + past participle so the sequence is clear against the when-clause arrival.

That sequencing is sound — past perfect marks the earlier of two past events.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are sound. Use this card as a model set for closed past time, "be used to," unfinished-period present perfect, future perfect with "by," and past-perfect sequencing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Last week" locks past simple. "Are used to training" means familiarity with a routine. "This semester" keeps present perfect alive. "By Friday noon" wants future perfect. When one past action finishes before another, past perfect marks the earlier one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each line as a clean template. Confirm the time cue and the verb form agree; do not invent a problem where the pairing is already standard.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have seen that documentary twice already this month.
They are believing the rumours about the new café.
By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.
Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.
We are knowing each other since primary school.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I have seen that documentary twice already this month.**

Present perfect "have seen" with "already" and an unfinished month fits repeated experience that still matters now. The viewings count toward the current month, so present perfect is right — past simple would close the period too early.

Keep this: unfinished time plus "already" correctly takes present perfect.

**B) They are believing the rumours about the new café.**

"Believe" is stative here, so "are believing" is wrong. Opinion verbs (believe, think = opinion) stay simple in careful exam English when they report a held view. Repair to "They believe the rumours about the new café."

Reject the continuous opinion verb — rewrite as "They believe the rumours about the new café."

**C) By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.**

Future perfect "will have reached" places the team's arrival before dawn. The cue "by + future point" demands completion ahead of that moment, not merely a plan to reach it at dawn.

Accept the line: "by + future point" correctly takes will have + past participle.

**D) Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.**

"Used to hate" correctly marks a past taste that no longer holds, and the contrast with "now he loves it" makes the change explicit. That is textbook discontinued habit or state with a present contrast.

That contrast works — "used to" correctly signals a preference that has ended.

**E) We are knowing each other since primary school.**

"Know" is stative, and a continuing relationship with "since" needs present perfect, not continuous. Duration with "since" takes present perfect simple for stative verbs. Repair to "We have known each other since primary school."

**Trap:** Continuous looks tempting for a long relationship, but stative "know" + "since" wants have known.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We have known each other since primary school."
tasks.solution_overview:
Three survivors and two stative continuous fails. Trust present perfect for unfinished time, future perfect for "by," and "used to" for abandoned habits — then reject -ing on believe and know.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Already" and "this month" support present perfect for repeated experience. Opinion "believe" and stative "know" stay simple (or present perfect for continuing "know"). "By dawn" wants future perfect. "Used to hate" marks a past taste that no longer holds.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First lock the clean tense pairings, then scan for illegally continuous stative verbs — those are the false lines here.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.
The trail was still wet when we have arrived.
I am used to the noise from the tram line.
He used to be afraid of public speaking.
By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.**

Present perfect "has lived" with "for six years" correctly shows a Lisbon situation that continues now. The duration is measured up to the present, which is present-perfect territory rather than a finished past stretch.

Keep this: "for + duration" with present perfect marks a situation still true.

**B) The trail was still wet when we have arrived.**

A completed arrival inside a past narrative needs past simple, not present perfect. Mixing a past continuous/simple story with present perfect for the same closed past breaks the timeline. Repair to "The trail was still wet when we arrived."

**Trap:** "Have arrived" can feel "recent," but a past narrative locks the arrival in past simple.

That timeline fails — rewrite as "The trail was still wet when we arrived."

**C) I am used to the noise from the tram line.**

"Am used to the noise" correctly means accustomed to the tram line. After "be used to," a noun works just as well as a gerund — both patterns mark familiarity, not past habit.

**Tip:** After "be used to," use a noun or an -ing form — both are fine.

Accept the line: "be used to + noun" correctly marks familiarity.

**D) He used to be afraid of public speaking.**

"Used to be afraid" correctly describes a past state of fear that has changed. "Used to + be + adjective" is a clean pattern for former feelings or identities, parallel to "used to + V1" for former habits.

This is sound: a former state is correctly marked with "used to be."

**E) By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.**

Future perfect "will have found" places finding seats before the concert begins. Even though the time clause uses present "starts" for future reference, the main clause still needs will have for prior completion.

That works: "by the time + present" correctly takes will have in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch the one timeline clash: a finished past arrival cannot wear present perfect. Everything else — "for," "be used to," "used to be," and future perfect — is clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Present perfect + "for" shows a situation that continues now. A closed past narrative needs past simple for the arrival, not present perfect. "Be used to" + noun means accustomed to. "Used to be" describes a past state that changed. "By the time + present" for future reference still wants will have in the main clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate open duration and future-before-future from closed past storytelling. Only the mixed past narrative fails.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.
She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.
Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.
We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.
My cousins used to visit us every summer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.**

Past simple "closed" with "last Sunday" correctly closes a finished bakery event. The day/date anchor makes past simple the only natural choice — there is no open present span.

Keep this: a day anchor correctly takes past simple.

**B) She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.**

Present perfect "has just baked" marks a recent action with present relevance — the loaf is newly done. "Just" is a classic present-perfect companion in exam English for recent completion that still matters now.

Accept the line: "just" correctly pairs with present perfect for recent baking.

**C) Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.**

"Prefer" is stative, so "is preferring" is wrong. Likes and preferences stay simple unless you force a rare temporary "acting" sense, which exams almost never want. Repair to "Tom prefers tea to coffee these days."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Tom prefers tea to coffee these days."

**D) We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.**

Future perfect "will have walked" correctly projects ten kilometres covered before lunchtime. Quantity completed by a future point is will have territory rather than plain will walk.

This is sound: distance completed "by" a future point takes will have + V3.

**E) My cousins used to visit us every summer.**

"Used to visit" correctly reports a repeated past summer habit. Frequency phrases such as "every summer" sit naturally with "used to" when the visits no longer happen (or are framed as former habit).

That habit reading works — "used to + base verb" fits the summer visits.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four good lines and one stative continuous. Separate closed past ("last Sunday") from recent present perfect ("just"), keep future perfect and past habit, then reject "is preferring."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Day anchors such as "last Sunday" lock past simple. "Just" marks a recent action with present relevance in present perfect. "Prefer" is stative and stays simple. Distance covered "by lunchtime" wants future perfect. Frequency phrases sit naturally with "used to."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each time cue against its usual tense, then scan preferences and likes for illegal continuous forms.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did you ever climb a volcano?
Have you ever climbed a volcano?
While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.
They are used to get up early for rowing practice.
By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Did you ever climb a volcano?**

Life experience up to now needs present perfect in careful exam English. Past simple "Did you ever" is non-standard for open lifetime experience when no finished period is named. Repair to "Have you ever climbed a volcano?"

**Trap:** "Did you ever…?" is common in casual speech, so it looks almost right on the page.

Reject the past-simple experience question — prefer "Have you ever climbed a volcano?"

**B) Have you ever climbed a volcano?**

Present perfect "Have you ever climbed" correctly asks about experience at any time up to now. "Ever" with present perfect is the standard life-experience pattern, contrasting with the broken A-line.

**Tip:** "Ever / never" + present perfect = life experience.

Keep this: "ever" correctly pairs with present perfect for life experience.

**C) While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.**

Past continuous "was reading" sets the balcony background; past simple "started" marks the snow interrupt. Reading was in progress; snow was the sudden change — the standard while-pairing.

That while-pairing is sound — continuous reading plus a simple snow interrupt.

**D) They are used to get up early for rowing practice.**

Familiarity needs "be used to" + -ing (or a noun), never a bare infinitive. Repair to "They are used to getting up early for rowing practice." The bare infinitive after "be used to" is a classic mix-up with "used to get up" (past habit).

**Trap:** "Are used to get" blends familiarity "be used to" with habit "used to + V1."

That form fails — rewrite as "They are used to getting up early for rowing practice."

**E) By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.**

Future perfect "will have completed" places marathon completion before next winter. Seasonal "by next …" deadlines routinely take will have + past participle for prior completion.

Accept the line: "by next + season" correctly takes future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview:
Compare the two experience questions side by side, keep the continuous–simple pair, fix "be used to" + -ing, and lock future perfect with "by next winter."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Lifetime experience up to now needs present perfect with "ever," not past simple "Did you ever" in careful exam English. Background continuous plus simple interrupt stays textbook. After "be used to," you need a gerund, never a bare infinitive. "By next winter" wants future perfect.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat A and B as a minimal pair, then check gerund form after "be used to" and the future-perfect deadline.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app update has crashed twice since midnight.
I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.
We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.
By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.
Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The app update has crashed twice since midnight.**

Present perfect "has crashed" with "since midnight" fits repeated glitches that still matter now. Tech problems counted from a start point into the present stay in present perfect rather than a closed past count.

Keep this: repeated crashes with "since" correctly stay in present perfect.

**B) I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.**

"Understand" is stative, so "was understanding" is wrong in exam English. Use past simple for the sense before the interrupt: "I understood the lecture until the fire alarm rang." Stative verbs rarely take past continuous in exam answers.

**Trap:** Continuous seems to match "until," but stative "understand" still wants simple form.

Mark it wrong and prefer "I understood the lecture until the fire alarm rang."

**C) We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.**

"Used to take" correctly marks a coastal-path habit that ended after the landslide. A later change that blocks the old routine is exactly what "used to" signals, with the base verb in place.

This is sound: a past habit blocked by a later change takes "used to + base verb."

**D) By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.**

Future perfect "will have set up" places the lighting ready before eight o'clock. A clock deadline with "by" is a classic future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that time.

Accept the line: clock "by" correctly takes will have + past participle.

**E) Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.**

Present perfect "has known" with "for a decade" correctly shows a continuing relationship. For stative "know," duration up to now takes have/has known — never "am knowing" or other continuous forms.

**Tip:** "Have known … for" beats any continuous "knowing."

That duration is right — stative "know" with "for" correctly takes present perfect simple.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four keepers and one stative continuous. Trust "since," "used to," future perfect, and "have known" — reject "was understanding."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Present perfect with "since midnight" fits repeated crashes still relevant now. "Understand" is stative and rarely takes past continuous in exams. "Used to take" marks a discontinued route. Clock "by" wants future perfect. Stative "know" with "for" takes present perfect simple.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Approve the four standard tense pairings, then ask whether continuous is trying to attach to a stative verb — that is the false line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.
When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.
She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.
I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.
They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.
tactical_explanations:
**A) When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.**

Both events are in the past, so the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect. Closed past narrative wants had + V3 for the action that finished first. Repair to "When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen."

**Trap:** "Already" tempts present perfect, but a finished past story still needs past perfect for the earlier event.

Reject present perfect in a closed past story — rewrite as "…the sun had already risen."

**B) When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.**

Past perfect "had already risen" correctly places sunrise before the summit arrival. "Already" with past perfect marks the prior completed state clearly against the when-clause past simple.

Keep this: past perfect correctly marks the earlier sunrise.

**C) She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.**

"Seem" is stative, so "is seeming" is wrong. Appearance verbs (seem, appear = look like) stay simple in exam prose when they report how someone looks or comes across. Repair to "She seems tired after the long rehearsal."

Mark it wrong and prefer "She seems tired after the long rehearsal."

**D) I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.**

"Getting used to" correctly means becoming accustomed to the new keyboard. This is the process of adapting, which differs from "be used to" (already adapted). Continuous "getting" fits that in-progress adaptation.

**Tip:** "Get used to" = adapting; "be used to" = already familiar.

That works — "get used to" correctly marks the process of adapting.

**E) They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.**

Future perfect "will have reheated" places the reheating before your arrival. "By the time you arrive" is a standard cue for will have + past participle in the main clause.

Accept the line: "by the time + present" correctly takes will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview:
Contrast the two summit lines carefully, reject stative "seeming," and accept "get used to" plus future perfect as clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

In a closed past narrative, the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect. "Seem" is stative and stays simple. "Get used to" means becoming accustomed — the process of adapting. "By the time you arrive" wants will have in the main clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read A and B as a minimal pair for past perfect versus present perfect, then check stative continuous and the adapting / future-perfect lines.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: How long are you waiting for the night bus?
How long have you been waiting for the night bus?
The river flooded the towpath three times last winter.
Jonas used to living near the botanical gardens.
By Thursday evening, we will have curated the exhibition labels.
tactical_explanations:
**A) How long are you waiting for the night bus?**

Duration up to now with "how long" needs present perfect continuous for an ongoing wait. Present continuous alone describes the current scene but does not cover the stretch from past into now. Repair to "How long have you been waiting for the night bus?"

**Trap:** Present continuous answers "what now?" but not "for how long up to now?"

That duration question fails — prefer "How long have you been waiting for the night bus?"

**B) How long have you been waiting for the night bus?**

Present perfect continuous "have you been waiting" correctly asks about waiting that started earlier and continues. Visible temporary activity plus duration is exactly this form's job — the repaired pair to A.

**Tip:** Ongoing action + duration up to now → have/has been + -ing.

Keep this: duration up to now correctly takes present perfect continuous.

**C) The river flooded the towpath three times last winter.**

Past simple "flooded" with "last winter" correctly counts finished floods in a closed season. Numbered past events inside a finished period take past simple, not present perfect.

This is sound: a finished winter plus an event count correctly takes past simple.

**D) Jonas used to living near the botanical gardens.**

Past habit needs "used to live," not "used to living." Never put -ing after "used to" when you mean habit — that -ing pattern belongs to "be used to." Repair to "Jonas used to live near the botanical gardens."

**Trap:** "Used to living" mixes past-habit "used to" with familiarity "be used to + -ing."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Jonas used to live near the botanical gardens."

**E) By Thursday evening, we will have curated the exhibition labels.**

Future perfect "will have curated" places the labels ready before Thursday evening. An art-deadline "by" is another future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that point.

Accept the line: deadline "by" correctly takes will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview:
Duration questions need present perfect continuous, closed seasons need past simple, and "used to" never takes -ing for habit. Future perfect with "by" stays solid.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"How long" for an ongoing wait wants have/has been + -ing. "Last winter" locks numbered past events into past simple. Past habit is "used to live," never "used to living." Thursday-evening "by" wants future perfect.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Compare the two duration questions as a pair, then check the past-season count, the "used to" form, and the curation deadline.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have been meaning to call you all week.
This jacket is fitting me perfectly today.
We had finished dinner before the guests rang the doorbell.
She is used to cook for large family gatherings.
By the time the podcast drops, the host will have recorded three more episodes.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I have been meaning to call you all week.**

Present perfect continuous "have been meaning" is an accepted fixed pattern for an intention delayed all week. Exams usually treat this rare continuous as correct even though "mean" is often stative elsewhere. The duration cue "all week" supports the stretch.

**Tip:** "Have been meaning to…" is one continuous form examiners routinely accept.

Keep this: idiomatic "have been meaning to" is accepted for delayed intention.

**B) This jacket is fitting me perfectly today.**

"Fit" as a size/state is stative, so "is fitting" is wrong for a current size fact. Clothing size statements stay simple: It fits me. Repair to "This jacket fits me perfectly today."

**Trap:** "Today" tempts continuous, but size "fit" is still a state verb in exams.

Reject stative continuous size — rewrite as "This jacket fits me perfectly today."

**C) We had finished dinner before the guests rang the doorbell.**

Past perfect "had finished" correctly shows dinner ended before the doorbell. The word "before" helps you spot which past action is earlier and keeps the sequence clear with past simple for the later ring.

That sequencing works — "before" correctly cues past perfect for the earlier dinner.

**D) She is used to cook for large family gatherings.**

Familiarity needs "is used to cooking," not "is used to cook." After "be used to," use -ing or a noun — never a bare infinitive. Repair by swapping the bare infinitive for a gerund.

**Trap:** Bare infinitive after "be used to" is a near-miss blend with "used to cook."

Mark it wrong and prefer "She is used to cooking for large family gatherings."

**E) By the time the podcast drops, the host will have recorded three more episodes.**

Future perfect "will have recorded" places the three extra episodes before the podcast drops. Release schedules with "by the time" routinely take will have for prior completion in the main clause.

Accept the line: "by the time" correctly takes will have + V3 before a future drop.
tasks.solution_overview:
Accept the idiomatic "have been meaning," keep past perfect and future perfect, and reject stative "fitting" plus the bare infinitive after "be used to."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Have been meaning to" is an accepted continuous for delayed intention. Clothing-size "fit" is stative and prefers simple "fits." "Before" often flags past perfect for the earlier action. "Be used to" needs -ing, not a bare infinitive. Media schedules with "by the time" invite will have.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep the idiomatic and sequencing lines; fail only the stative continuous and the broken "be used to" pattern.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Since moving abroad, Lara is making friends more easily.
Since moving abroad, Lara has been making friends more easily.
The museum used to open only on weekdays.
I am tasting the soup to check the seasoning.
By noon tomorrow, the drones will have mapped the whole coastline.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since moving abroad, Lara is making friends more easily.**

"Since" with a continuing social change needs present perfect (continuous), not present continuous alone. Present continuous covers "now" but misses the span from the move into the present. Repair to "Since moving abroad, Lara has been making friends more easily."

**Trap:** "Is making" looks current, but "since" demands a perfect form for the open span.

Reject bare present continuous after "since" — prefer "…has been making friends more easily."

**B) Since moving abroad, Lara has been making friends more easily.**

Present perfect continuous "has been making" correctly links the move abroad to an ongoing change in how easily Lara makes friends. Process + since is classic have been + -ing territory — the repaired A-line.

**Tip:** Ongoing process after "since" → have/has been + -ing.

Keep this: "since" plus an ongoing process correctly takes have been + -ing.

**C) The museum used to open only on weekdays.**

"Used to open" correctly reports a former weekday-only schedule. Former rules and timetables take used to + base verb when that schedule no longer applies.

This is sound: an old timetable is correctly marked with "used to + V1."

**D) I am tasting the soup to check the seasoning.**

"Am tasting" is allowed because "taste" here is a deliberate action — sampling to check seasoning — not a permanent stative property. Dynamic senses of sense verbs can take continuous when you taste, smell, or feel on purpose.

**Tip:** When you taste/smell/feel on purpose, -ing is fine.

Accept the line: deliberate sampling correctly allows continuous "tasting."

**E) By noon tomorrow, the drones will have mapped the whole coastline.**

Future perfect "will have mapped" places coastline mapping complete before noon tomorrow. Science deadlines with "by" take will have + past participle for prior completion.

That deadline reading works — "by" correctly takes will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pair the "since" lines carefully, keep "used to" and future perfect, and notice when a sense verb becomes dynamic ("am tasting") so continuous is fine.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Since" with a continuing change needs present perfect (continuous), not present continuous alone. "Used to open" reports a former timetable. Deliberate "taste" (sampling) can take continuous. Mapping completion "by noon tomorrow" wants future perfect.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat A/B as a minimal pair for "since," then accept the remaining three as clean once you see the dynamic tasting sense.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.
He has been to the allotment three times this week.
We are loving this new pottery class.
They will have been travelling for fourteen hours by the time they land.
I used to be used to the cold winters, but I am not any more.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.**

"Has gone" correctly means he went to the allotment and is still away, with return expected by dusk. The present result is absence, which is what "has gone" encodes — unlike "has been," which would imply a completed visit and return.

**Tip:** Has gone = left and not back yet.

Keep this: "has gone" correctly marks absence with expected return.

**B) He has been to the allotment three times this week.**

"Has been to" correctly means visited and returned — three completed visits this week. That experience/count reading is different from "has gone," which would leave him still there. The unfinished week keeps present perfect natural.

**Tip:** Has been to = visited; has gone to = still there.

That visit count is sound — "has been to" correctly marks completed trips this week.

**C) We are loving this new pottery class.**

In careful exam English, "love" stays stative. Marketing "I'm loving it" is too informal for the default exam standard. Repair to "We love this new pottery class."

**Trap:** Advertising continuous "loving" is familiar in speech but fails careful exam style.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We love this new pottery class."

**D) They will have been travelling for fourteen hours by the time they land.**

Future perfect continuous "will have been travelling" correctly stresses fourteen hours of travel completed before landing. Duration up to a future point is will have been + -ing territory rather than plain future continuous.

**Tip:** "By the time" + duration → will have been + -ing.

Accept the line: duration before a future landing correctly takes will have been + -ing.

**E) I used to be used to the cold winters, but I am not any more.**

The sentence deliberately contrasts "used to be" (a past state of cold-hardiness) with "be used to" (familiarity) and uses both forms correctly. The closing "I am not any more" shows the familiarity has ended, which justifies stacking the two patterns.

**Tip:** Used to be ≠ be used to; combining them is fine when meaning needs both.

This works: both "used to be" and "be used to" are correctly combined.
tasks.solution_overview:
Master "gone" versus "been," reject informal continuous "loving," accept future perfect continuous for duration, and parse the double "used to" contrast carefully.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Has gone" means left and still away; "has been to" means visited and returned. In careful exam English, "love" stays stative. Duration before landing wants will have been + -ing. You can correctly combine "used to be" (past state) with "be used to" (familiarity) when the meaning requires both.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate the allotment pair first, reject marketing-style "are loving," then confirm duration and the nested used-to contrast.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This is the first time I have ever tried paddleboarding.
This is the first time I ever tried paddleboarding.
While the barista was frothing milk, the espresso machine jammed.
People are depending on the coastal path for weekend walks.
By the end of the festival, performers will have given forty shows.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This is the first time I have ever tried paddleboarding.**

"This is the first time" requires present perfect for the new paddleboarding experience. The pattern first/second/third time + have/has + past participle is fixed in exam English and does not take past simple after "this is."

**Tip:** First/second/third time + present perfect.

Keep this: "this is the first time" correctly takes present perfect.

**B) This is the first time I ever tried paddleboarding.**

Past simple after "this is the first time" breaks the fixed pattern. If the sentence starts with "This is the first time," expect have/has + V3. Repair to "This is the first time I have ever tried paddleboarding."

**Trap:** Past simple feels natural next to "ever," but "this is the first time" still demands present perfect.

Reject past simple after that frame — rewrite as "…I have ever tried paddleboarding."

**C) While the barista was frothing milk, the espresso machine jammed.**

Past continuous "was frothing" sets the barista's background; past simple "jammed" marks the short machine interrupt. Café chaos still follows the same continuous–simple pairing as any while-interrupt story.

That café pairing is sound — continuous frothing plus a simple jam interrupt.

**D) People are depending on the coastal path for weekend walks.**

"Are depending" describes a current community pattern of reliance on the coastal path, so continuous is acceptable here (simple "depend" would also work). Some verbs allow continuous when you stress the present situation rather than a permanent truth.

Accept the line: situational continuous "are depending" is acceptable here.

**E) By the end of the festival, performers will have given forty shows.**

Future perfect "will have given" totals forty shows before the festival ends. Quantity completed "by the end" is will have territory for prior completion of a count.

This is sound: a count completed "by the end" correctly takes will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lock the "first time" + present perfect rule, keep the café interrupt pair and future perfect, and treat "are depending" as an acceptable current-situation continuous.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"This is the first time" requires present perfect for the new experience. Background continuous plus simple interrupt works in the café scene. "Depend" can take continuous when you stress a current community reliance. Quantity completed "by the end" wants future perfect.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Fail only the past-simple "first time" line; keep the rest once each cue matches its usual form.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have packed a warmer coat yesterday.
I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday.
She has been working on the mural all morning and still isn’t finished.
The soup is smelling of garlic and thyme right now.
By next spring, we will have been volunteering at the shelter for five years.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish I would have packed a warmer coat yesterday.**

After "I wish" for a past regret, use past perfect, not "would have packed." Save would for present wishes about someone else's behaviour (I wish you would…), not for your own past regret. Repair to "I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday."

**Trap:** "Would have" after "I wish" is a common transfer from conditional regret patterns.

Mark it wrong and prefer "I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday."

**B) I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday.**

Past perfect "had packed" correctly expresses regret about yesterday's packing choice. "I wish + had + past participle" is the standard past counterfactual — the repaired A-line.

**Tip:** I wish + had + V3 = past regret.

Keep this: past regret after "I wish" correctly takes past perfect.

**C) She has been working on the mural all morning and still isn’t finished.**

Present perfect continuous "has been working" correctly stresses mural work that has run all morning and is still unfinished. Duration plus "still isn't finished" is classic have been + -ing for activity stretching into now.

That stretch is right — all-morning unfinished work correctly takes have been + -ing.

**D) The soup is smelling of garlic and thyme right now.**

"Is smelling" reports a temporary sensory impression right now, so continuous is natural. The dynamic sense (how the soup smells at this moment) can take -ing; stative "It smells of garlic" would also be fine as an alternative.

Accept the line: a temporary how-it-smells-now reading correctly allows continuous.

**E) By next spring, we will have been volunteering at the shelter for five years.**

Future perfect continuous "will have been volunteering" correctly projects five years completed by next spring. Duration stretching up to a future point wants will have been + -ing rather than plain future perfect alone when the stretch is the point.

**Tip:** Long duration up to a future point → will have been + -ing.

This works: long duration by a future point correctly takes will have been + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fix the wish-regret pattern, then accept present perfect continuous, a dynamic sensory continuous, and future perfect continuous for long-running volunteering.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After "I wish" for a past regret, use past perfect — not "would have." All-morning unfinished work wants have been + -ing. Temporary "smell" impressions can take continuous. Five years of volunteering by next spring wants will have been + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat A/B as the regret minimal pair, then confirm the three advanced continuous patterns on C–E.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It’s high time we have updated the club website.
It’s high time we updated the club website.
After the storm had passed, birds began singing again.
I am seeing what you mean about the plot twist.
They will finish the crossword by tonight — in fact, they will have finished it by six.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It’s high time we have updated the club website.**

"It's high time" takes a past-simple form with present meaning, not present perfect. High time / about time + past simple marks overdue action now. Repair to "It's high time we updated the club website."

**Trap:** Present perfect feels "up to now," but high time still wants a past-simple form.

Reject present perfect after high time — rewrite as "It's high time we updated the club website."

**B) It’s high time we updated the club website.**

Past simple "updated" after "It's high time" correctly marks overdue action with present urgency. Treat "high time" like a mini-unreal: past form, present pressure — the repaired A-line.

**Tip:** High time + past simple = overdue now.

Keep this: "high time" correctly takes past simple with present urgency.

**C) After the storm had passed, birds began singing again.**

Past perfect "had passed" marks the earlier storm; past simple "began" covers the later singing. After + past perfect, then simple past for the next event, is a clean sequence of two past stages.

That sequence is sound — after + past perfect correctly precedes simple past.

**D) I am seeing what you mean about the plot twist.**

"Am seeing" here means understanding gradually, and continuous is accepted in modern careful English for that unfolding sense (simple "see" is also fine). Mental "see" can take continuous when comprehension is in progress rather than a finished grasp.

Accept the line: understanding-as-process correctly allows continuous "seeing."

**E) They will finish the crossword by tonight — in fact, they will have finished it by six.**

The second clause correctly upgrades to future perfect for clearer completion by six. "Will finish by" is acceptable; "will have finished by" is more precise when you mean already done at that clock time — so the sentence as written is fine.

**Tip:** Prefer will have + V3 when "by" means completion before the deadline.

This is sound: the upgrade to will have finished by six correctly marks prior completion.
tasks.solution_overview:
Apply the "high time" + past simple rule, keep past-perfect sequencing, accept gradual "am seeing," and prefer future perfect for precise "by" completion.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"It's high time" takes a past-simple form with present urgency — not present perfect. After a storm that had passed, past simple covers the next event. Mental "see" (= understand) can take continuous as understanding unfolds. "Will have finished by six" is more precise than plain will for prior completion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Fail only the broken high-time line; keep B–E as clean advanced patterns.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner the train had left than the platform announcement began.
No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began.
I have yet to try the new climbing wall downtown.
We are having a brilliant time at the street festival.
By the time you read this postcard, we will already arrive in Lisbon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) No sooner the train had left than the platform announcement began.**

"No sooner" needs inversion with the auxiliary fronted: had before the subject. Subject–verb order without fronted had is the classic mistake. Repair to "No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began."

**Trap:** Keeping "the train had" after "no sooner" looks almost grammatical until you check inversion.

Mark it wrong and prefer "No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began."

**B) No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began.**

Inverted past perfect "No sooner had the train left" correctly pairs with "than" for an immediate follow-up announcement. Inversion after no sooner / hardly / scarcely is exam gold — the repaired A-line.

**Tip:** No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than…

Keep this: inverted "no sooner had… than…" is correctly formed.

**C) I have yet to try the new climbing wall downtown.**

"Have yet to try" is a present-perfect pattern meaning you still have not done it. The climbing wall remains outstanding experience, which is exactly what the construction encodes.

**Tip:** Have yet to + base verb = still outstanding.

That pattern works — "have yet to" correctly marks an outstanding experience.

**D) We are having a brilliant time at the street festival.**

"Are having" for enjoyment is dynamic, so continuous is fine — you are experiencing the festival, not "owning" a time. Contrast this with stative possession "have," which stays simple.

**Tip:** Having a good time / having lunch = action; owning = stative.

Accept the line: experiential "having a brilliant time" correctly takes continuous.

**E) By the time you read this postcard, we will already arrive in Lisbon.**

"By the time" with a future reading needs future perfect for completion before the reading moment. Plain "will already arrive" fails to mark that Lisbon arrival as already done when the postcard is read. Repair to "By the time you read this postcard, we will already have arrived in Lisbon."

**Trap:** "Already" next to will feels complete, but "by the time" still wants will have.

Reject plain will after "by the time" — rewrite as "…we will already have arrived in Lisbon."
tasks.solution_overview:
Force inversion after "no sooner," keep "have yet to" and dynamic "having," and repair the broken future perfect after "by the time."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"No sooner" needs auxiliary inversion: No sooner had + subject + V3 + than. "Have yet to" means still have not done something. Experiential "having a brilliant time" is dynamic, so continuous is fine. "By the time" with a future reading needs will have, not plain will arrive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Compare A/B as the inversion minimal pair, keep C/D, and fix E's missing future perfect.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly I had sat down when my phone buzzed.
Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed.
She has been wanting a pottery wheel for months.
I’m thinking that the gallery closes too early on Mondays.
In two hours’ time, the tide will have turned and the rock pools will be underwater.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Hardly I had sat down when my phone buzzed.**

"Hardly" needs inversion with past perfect: had before the subject. Without fronted had, the formal immediate-sequence pattern collapses. Repair to "Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed."

**Trap:** Ordinary order after "hardly" is the twin of the broken "no sooner" line.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed."

**B) Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed.**

Correct inverted past perfect "Hardly had I sat down" marks sitting as complete just before the buzz. Match hardly … when with had + V3 after the fronted adverb — the repaired A-line.

**Tip:** Hardly / scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when…

Keep this: inverted "hardly had… when…" is correctly formed.

**C) She has been wanting a pottery wheel for months.**

"Has been wanting" is accepted in modern exam-tolerant English for a desire lasting for months up to now. The continuous stresses the ongoing stretch of that wish rather than a one-off decision.

**Tip:** Have been wanting = desire lasting up to now.

That stretch is sound — long-running desire correctly allows "has been wanting."

**D) I’m thinking that the gallery closes too early on Mondays.**

Opinion "think" (= believe) is stative, so "I'm thinking that…" is wrong here. Continuous "thinking" is for mental process ("I'm thinking about a title"), not for stating a belief. Repair to "I think that the gallery closes too early on Mondays."

**Trap:** "I'm thinking that…" is common in speech for soft opinion, but exams keep belief "think" simple.

Reject opinion continuous — rewrite as "I think that the gallery closes too early on Mondays."

**E) In two hours’ time, the tide will have turned and the rock pools will be underwater.**

Future perfect "will have turned" correctly places the tide's turn before the two-hour mark, with rock pools underwater as the clear present-result consequence. Nature timing with "in … time" pairs well with will have for prior completion.

Accept the line: "in … time" plus prior completion correctly takes will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview:
Close with inversion after "hardly," accept long-running "has been wanting," reject opinion continuous "I'm thinking that," and keep future perfect for the tide.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Hardly" needs inversion: Hardly had + subject + V3 + when. "Want" can take present perfect continuous for a long-standing desire. Opinion "think" (= believe) stays simple; continuous "thinking" is for considering. Tide turning "in two hours' time" wants future perfect for prior completion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat A/B as the inversion pair, keep C and E, and fail D when "think" is pure opinion.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.
If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.
If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If you heat ice, it melts.**

This is a clean zero conditional: a general scientific fact uses present simple on both sides. Heating ice always leads to melting, so there is no need for will. The sentence reads like a law of nature, which is exactly when zero is the right frame.

Keep this: present + present correctly marks the timeless ice-melting fact.
**B) If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.**

A real morning plan: present simple after if, will + base verb in the result. Opening early is possible, and finishing before lunch is an open future outcome. That present-plus-will pairing is the classic first conditional.

That pairing works — present after if plus will finish for the open morning plan.
**C) If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.**

After will the verb must stay bare — will cancel, not will cancels. The if-clause is fine (present for a real future); only the result form is broken. Modals never take a third-person -s on the following verb.

**Trap:** will cancels looks almost like ordinary present, but will freezes the next verb as V1.

Mark it wrong and prefer "If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic."
**D) If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.**

A real future result pinned to next week needs will pass (or similar), not bare present passes. Present + present would only fit a zero-style habit or general truth. This next-week quiz is an open plan, not a law of nature.

**Trap:** bare present in the result can look tidy, but next week forces a will result.

That result tense fails — rewrite as "If Leo studies tonight, he will pass the quiz for certain next week."
**E) If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.**

Will takes the base form bake, not bakes. The condition is a fine first-conditional if-clause; only the -s after will wrecks the result. Strip the inflection and the open-future plan is clean.

Reject this -s after will; the clean line is "If the oven is ready, Sara will bake the muffins."
tasks.solution_overview:
Ice, library hours, rain, study night, and muffins — a starter round on zero versus first conditionals.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Zero conditionals state general facts with present simple in both clauses (heat ice → it melts). First conditionals state open, real futures: present after if, will + base verb in the result. The broken lines either glue an -s onto the verb after will, or use bare present where a next-week future result needs will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask: always true, or a real plan? Facts stay present + present. Real plans keep present in the if-clause and will + V1 in the result. If you see will cancels / will bakes, strip the -s. If the result is pinned to next week and the condition is real, prefer will pass over passes.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If plants get no water, they die.
If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.
If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.
If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.
If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If plants get no water, they die.**

Zero conditional correctly states a general consequence with present simple on both sides. No water → death is a habitual natural truth, not a one-off future plan. Will would wrongly pull this permanent result into a first-conditional frame.

Accept the line: present + present states the habitual no-water consequence as a law.
**B) If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.**

First conditional links a real booking decision today to a future seating plan. Present in the if-clause, will + base verb in the result — textbook open future. Both halves stay aligned with a possible today→later chain.

This is sound — present booking today with will sit for the open train plan.
**C) If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.**

Will misses is ungrammatical; use will miss. The late-bus condition is fine first-conditional material — only the -s after will is wrong. Keep the verb after will in the bare infinitive.

**Trap:** will misses mirrors third-person present, so it looks almost right at speed.

Mark it wrong and prefer "If the bus is late, Tom will miss his lecture."
**D) If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.**

A timeless colour fact belongs in zero conditional (you get purple), not first with will. The phrase as a law of nature is a strong clue that will is the wrong mood for a permanent truth. Drop will and keep both clauses in present simple.

**Trap:** will get feels natural for results, but a named law of nature wants zero, not first.

That will result fails a named law of nature — rewrite as "If you mix red and blue, you get purple every time as a law of nature."
**E) If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.**

Clean first conditional for a real morning timetable and intention. Opens is present; will train is the open future result. Nothing in the line forces a zero-style habit frame.

Keep this: opens + will train correctly frames the real early-gym intention.
tasks.solution_overview:
Plants, train seats, a late bus, mixing colours, and an early gym — more zero-versus-first practice, including a fact wrongly dressed in will.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Always-true consequences belong in zero (present + present). Open plans belong in first (present + will). One line fails with will + -s; another states a permanent colour law with will get, which pulls a timeless fact into first conditional.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each sentence fact or plan. Facts: drop will and keep both presents. Plans: keep will + bare verb. Reject will misses on sight, and reject will when the result is framed as a law of nature.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If I were you, I would take the earlier train.
If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.
If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.
If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.
If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If I were you, I would take the earlier train.**

Second conditional with formal were after if I, plus would + base verb for unreal advice. The speaker is not claiming to be you — the role is hypothetical. This is the classic advice pattern exams reward.

That advice pattern is sound — If I were … would take marks the unreal role.
**B) If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.**

Past/were in the if-clause plus would marks an unreal present wish about the weather. We are not claiming the weather is better — we are imagining it. Would cycle is the unreal result that depends on that imagined improvement.

Accept the line: were + would correctly frames the unreal better-weather wish.
**C) If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.**

Do not put would in the if-clause; write If she had more free time, she would join the choir. Keep would for the result only; the condition wants past simple. Stacking would on both sides is a classic second-conditional break.

**Trap:** If she would have … looks polite, but standard conditionals ban would in the if-clause.

Reject the would-in-if slip; prefer "If she had more free time, she would join the choir."
**D) If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.**

Standard second conditional for a counterfactual present about distance and commuting. Lived + would walk is the default unreal-present frame. Dan does not live closer; the daily walk is only imagined.

Keep this: lived + would walk marks Dan’s counterfactual closer commute.
**E) If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.**

Careful exam English prefers were for unreal be after if, not was, especially in formal true/false items. The rest of the pattern (would change) is fine; only was is the fail. Swap was → were and the hypothetical captain role is exam-safe.

**Trap:** If I was is common in speech, so it can feel acceptable — exams still prefer were here.

That was fails careful exam be — rewrite as "If I were the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation."
tasks.solution_overview:
Trains, weather, choir, campus walks, and team captain — unreal present (second conditional) with exam-style were and a would-in-the-if trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional marks unreal or hypothetical present/future: past simple or were in the if-clause, would + base verb in the result. Do not park would inside the if-clause. Careful exam English prefers were over was for unreal be after if.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check where would sits — result only. Prefer If I were / If the weather were for hypothetical be. Keep past simple + would for counterfactual present lifestyle wishes (distance, commuting).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.
As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.
Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.
If only I knew her phone number now.
I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.**

Unless (= if not) + present simple pairs cleanly with will for a real future sports plan. The match goes ahead if rain does not intervene. Will sits in the result, not in the unless-clause.

This works: unless + present + will correctly frames the open match-ahead plan.
**B) As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.**

As long as (= provided that) takes present simple for a real ongoing condition, then will in the result. Watering is the proviso that keeps the herbs fine. The connector behaves like if for open conditions.

Keep this — as long as + present + will is the right proviso for the herbs.
**C) Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.**

After unless, avoid will; use present — Unless you hurry, we will miss the opening credits. Will belongs in the result, not stacked into the condition. The double will makes the polarity and timing messy.

**Trap:** Unless you will hurry mirrors ordinary future talk, but unless rarely takes will.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Unless you hurry, we will miss the opening credits."
**D) If only I knew her phone number now.**

If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present lack of knowledge. Knew is the backshifted form for a present gap. The speaker does not have the number now, so past form carries the regret.

Accept the wish: if only + past simple marks the unreal present lack of her number.
**E) I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.**

Wish about present ability needs past form — I wish I could speak…, not can. After wish, shift the tense back one step from reality. Ordinary present modal can does not belong after wish.

**Trap:** I wish I can … keeps everyday present can, which looks fluent but fails the backshift.

That can after wish fails the backshift — rewrite as "I wish I could speak Italian fluently this semester."
tasks.solution_overview:
Match day, herbs, film credits, a missing number, and Italian — unless, as long as, and wish / if only at entry level.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unless and as long as behave like if for real conditions: present in the condition clause, will (or another realistic result) in the main clause. Wish and if only for present unreal situations shift the tense back — past simple, and can becomes could.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip will from unless / if / as long as conditions. For present regrets with wish / if only, use past simple. Reject I wish I can… on sight.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.
If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.
If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.
Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.
As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.**

Second conditional for an unreal present about the cinema timetable. Had (past meaning) + would go imagines a better schedule that does not actually exist. The go-more-often result depends on that counterfactual slots claim.

Keep this: past + would correctly marks the unreal present cinema-slots wish.
**B) If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.**

Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle for a missed past opportunity. The sale is over; the jacket stays unbought in this alternate past. Both halves stay locked in closed unreal past.

That third-conditional chain is sound — had known / would have bought for the missed sale.
**C) If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.**

Would does not belong in the if-clause; use If they practised every day, they would improve faster. Ban would from the condition; leave it for the result. Double would is the signature second-conditional error here.

**Trap:** If they would practise … can sound like polite pressure, but the if-clause wants past simple.

Reject the double-would if-clause; prefer "If they practised every day, they would improve faster."
**D) Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.**

Unless + present correctly sets a real study condition before a future entertainment plan. Finishes is present; will not watch is the open future result. Unless already means if not, so one layer of negation is enough.

Accept the line: unless + present + will not fits Mia’s real study-before-film proviso.
**E) As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.**

As long as + present states a real proviso that enables present ability with can. Not every as long as line needs will — can / may work when the result is present capability. Keep quiet stays present; can revise is the enabled present result.

This works — as long as + present + can correctly enables the midnight revision.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cinema slots, a missed sale, daily practice, a lab report, and quiet neighbours — blending second, third, unless, and as long as.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional = unreal present (past + would). Third = unreal past (had + V3 / would have + V3). Unless and as long as keep present for real provisos. The clear fail is would parked inside the if-clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate would: only the result may have it in these patterns. Match unreal-present cinema wishes to past + would, and missed past shopping to past perfect + would have. Trust unless / as long as when the condition stays present.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.
Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.
If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.
I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.
If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.**

Classic third conditional for a missed travel outcome in the past. Had left + would have reached keeps both halves in unreal past. The ferry did not leave on time, and the island arrival before dusk did not happen.

Keep this: past perfect + would have correctly marks the missed on-time ferry outcome.
**B) Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.**

Inverted third conditional (Had she set…) correctly replaces If she had set… The meaning and the would not have overslept result stay fully unreal past. Inversion is a formal shortcut, not a different tense.

Accept the inversion — Had she set … would not have overslept is valid third-conditional shorthand.
**C) If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.**

The result must stay in the unreal past — would have won, not will have won. Will have is ordinary future perfect, not third-conditional regret. Past perfect in the if-clause forces would have in the result.
