**Trap:** will have won looks like a polished perfect form, but third conditional needs would have.

That will have result fails unreal past — rewrite as "If Ben had trained harder, he would have won the race."
**D) I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.**

Wish + past perfect correctly regrets a past packing choice. Yesterday locks the regret in closed past, so past perfect is the right shift. A present wish would use past simple instead.

That regret is sound: wish + past perfect correctly locks yesterday’s packing miss.
**E) If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.**

If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present problem. Right now signals present inconvenience, so worked (past form) is the backshift — not past perfect. Past perfect would wrongly push the café Wi-Fi problem into finished past.

Keep this: if only + past simple fits the present café Wi-Fi inconvenience.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ferry timing, a missed alarm, a race, an umbrella, and café Wi-Fi — unreal past with third conditional, Had-inversion, and wish / if only.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unreal past uses had + V3 in the condition and would have + V3 in the result. Had she set… is a formal inversion of If she had set… Wish / if only take past perfect for closed past regrets and past simple for present inconvenience. Reject will have where would have is required.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the regret is finished (past perfect / would have) or present (past simple after if only). Accept inversion as a shortcut for if + past perfect. Swap will have won → would have won in third-conditional results.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.
I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.
If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.**

First conditional with a negative if-clause correctly predicts a real future result. Don't water is still present tense after if; will wilt is the open outcome. Negation in the condition does not force a different conditional type.

Accept the line: if + present negative + will correctly predicts the open wilting result.
**B) Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.**

Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative. Use Unless you water… or If you don't… — not both layers of negation. The intended polarity becomes unclear, and exam English rejects the stack.

**Trap:** Unless you don't … can look carefully cautious, but the double negation is the fail.

Mark the double negative wrong and prefer "Unless you water the tomatoes, they will wilt."
**C) As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.**

As long as + present correctly sets a real academic condition for a future result. Submit is present; will give is the open Monday plan. Provided / as long as behave like if for real conditions.

This is sound — as long as + present + will frames the Friday-draft feedback plan.
**D) I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.**

Wish + would correctly complains about someone else's annoying present habit and asks for a change. This is the behaviour-change use of wish, not a simple state wish. Would stop is the plea for different neighbour behaviour.

Keep this: wish + would correctly presses the neighbours to stop the dawn drilling.
**E) If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.**

If only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not will — If only she would listen… / If only she listened… Ordinary will does not belong after if only. Keep will for ordinary first-conditional results, not wishful if only clauses.

**Trap:** If only she will … feels like urgent future hopes, but if only rejects ordinary will.

That will after if only fails — rewrite as "If only she would listen to the podcast before the seminar."
tasks.solution_overview:
Tomatoes, drafts, dawn drilling, and a podcast — polarity with unless, as long as for real plans, and wish / if only + would for behaviour change.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If + negative present + will is fine for open futures. Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative. Wish + would complains about someone else's habit; if only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not ordinary will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Avoid stacking unless with another negative. Keep as long as in present for real academic plans. Prefer wish / if only + would (or past) when you want a change in behaviour — reject if only … will.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.
If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.
If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.
Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.
I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.**

Second conditional with were for an unreal present outdoor scenario. The trail is muddy; we only imagine it cleaner. Would hike is the unreal result that depends on that cleaner trail.

That pairing works — were + would marks the unreal cleaner-trail hiking wish.
**B) If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.**

First conditional: a real possible price change pairs with will switch. Fall is present; will switch is the open future lifestyle result. Nothing here is hypothetical enough to force second conditional.

Keep this: present + will correctly frames the real price-drop possibility.
**C) If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.**

Never write If I would be; use If I were / If I was (exam: were). Would stays out of the if-clause in standard conditionals; only the result may keep would reach. The height wish is unreal present, so were is the safe condition form.

**Trap:** If I would be … doubles would and looks like cautious future English — it is still wrong.

Reject If I would be; prefer "If I were taller, I would reach the top shelf easily."
**D) Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.**

Unless + present + will correctly frames a real museum visit plan. Closes is present; will see is the open result if early closing does not intervene. Unless already means if not, so the polarity is clear.

Accept the plan: unless + present + will fits the real museum-visit proviso.
**E) I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.**

Wish + were correctly marks an unreal present ability. Formal exam English likes were here for present counterfactuals with be. The speaker is not better at mental arithmetic now — were carries that gap.

This is sound — wish + were correctly frames the present mental-arithmetic counterfactual.
tasks.solution_overview:
Muddy trails, seasonal produce, shelf height, a museum wing, and mental arithmetic — consolidating second conditional, unless, wish + were, and one real first-conditional line.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unreal present keeps were / past + would. Real futures keep present + will. Unless + present + will frames real visit plans. The signature trap is If I would be… — would must not sit in the if-clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept were for unreal outdoor and ability wishes. Accept one clean first-conditional price/lifestyle line. Rewrite If I would be → If I were. Trust unless when the condition stays present.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.
If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.
If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.
If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.
If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.**

Mixed conditional: past unreal cause (had taken) with present result (would be). The missed bus is finished; the empty seat at the theatre is the present consequence. Matching cause time to result time is what makes the mix legal.

**Tip:** Past perfect in if + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

Keep this: the mixed past-cause → present-effect pattern (had taken / would be) is aligned.
**B) If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.**

Mixed conditional: unreal present character (were) with past result (would have handed). The trait is imagined as present; the missed Friday deadline is the past fallout. Were keeps the personality claim unreal now; would have locks the Friday fail in the past.

**Tip:** If + past / were + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

Accept the mix — present unreal were feeding would have handed for Friday’s miss.
**C) If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.**

A finished past result needs would have arrived, not would arrive, after a past perfect condition. Yesterday evening locks the outcome in the past, so plain would + V1 is the wrong half of the mix. Past condition plus past result wants full third conditional.

**Trap:** would arrive can look like a sleek mix, but yesterday evening forces would have arrived.

That would arrive fails yesterday evening — rewrite as "If they had left earlier, they would have arrived yesterday evening."
**D) If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.**

A childhood past state needs past perfect — If I had had more patience as a child… Pure past regrets need had + past participle in the if-clause when the cause itself is past. Bare had + noun underpowers the childhood timeline here.

**Trap:** If I had more patience as a child looks almost second-conditional, but as a child pushes it into past.

Mark the childhood cause underpowered; prefer "If I had had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner."
**E) If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.**

Second conditional can use past simple heated for an unreal or unlikely present suggestion. Now softens into a hypothetical offer rather than a firm first-conditional plan. Would taste is the imagined better result under that soft suggestion.

That soft suggestion works: past heated + would taste for the present soup hypothetical.
highlights: If I had more patience as a child
tasks.solution_overview:
Theatre arrival, a late portfolio, yesterday's arrival, childhood patience, and soup — mixed conditionals and time alignment.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Mixed conditionals match the time of the cause to the time of the result: past perfect cause + present would result, or unreal present trait + would have past result. Reject would + V1 with clear past time markers like yesterday, and reject weak past-perfect gaps when the story is a childhood past state.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline time cues (now, last Friday, yesterday, as a child). Build the if-clause for the cause's time and the result for the effect's time. Soft hypothetical now can still use second conditional (heated / would taste).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.
Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.
I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.
If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.
Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.**

As long as takes present for real conditions — As long as you follow…, not will follow. Will belongs in the result (will rise), not twice. The double will breaks the open-condition connector pattern.

**Trap:** as long as you will follow feels like careful future English, but the proviso wants present.

Reject will in the as-long-as clause; prefer "As long as you follow the recipe, the cake will rise."
**B) Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.**

Provided that + present + will is a clean real-future proviso. Is open sets the condition; will swim is the plan. Provided that ≈ if / as long as for open conditions.

Keep this: provided that + present + will correctly frames the open swim plan.
**C) I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.**

Wish + past simple correctly regrets a present obligation. Didn't have to is the backshift from present have to. Tonight keeps the annoyance in present time, so past simple — not past perfect — is enough.

Accept the regret — wish + past simple marks tonight’s present have-to annoyance.
**D) If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.**

If only + past perfect correctly regrets a finished past cancellation. Last Saturday closes the event in the past. Present-backshift past simple would underpower that closed-date regret.

This is sound: if only + past perfect correctly regrets last Saturday’s cancellation.
**E) Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.**

The timelines clash. A past-perfect unless-clause wants a past result (would have answered), or rephrase carefully as a matching mixed / first pattern. Do not paste past perfect onto plain would + V1 present without a clear mixed design.

**Trap:** Unless she had missed… would answer now looks mixed at a glance, but the times do not lock cleanly.

That time match fails — prefer something aligned like "Unless she had missed the call, she would have answered it."
tasks.solution_overview:
Cake rising, a swim plan, revision, a cancelled concert, and a missed call — connectors plus wish / if only tense shifts, with one messy unless timeline.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

As long as / provided that take present for real conditions, not will. Wish + past simple regrets present obligations; if only + past perfect regrets finished past cancellations. Unless + past perfect wants a time-matched result — not a casually pasted present would + V1 without a clear mixed pattern.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep will out of as long as / provided that. Trust didn't / hadn't after wish / if only when the time cue is clear. For unless + had missed, either go fully past (would have answered) or rebuild a clean mixed / first pattern — do not leave the clash.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the tutor explained the theorem more slowly, more students would have passed last week's test.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly, more students would pass the resit next month.
If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly last term, more students would understand it now.
Had the trail been clearer, we would not have got lost.
If it weren't for the fog, we could see the harbour lights.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the tutor explained the theorem more slowly, more students would have passed last week's test.**

Mixed conditional: unreal present teaching style (explained) with a finished past result (would have passed). The slow-explanation habit is imagined as a present trait; last week's scores are the past consequence. Cause time and result time each get the form that matches them.

**Tip:** If + past + would have + V3 = present unreal trait, past consequence.

Keep this: present-trait past form + would have passed correctly mixes to last week’s scores.
**B) If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly, more students would pass the resit next month.**

A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with plain future would pass next month. Use would have passed for a past test, or If she explained… would pass for unreal present/future. The times of cause and result must align before the line can pass.

**Trap:** had explained + would pass next month mixes closed past with open future without a legal hinge.

Mark it wrong — align times (past test → would have passed, or unreal now → explained / would pass).
**C) If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly last term, more students would understand it now.**

Mixed: past unreal teaching (had explained) with present result (would understand now). Last term is the cause; now is the effect. Past perfect in the if-clause and would + V1 in the result is the standard past→present mix.

Accept the mix: past perfect had explained + would understand now for last term → now.
**D) Had the trail been clearer, we would not have got lost.**

Inverted third conditional correctly reports a past hiking mishap avoided in an alternate past. Had the trail been… replaces If the trail had been… Would not have got lost keeps the result in unreal past.

That inversion is sound — Had the trail been … would not have got lost stands for if + past perfect.
**E) If it weren't for the fog, we could see the harbour lights.**

If it weren't for + noun correctly introduces an unreal present obstacle, with could in the result. Without the fog, the lights would be visible now. Weren't for marks the fog as the present barrier.

Keep this: If it weren’t for correctly marks fog as the unreal present obstacle.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tutor explanations, a hiking trail, and harbour fog — mixed timelines, Had-inversion, and If it weren't for.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Mixed lines succeed when cause time and result time match (present unreal teaching + past test result; past unreal teaching + present understanding). A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with a plain would pass next month. Inversion and If it weren't for are standard alternate forms.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check last week's test versus next month's resit versus now. Accept Had the trail been… as third-conditional inversion. Accept If it weren't for + noun for an unreal present obstacle with could / would.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.
I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.
If only the semester break were longer.
If water freezes, it will expands.
If water freezes, it expands.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.**

Wish + would correctly asks for a change in habitual annoying behaviour. The shoes keep appearing; wouldn't leave is the plea to stop. This behaviour-change use is distinct from a simple state wish.

Accept the plea: wish + would correctly seeks a change in the hallway shoe habit.
**B) I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.**

Wish does not take present simple like a command; use wouldn't leave or didn't leave. After wish, shift the tense — don't keep ordinary present. The hallway complaint needs a backshift, not a direct present imperative shape.

**Trap:** I wish you don't … sounds like a firm request, but wish still demands the backshift.

That present after wish fails — rewrite as "I wish you wouldn’t leave your shoes in the hallway."
**C) If only the semester break were longer.**

If only + were correctly wishes for an unreal present length of break. The break is not longer; were marks the counterfactual. Past perfect would wrongly push the semester-break wish into finished past.

Keep this: if only + were marks the present counterfactual longer-break wish.
**D) If water freezes, it will expands.**

A scientific fact belongs in zero conditional, and will expands is doubly wrong (will + -s). Write it expands — present + present, no will. Permanent physical laws do not take first-conditional will.

**Trap:** will expands piles a wrong mood and a wrong -s onto a timeless fact.

Reject will expands on a physical law; prefer "If water freezes, it expands."
**E) If water freezes, it expands.**

Clean zero conditional for a physical law. Both clauses stay in present simple for a permanent truth. Freezing → expanding is always true, so will is unnecessary.

This is sound — present + present correctly states the freezing→expanding law.
highlights: If only the semester break were
tasks.solution_overview:
Hallway shoes, semester break, and freezing water — wish + would versus illegal wish + present, if only + were, and a return to zero conditional form.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wish + would asks someone to change a habit; wish does not take ordinary present like a command. If only + were marks present counterfactuals. Scientific facts belong in zero (present + present); will expands is doubly wrong (wrong mood and will + -s).

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer wouldn't / didn't after wish for behaviour and states. Accept were after if only for present unreal length. For physical laws, keep both clauses present and never write will + -s.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.
If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.
Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.
Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.
Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.**

Second conditional can mark an unlikely or tentative future plan (studied / would improve). Next year does not force first conditional when the speaker treats the plan as remote. Past + would softens the abroad year into a hypothetical step.

**Tip:** Unlikely future → past + would, even with a future time cue like next year.

Keep this: past + would correctly softens next year’s abroad plan into a remote hypothesis.
**B) If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.**

Will in the if-clause plus bare present improves is a broken first-conditional attempt. Real future: If she studies… she will improve… Keep will out of the if-clause and put it in the result.

**Trap:** If she will study … she improves flips the will into the wrong clause and drops it from the result.

That will-in-if fails — rewrite as "If she studies abroad next year, she will improve her Spanish dramatically."
**C) Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.**

Should you need… is a polite inverted first-conditional alternative to If you need… Formal offers often prefer this shape. Will help keeps the open real result.

Accept the offer: Should you need … will help is polite first-conditional inversion.
**D) Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.**

Were the path safer… correctly inverts a second-conditional if-clause. It replaces If the path were safer… with the same unreal-present meaning. Would use is the unreal result after dark.

That Were-inversion works — it correctly marks the unreal safer-path wish after dark.
**E) Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.**

Inverted past perfect needs would have visited for a past result, not would visit yesterday. Yesterday forces third-conditional result shape. Had we known… only works when the result stays in unreal past.

**Trap:** would visit yesterday looks like a light mix, but yesterday locks the result into would have + V3.

Mark yesterday’s result wrong; prefer "Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would have visited yesterday."
tasks.solution_overview:
Study abroad, hotel towels, a safer path, and a free gallery day — unlikely futures plus Should / Were / Had inversion.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional can mark an unlikely future (studied / would improve) even with next year. Real futures keep will out of the if-clause. Should you need… and Were the path safer… are polite inverted forms. Had-inversion for past knowledge needs would have + V3 for a yesterday result.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject If she will study… she improves…. Accept Should / Were inversion as formal if-alternatives. Pair Had we known… with would have visited for finished past outcomes — not would visit yesterday.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
But for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.
If it was not for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago.
As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.**

Mixed pattern: past obstacle (had not been) with present/future-facing result (would be camping tonight). The puncture is finished; tonight's campsite is the imagined present. If it had not been for X is the formal past-cause frame for that mix.

**Tip:** If it had not been for X + would + V1 = past cause, present effect.

Keep this: past obstacle had not been + would be camping tonight is a clean mixed frame.
**B) But for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.**

But for + noun is a compact equivalent of if it were not / had not been for. Same camping counterfactual, tighter wording. The flat tyre remains the blocking condition for tonight's campsite.

Accept the compact form — But for correctly compresses the same flat-tyre counterfactual.
**C) If it was not for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago.**

Prefer If it hadn't been for… would have arrived… (past) or If it weren't for… would be… (present). Was not for with would have is non-standard for this item. Keep weren't for and hadn't been for distinct by time.

**Trap:** If it was not for … would have arrived mixes present-looking was not for with a past result.

That was-not-for shape fails — rewrite as "If it hadn’t been for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago."
**D) As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

As long as + present + can correctly sets a real group condition. Objects is present; can move is present capability under that proviso. As long as supports present modal results as well as will.

This works: as long as + present + can fits the rehearsal-move proviso.
**E) Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

Unless + will is wrong; use Unless anyone complains… Will does not belong in the unless-clause. Keep the condition in present for this open group plan.

**Trap:** Unless anyone will complain inserts future will where unless wants present.

Reject will after unless; prefer "Unless anyone complains, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday."
highlights: If it had not been for
tasks.solution_overview:
Flat tyre camping plans and a Thursday rehearsal — If it had not been for / But for, weren't for versus hadn't been for, and no will after unless.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If it had not been for + would + V1 mixes past obstacle with present/future-facing result. But for + noun is a compact equivalent. Keep If it weren't for (present) distinct from If it hadn't been for (past). As long as + present can support can; unless must not take will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept had not been for / But for when the tyre story lands on tonight. Reject was not for + would have as non-standard here. Strip will from unless anyone will complain.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have more free evenings.
I wish I had more free evenings.
If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.
Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish I would have more free evenings.**

Wish + would have is wrong for a present lack; use wish + past simple (had). Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes about states. Free evenings are a present desire, so had — not would have — is the backshift.

**Trap:** I wish I would have … borrows third-conditional furniture for a present state wish.

Mark the would-have present wish wrong; prefer "I wish I had more free evenings."
**B) I wish I had more free evenings.**

Wish + past simple correctly expresses an unreal present desire about free time. Had is the backshift from present have. The speaker does not have those free evenings now.

Keep this: wish + past simple correctly marks the present free-evenings desire.
**C) If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

If only + past perfect cause with wouldn't be now is a valid mixed regret linking past delay to present queue. The delay is finished; the queue is happening. Past perfect after if only can feed a present would/wouldn't result when times match.

Accept the mix — if only + past perfect feeding wouldn’t be now for delay → queue.
**D) If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

Same mixed pattern with ordinary if instead of if only. Past unreal cause → present continuous-looking result with wouldn't + be + -ing. If and if only both allow this past→present mix when the times are clear.

That parallel if-mix is sound: past perfect cause → present queueing result.
**E) Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?**

Supposing + past simple introduces a second-conditional hypothesis with would in the question. Closed + would we study is the tentative-scenario frame. Supposing / suppose ≈ if for tentative scenarios.

This works: supposing + past + would correctly frames the closed-café hypothesis.
tasks.solution_overview:
Free evenings, delayed coaches, and a café that might close — killing wish I would have, keeping mixed past→present, and welcoming supposing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes; use wish + past simple (had). If only / if + past perfect can feed a present would/wouldn't be … now result. Supposing + past introduces second-conditional hypotheses with would in the question.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For present state wishes, choose had over would have. Accept mixed delay→queue lines with if or if only. Treat supposing like if + past for tentative scenarios.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.
Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.
Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.
If so be the weather improves, we will hike.
If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.**

Even if + present + will correctly means the result holds despite the condition. Expense does not block the festival plan. Even if is not ordinary if — the main clause still uses real-future will here.

Keep this: even if + present + will correctly holds the festival plan despite cost.
**B) Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.**

Even if + past (were) wants would stay, not will stay. Match even if tense to the result: past → would; present → will. Were free clashes with will stay and breaks the unreal/real pairing.

**Trap:** Even if the tickets were free, we will still… mixes second-conditional were with first-conditional will.

That were / will clash fails — rewrite as "Even if the tickets were free, we would still stay home."
**C) Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.**

Whether or not + present + will correctly says the run happens regardless of rain. The start time is fixed either way. Whether or not = no matter if.

Accept the line: whether or not + present + will correctly ignores the rain alternative.
**D) If so be the weather improves, we will hike.**

If so be is archaic and not exam-standard; use If the weather improves… Stick to standard if + present for real futures. Modern keys do not reward this set-phrase fossil.

Reject archaic If so be; prefer "If the weather improves, we will hike."
**E) If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.**

If need be is an accepted fixed phrase meaning if it is necessary, here with can. Do not "correct" it to if needs be in formal keys. The idiom stands as a set form for this open contingency.

**Tip:** If need be is a set idiom — leave the wording alone.

This is sound — if need be correctly stands for if it is necessary.
highlights: Even if the tickets were, we will
tasks.solution_overview:
Festival tickets, a charity run, weather, and taxis — even if, whether or not, and fixed if need be, while rejecting tense clashes and archaic if so be.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Even if + present + will means the result holds despite the condition; even if + past wants would, not will. Whether or not + present + will says the plan happens regardless. If so be is archaic; if need be is an accepted idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match even if tense to the result mood. Accept whether or not for rain-proof plans. Prefer standard If the weather improves… over if so be, and leave if need be alone as a set phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.
If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.
Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.
If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional way to mark a hypothetical future step. Were to + V1 softens the plan into something remote or tentative. Would need keeps the unreal/formal result about references.

**Tip:** If + were to + V1 ≈ unlikely/formal if + past.

Keep this: were to correctly softens the scholarship application into a remote step.
**B) If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.**

Was to have applied mixed with would need now is over-stacked and non-standard for this item. Prefer clear mixed or third forms; avoid was to have + mismatched results. Formal keys stay on clear were to / had + V3 patterns.

**Trap:** was to have applied + would need now piles formal layers without a clean time match.

Mark the stacked was-to-have line wrong — rebuild with clear were to / had + V3 and matching result time.
**C) Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.**

Were he to practise… correctly inverts were to for a hypothetical training plan. Same meaning as If he were to practise… Would improve stays the remote/formal result within weeks.

Accept the inversion: Were he to practise … would improve replaces if + were to cleanly.
**D) If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

Knew then is underpowered for a clear past knowledge gap; the standard line uses had known then. Past counterfactual knowledge → past perfect in the if-clause. Would have chosen already locks the module decision in the past, so the if-clause must match.

**Trap:** If I knew then … looks idiomatic, but then + past ignorance wants had known.

That bare knew then fails — rewrite as "If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module."
**E) If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

Classic form: past perfect for past ignorance, would have chosen for the past decision. This is the polished exam hindsight pattern. Then and the closed module choice stay fully aligned in unreal past.

This hindsight form is sound: had known then … would have chosen keeps both halves in unreal past.
tasks.solution_overview:
Scholarships, serving practice, and module choices — advanced were to / Were … to inversion and the polished had known then pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional hypothetical. Were he to practise… inverts the same idea. Was to have applied stacked with a mismatched result is overcomplicated. Past counterfactual knowledge wants had known then, not underpowered knew then.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept were to / Were … to for formal unlikely steps. Prefer clear mixed or third forms over was to have stacks. Choose If I had known then… would have chosen… for hindsight module regrets.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.
It's time we left for the airport.
It's time we leave for the airport.
Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'd rather you didn't stream loud videos while I'm revising.**

Would rather + past simple correctly softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour. Didn't stream is the polite backshift, not a past-time narrative. The revising scene is happening now; the past form is only the courtesy shift.

Keep this: I’d rather you + past correctly softens the present loud-video preference.
**B) I'd rather you don't stream loud videos while I'm revising.**

After I'd rather you, use past simple, not present don't. Same backshift habit as wish — prefer past after I'd rather you. Present don't leaves the line looking like a flat present command.

**Trap:** I'd rather you don't … keeps ordinary present and misses the required backshift.

That present don’t after rather fails — rewrite as "I’d rather you didn’t stream loud videos while I’m revising."
**C) It's time we left for the airport.**

It's time + past simple is the standard formal pattern for present urgency. Left means we should leave now, not that we already departed. The past form is the marked formal choice after it's time.

Accept the urgency: it’s time + past correctly marks present airport leave-now pressure.
**D) It's time we leave for the airport.**

Careful exam keys usually want It's time we left, not leave. It's time + past is the marked formal choice. Present leave is too bare for this set pattern in formal true/false items.

**Trap:** It's time we leave sounds natural in speech, but formal keys prefer left.

Mark bare leave wrong for formal keys; prefer "It’s time we left for the airport."
**E) Suppose you won free concert tickets — what would you do?**

Suppose + past + would correctly frames a second-conditional daydream. Won + would you do matches if + past + would. Suppose / supposing pattern like if + past for tentative scenarios.

That suppose frame works — past + would correctly daydreams the concert-ticket scenario.
tasks.solution_overview:
Loud videos, airport departures, and free concert tickets — extending conditional logic into I'd rather you, it's time + past, and suppose.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

I'd rather you + past softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour. It's time + past marks present urgency in careful exam English. Suppose + past + would frames a second-conditional daydream. These share the same backshift instinct as wish and second conditionals.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject I'd rather you don't… and It's time we leave… in favour of past forms. Accept Suppose you won… what would you do? as if + past with would.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.
Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.
If only I could have attended the reunion last month.
I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.
Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.**

First conditional with a real possible macro change and a future lifestyle effect. Drops is present; will feel is open future. Next quarter keeps the budget relief in open future time.

Keep this: present + will correctly frames the real inflation→budget relief chain.
**B) Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.**

Mixed: past unreal storm (Had … not hit) with present result (would still be open). Negative inversion can feed a present would result when this afternoon is the effect time. The storm is finished; the market's open state is the present counterfactual.

**Tip:** Had … not + V3 can pair with present would + V1 when the effect time is now.

Accept the mix — past storm inversion feeding would still be open this afternoon.
**C) If only I could have attended the reunion last month.**

If only + could have + V3 correctly regrets a missed past ability or opportunity. Last month locks the regret in closed past. Could have attended carries both ability and the missed chance.

This regret is sound: if only + could have correctly mourns last month’s missed reunion.
**D) I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.**

Wish + could have + V3 matches the same past missed opportunity. Wish and if only parallel here for past ability regrets. Last month again keeps the reunion firmly in closed past.

Keep this parallel: wish + could have correctly regrets the same closed past opportunity.
**E) Unless having finished the essay, she will not join us.**

Unless needs a finite clause (Unless she has finished…), not Unless having finished… Avoid a dangling -ing after unless. Rebuild with subject + finite verb before you attach will not join us.

**Trap:** Unless having finished … looks like a compressed participle clause, but unless rejects bare -ing.

Reject bare -ing after unless; prefer "Unless she has finished the essay, she will not join us."
tasks.solution_overview:
Household budgets, a storm-hit market, a missed reunion, and a dangling unless -ing — advanced first, mixed inversion, and could have regrets.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A light economy first conditional stays present + will. Had … not hit can feed a present would still be… result. Wish / if only + could have + V3 regrets missed past ability. Unless needs a finite clause — not Unless having finished…

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept real-future inflation → budget relief. Accept negative Had-inversion into a present market result. Parallel if only / wish + could have for last month. Rebuild unless with subject + finite verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It's high time we booked the campsite.
If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.
I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.
No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It's high time we booked the campsite.**

It's high time + past simple correctly marks present urgency with the same backshift as wish / it's time. Booked means we should book now. The past form does not claim that the campsite is already booked.

Accept the urgency: it’s high time + past correctly marks present campsite-booking pressure.
**B) If you come to the hike, bring a reusable bottle.**

Clear first-conditional imperative result: if + present, imperative bring… Instructions work fine as first-conditional results. Come is present; bring is the real-instruction outcome.

Keep this: if + present + imperative is a valid first-conditional instruction.
**C) I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds.**

Provided + present (holds) correctly sets a real weather condition for a future plan with will come. Holds stays present in the proviso. Provided / providing take present, not will, just like if / as long as.

This works — provided + present correctly conditions the Sunday cycling plan.
**D) I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.**

Provided the weather will hold wrongly inserts will into the condition. Same rule as if / as long as: no will in the proviso clause. Keep will come in the main clause and strip will from the weather proviso.

**Trap:** provided the weather will hold doubles future will and breaks the connector pattern.

Mark will in the proviso wrong; prefer "I’ll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather holds."
**E) No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.**

No sooner… than needs a simple past result (went off), not conditional would go off. No sooner is past sequencing, not a conditional frame. Leave would out of this narrative pattern.

**Trap:** would go off sneaks conditional mood into a past-sequencing idiom that wants went off.

That would go off fails the sequencing idiom — rewrite as "No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm went off."
highlights: If you come to the hike, bring
tasks.solution_overview:
Campsite booking, hike bottles, Sunday cycling, and a fire alarm — it's high time, imperative first conditionals, provided + present, and a no sooner false friend.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

It's high time + past marks present urgency. First conditionals may use an imperative result (bring…). Provided takes present, not will. No sooner… than is past sequencing with simple past (went off), not conditional would go off.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept booked / bring / holds as clean backshift, imperative, and proviso patterns. Reject will after provided. Do not force would onto a no sooner narrative.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of overdue library books has risen since March.
A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.
Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.
Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.
There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of overdue library books has risen since March.**

The head of this sentence is "the number," which names one count of overdue books, not the books themselves. Singular subjects take singular verbs, so "has risen" is the right match. Mentally swapping in "that total has risen" makes the agreement feel natural.

That agreement is clean — singular "the number" correctly pairs with "has risen."
**B) A number of neighbours was unable to join the street clean-up.**

"A number of neighbours" means several neighbours, so the verb must be plural. The written "was unable" wrongly treats "number" as a singular head. Flip the article test: a number = many people, so the repair is "were unable."

Mark it wrong and prefer "A number of neighbours were unable to join the street clean-up."
**C) Neither the coach nor the players were copied on the match email.**

With neither…nor, agreement follows the nearer subject — the one sitting just before the verb. Here that noun is plural "players," so "were copied" is correct. Ignore "coach" when you choose the verb; proximity, not the first noun, decides.

**Tip:** Cover the first noun and read only from "nor" onward.

Accept the line — nearer plural "players" after nor rightly takes "were copied."
**D) Each of the flatmates have filed a chore preference form.**

"Each of the flatmates" is singular even though "flatmates" looks plural. "Each" picks out one member at a time, and the of-phrase never takes control of the verb. The written "have filed" agrees with the wrong noun.

That agreement fails — rewrite as "Each of the flatmates has filed a chore preference form."
**E) There are several typos in the potluck recipe list.**

The delayed subject after "there" is plural "typos," so "there are" agrees correctly. In there-constructions the real subject follows the verb — match that noun's number. Here several typos make the plural verb unavoidable.

That works: plural "typos" after there correctly calls for "there are."
tasks.solution_overview:
You are judging five everyday sentences for subject-verb agreement. Library books, a street clean-up, a match email, flatmate chores, and a potluck list supply the setting — the verbs are what matter.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set mixes four classic traps: the number of versus a number of, neither…nor proximity, each of, and there is/are. Distracting plurals sit next to the verb on purpose, so your job is to name the true grammatical subject first. Once that subject is clear, the right verb number usually follows without debate.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cross out of-phrases and insert material, then ask whether the leftover head is singular or plural. For neither…nor, check only the noun sitting next to the verb. For there-constructions, look past the verb to the delayed subject and match that.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Every applicant for the baking class receives a starter kit.
The chef, along with two helpers, were present at the tasting.
There is a backlog of laundry waiting for the dryer.
Neither the twins nor their aunt has signed the permission slip.
A number of guests have requested a later checkout.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Every applicant for the baking class receives a starter kit.**

"Every applicant" is grammatically singular even though many people are implied. Singular "receives" is therefore correct with "a starter kit." Words like every and each always pick units one at a time in formal exam English.

This is sound — "every applicant" locks in singular "receives."
**B) The chef, along with two helpers, were present at the tasting.**

"Along with two helpers" is only a parenthetical add-on; the subject remains singular "The chef." Inserts introduced by along with, as well as, or together with never create a compound plural subject. The written "were present" wrongly steals plurality from the helpers.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "The chef, along with two helpers, was present at the tasting."
**C) There is a backlog of laundry waiting for the dryer.**

The delayed subject is singular "a backlog," so "there is" agrees. Do not let the plural idea inside "of laundry" steal the agreement — the head noun is backlog. Once you isolate that head, the singular verb is obvious.

Hold onto this: singular "backlog" after there correctly takes "there is."
**D) Neither the twins nor their aunt has signed the permission slip.**

After neither…nor the nearer subject is singular "aunt," so "has signed" is right. Proximity overrides the plural feel of "twins" at the front of the chain. Read only from "nor" to the verb when you decide number.

**Tip:** Neither…nor: last noun wins.

Call this correct: nearer singular "aunt" after nor takes "has signed."
**E) A number of guests have requested a later checkout.**

"A number of guests" means several guests, so plural "have requested" is correct. Flip the article test if you hesitate: a number = many, the number = one figure. Here the plural verb matches the plural sense cleanly.

The plural reading works: "a number of guests" rightly takes "have requested."
tasks.solution_overview:
Five more agreement checks, this time around a baking class, a tasting, laundry, a permission slip, and a hotel checkout. Same game: decide whether the sentence as written is fine.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

That proximity miss fails — prefer "Neither the kitchen nor the bathrooms were cleaned last week."
**C) There is three outstanding photos on the shared album.**

"Each partner" takes a singular verb even when "duo" suggests two people. The written "have veto rights" agrees with the wrong idea of plurality. Strip the of-phrase and hear "each has."

In formal usage "data" is treated as plural, so "support" is the agreed verb here. On exam papers, keep that plural default unless the prompt clearly marks informal style. The of-phrase "from the pilot survey" does not change the number.

Trust the verb here: formal plural "data" correctly takes "support."

Nearer singular "lawyer" correctly takes "has requested." A singular nearer noun wins even when plural sellers sit earlier in the chain. Delay content does not affect number.

**Tip:** Neither…nor: nearer noun, whatever its number.

That pairing works — nearer singular "lawyer" correctly takes "has requested."
**B) The head chef, along with the sous-chefs, reviews the specials nightly.**

Singular head chef governs "reviews" despite along with the sous-chefs. Strip the insert; "the head chef reviews" must stand alone. Nightly specials are just the object.

Accept the line: singular head chef stays head with "reviews."
**C) There are still a few outstanding RSVPs from classmates.**

Plural "RSVPs" correctly takes "there are." "A few" marks plurality after there. Classmates in the of-phrase do not change the head's number.

Leave it as written — plural "RSVPs" correctly take "there are."
**D) Each of the flatshare partners retains a spare key.**

"Each of the flatshare partners" takes singular "retains." Partners in the of-phrase do not control the verb. Spare-key content is irrelevant to agreement.

Call this correct: "each of" keeps singular "retains."
**E) The data underlying the fitness test suggest limited injury risk.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "suggest." Participial modifiers ("underlying the fitness test") never change data's formal plurality. Limited injury risk is the claim, not the subject.

**Tip:** Data stays plural under modifiers.

Trust it: formal plural "data" correctly takes "suggest."
tasks.solution_overview:
All five denser sentences — delay requests, nightly specials, classmate RSVPs, flatshare keys, and fitness-test data — are correct. Use them as benchmarks for the constructions you have been drilling.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Proximity after neither…nor with a singular nearer lawyer, along with with a singular chef, there are + a few, each of, and formal plural data with a participial modifier. Correct answers at this level still reward the same subject-finding habit, just with heavier noun phrases.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip inserts and modifiers, then confirm each head. Notice how a singular nearer noun after nor can win even when plural parties are nearby, and how "a few" marks plurality after there.

tasks.title: Task 14

statements: The number of unresolved tickets are alarming the helpdesk.
Neither the sponsor nor the team captains was invited to the closed meeting.

The managing editor, as well as the reporters, have approved the feature.
A number of clauses in the lease survive completion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of unresolved tickets are alarming the helpdesk.**

"The number of unresolved tickets" is a singular total alarming the helpdesk. Continuous forms still follow the head subject's number. The written "are alarming" wrongly agrees with "tickets."

**Trap:** Progressive "are alarming" after "the number of" is a polished near-miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The number of unresolved tickets is alarming the helpdesk."
**B) Neither the sponsor nor the team captains was invited to the closed meeting.**

Nearer plural "team captains" needs a plural verb after neither…nor. Long second nouns after nor are still plural when marked -s. Closed-meeting detail is irrelevant.

**Trap:** Singular "was invited" after a plural nearer noun is the classic proximity miss.

Reject this; the clean version is "Neither the sponsor nor the team captains were invited to the closed meeting."
**C) There seems to be several inconsistencies between the two diaries.**

Prefer "there seem to be several inconsistencies" to match the plural complement. Seem/appear after there must still track the real subject's number in careful usage. Two diaries make the plural clear.

**Trap:** "There seems to be several" looks formal while disagreeing with a plural complement.

That fails here — rewrite as "There seem to be several inconsistencies between the two diaries."
**D) The managing editor, as well as the reporters, have approved the feature.**

Singular managing editor plus as well as the reporters needs a singular verb. Reporters after as well as are not co-subjects. Feature approval is the object only.

**Trap:** As well as the reporters looks like and — but it never creates a plural compound subject.

**E) A number of clauses in the lease survive completion.**

"A number of clauses" correctly takes plural "survive." Present simple plural has no -s: survive, not survives. Completion timing does not change agreement.

Plural sense lands: "a number of clauses" correctly takes "survive."
tasks.solution_overview:
Helpdesk alarms, closed meetings, diary mismatches, a feature approval, and lease clauses: four failures and one clean "a number of" success. Soft connectors are designed to hide plural complements.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The number of with a wrong plural progressive, neither…nor with was, there seems to be several, as well as with a plural verb, and a correct plural survive after a number of. At this level, seems/appears after there must still track what follows.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Always check the complement after seems/appears to be. Progressive and perfect forms still follow the head subject's number. Present simple plurals after a number of take no -s on the verb (survive, not survives).

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15

tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the shop nor its branches is bound by the Sunday rule.**

**B) Every one of the contingent prizes has been disclosed in the notes.**

This is sound — "every one of" locks in singular "has been disclosed."
**C) There remain, after the rethink, three material open points.**

Plural "three material open points" correctly takes "remain," even with a mid-sentence insert. Ignore the comma aside ("after the rethink") and match the postponed plural subject. Rethink wording is padding only.

**Tip:** Delete the aside; match the plural subject after there.

Accept the line: plural "open points" correctly govern "there remain."
**D) The coach, together with the squad captains, was accountable for the overspend.**

**E) The data released this morning confirm the earlier forecast.**

tasks.solution_overview:
Sunday trading rules, prize disclosures, rethink asides, squad accountability, and morning data raise difficulty with inserts and passives — the agreement rules themselves stay fixed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Neither…nor with a false singular, every one of in the passive, there remain with a mid-sentence aside, together with, and formal plural data. Comma asides between there and the subject change nothing. Possessives before a nearer plural noun do not singularise it.

Find the subject first; the verb will usually announce itself. Ignore padding between there and the postponed subject, and keep every one singular even in passive perfect.

tasks.title: Task 16

statements: A number of practice drills was revised after the club meeting.
Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors has objected to the timetable.
There is, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge.
Each branch that operates abroad file a local safety certificate.
The number of noise complaints has stabilised since the quiet hours.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of practice drills was revised after the club meeting.**

"A number of practice drills" needs a plural verb. Long plural noun phrases after a number of still take plural verbs. Club-meeting timing does not singularise the drills.

**Trap:** Singular "was revised" after "a number of" is a near-miss that trusts the word number.

Don't accept that; rewrite as "A number of practice drills were revised after the club meeting."
**B) Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors has objected to the timetable.**

Nearer plural "mentors" needs a plural verb after neither…nor. "Students'" only marks possession; mentors remain plural. Timetable objections do not change number.

**Trap:** A possessive before the nearer noun often disguises a plural subject after nor.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Neither the tutor nor the students' mentors have objected to the timetable."
**C) There is, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge.**

Plural "bills" needs "there are," despite the interrupting phrase. Cross out the contrary-to aside before choosing is/are. Unpaid bills on the fridge stay plural.

**Trap:** A long aside after there is designed to hide a plural delayed subject.

That there-agreement fails — prefer "There are, contrary to the notice, several unpaid bills still on the fridge."
**D) Each branch that operates abroad file a local safety certificate.**

"Each branch" needs singular "files," not "file." Relative clauses after each ("that operates abroad") do not licence a plural verb. Local certificates are the object only.

**Trap:** A relative clause after each can make a plural verb look almost justified — it is not.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "Each branch that operates abroad files a local safety certificate."
**E) The number of noise complaints has stabilised since the quiet hours.**

"The number of noise complaints" correctly takes singular "has stabilised." Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural). Quiet hours describe the time frame, not the subject's number.

That works: singular "the number" correctly takes "has stabilised."
tasks.solution_overview:
Club drills, tutor mentors, fridge bills, overseas branches, and noise complaints use interruptions and relative clauses as noise. Mentally delete them, then apply the familiar tests.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A number of, neither…nor, there is with a contrary-to aside, each with a relative clause, and a clean the-number-of singular. Relative clauses after each do not licence a plural verb. Asides after there still leave the delayed subject's number in charge.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cross out interrupting phrases and relative clauses, then re-run a number / the number, proximity, there is/are, and each. Keep contrasting the number (singular) with a number (plural) on the last clean line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17

statements: Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams was named in the report.
The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approve large group bookings.
There appear to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow.
Every set of rehearsal notes for the cast is reviewed by the director.
The data on which the ranking rests are drawn from audited scores.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams was named in the report.**

Nearer plural "teams" needs a plural verb after neither…nor. Extra adjectives before the nearer noun do not change its plural number. Report content is irrelevant to agreement.

**Trap:** Satellite teams are still plural after nor, even with a singular club up front.

Score it false and use "Neither the parent club nor the satellite teams were named in the report."
**B) The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approve large group bookings.**

Singular "box office" plus along with stewards needs "approves," not "approve." Box office is a singular institutional subject here. Front-of-house stewards stay in the insert.

**Trap:** Institutional singulars plus human along-with inserts are a favourite reverse trap.

Strike this and write "The box office, along with the front-of-house stewards, approves large group bookings."
**C) There appear to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow.**

The complement "a single bottleneck" is singular, so write "there appears to be." Appear/seem after there must track a singular complement too — not only plurals. One bottleneck, singular verb.

**Trap:** Learners overcorrect to plural appear after there even when the complement is singular.

That number clash fails — prefer "There appears to be a single bottleneck in the check-in workflow."
**D) Every set of rehearsal notes for the cast is reviewed by the director.**

"Every set" is singular, so "is reviewed" is right. "Set of notes" is one unit; every keeps it singular. Director review is the passive agent, not the subject.

**Tip:** Every set of… → singular.

Accept the line: "every set" correctly takes singular "is reviewed."
**E) The data on which the ranking rests are drawn from audited scores.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "are drawn," even inside a which-clause sandwich. Relative clauses around data do not convert it to singular on formal papers. Audited scores are the source, not a singulariser.

Trust the exam default: formal plural "data" correctly takes "are drawn."

Top-band reverse traps: satellite teams, a box-office institution, a single bottleneck after appear, rehearsal-note sets, and audited ranking data. Read for the actual head noun, not the surrounding formality.

Neither…nor with a false singular, along with on an institutional singular, there appear with a singular complement (the reverse of the usual plural trap), every set, and formal plural data inside a which-clause sandwich. Name the head: teams, box office, bottleneck, set, data. Institutional singulars like "box office" stay singular despite human stewards in an along-with insert. "Every set of notes" is one unit.

tasks.solution_overview:
Five correct formal-register models: timetable acceptance, disclosure clearance, rules still in force, stepped fines, and school ranking data. Internalise how inserts still leave a single grammatical subject in charge.

Neither…nor with a plural nearer noun, together with, there remain with legalistic padding, each of, and formal plural data with a past participle. Dual adviser references and "for the avoidance of doubt" asides look heavy but change nothing about number.

Confirm proximity, strip together-with inserts, ignore padding between there and the subject, keep each singular, and keep data plural. These lines are what correct formal agreement looks like under exam conditions.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of material safety clauses was triggered overnight.
Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group was prepared to waive the rule.

The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of material safety clauses was triggered overnight.**

"A number of material safety clauses" needs a plural verb. Dense noun phrases still follow the a-number-of plural rule. Overnight timing does not singularise the clauses.

**Trap:** A long technical noun phrase makes singular "was triggered" look almost technical — it is not.

Mark it wrong and prefer "A number of material safety clauses were triggered overnight."
**B) Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group was prepared to waive the rule.**

Nearer plural "stewards" needs a plural verb after neither…nor. Extra modifiers after the nearer noun ("in the group") do not make it singular. Waiving the rule is content only.

**Trap:** Modifiers after the nearer noun invite a false singular after nor.

That proximity error fails — rewrite as "Neither the organiser nor the other stewards in the group were prepared to waive the rule."
**C) There is, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates.**

"More than two conflicting dates" is plural, so write "there are," not "there is." Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there. The long when-clause is only an interruption.

**Trap:** A long when-clause after there is designed to hide a plural quantity phrase.

Reject this; the clean version is "There are, when one examines the schedules carefully, more than two conflicting dates."
**D) The lead reviewer, as well as the marking team, were responsible for the opinion.**

Singular lead reviewer plus as well as the marking team needs a singular verb. Marking team after as well as is not a co-subject. Opinion content does not affect number.

**Trap:** As well as the marking team looks like a plural co-subject — agreement still follows the head.

Don't accept that; fix to "The lead reviewer, as well as the marking team, was responsible for the opinion."
**E) The data that the model relies on have been restated twice this year.**

Formal plural data correctly takes "have been restated." Prefer plural agreement with data on formal exams unless the paper allows informal singular data. The model-relies-on clause does not singularise data.

Leave the plural: formal "data" correctly takes "have been restated."
tasks.solution_overview:
Four agreement failures surround one clean formal-data line: overnight safety clauses, steward waivers, conflicting dates, a reviewer's opinion, and restated model data. Strip inserts before you judge.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A number of, neither…nor with extra modifiers, there is with a long when-clause, as well as with a false plural, and plural data with a present perfect passive. Quantity phrases greater than one take plural after there. As well as still never makes a co-subject of the marking team.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat plural data as the safe exam default on the last line. For the false lines, delete modifiers and asides, then re-apply a number, proximity, there is/are, and as well as. "More than two" is a plural cue after there.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

**C) There appear to be fewer exceptions in this month's checklist.**
