**C) Direct: "Dare I ask for a refund?" → "He asked if he dared ask for a refund.".**

Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive. "He asked if he dared ask for a refund" turns modal-like dare into a past lexical dare inside if. That is acceptable advanced reporting for "Dare I ask…?"

**Tip:** Dare I…? → asked if + subject + dared + bare infinitive.

That advanced dare report works — if he dared ask is acceptable.
**D) Direct: "The team will have been rehearsing for six hours by then." → "She said the team would have been rehearsing for six hours by then.".**

Future perfect continuous will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. "She said the team would have been rehearsing for six hours by then" changes only will to would; the rest of the stack stays. By then can remain because it is already relative.

Accept the line: only will→would moves inside the long perfect-continuous stack.
**E) Direct: "What if we delay the concert?" → "He asked what if we delayed the concert.".**

"What if…" hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb. "He asked what if we delayed the concert" is natural exam English for "What if we delay…?" You do not need to force a full if/whether paraphrase here.

Keep this: what if with delayed is a natural hypothetical report.
highlights: had been cleared the previous winter
tasks.solution_overview:
A clean advanced sweep: passive perfect reports, prefer + not to, dare, future perfect continuous, and what-if backshift — all grammatical.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Passive past yes/no → whether + past perfect passive + last→previous. Would prefer + object + not to keeps its skeleton while pronouns and this→that adjust. Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive. Will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. What if… hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm voice/stack retention where needed and only the layers that truly move (will→would, last→previous, this→that). Every line already does — use the set as a high-difficulty model bank.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog."
Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon."
Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first."
Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning."
Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog.".**

Negative inversion can survive inside the reported clause after said, with pronoun and tense already matching. "She said seldom had they seen such fog" keeps the inverted rhetorical shape. Reporting rare inverted rhetoric may keep that shape when the rest aligns.

**Tip:** Flashy inversion is optional but grammatical if tenses and pronouns fit.

This inverted rhetoric is allowed — seldom had they seen may keep its shape.
**B) Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon.".**

"Was to have + past participle" (unfulfilled plan) typically remains was to have…. This past-scheduled perfect form needs no further shift under said. "He said he was to have signed before noon" keeps the missed-plan meaning intact.

Keep this: was to have signed stays unchanged as an unfulfilled plan.
**C) Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first.".**

Embedded object questions need statement order — "who we should notify first," not "who should we notify first." Modal should still follows the subject after asked. Repair: She asked who we should notify first.

**Trap:** Modal should does not license question order once the clause is embedded after asked.

Mark it wrong and prefer "She asked who we should notify first."
**D) Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning.".**

Future will → would, and tomorrow morning → the next morning. "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning" moves both pieces after past said. Will and time words travel together.

Accept the line: would and the next morning both shifted with the report.
**E) Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours.".**

Yes/no might needs if or whether + subject + might, not "might the shop extend…" Bare modal inversion is still a direct question after asked. Repair: They asked whether the shop might extend its hours.

**Trap:** Leaving might before the subject looks modal-aware but skips if/whether entirely.

Reject bare might-inversion; rewrite as "They asked whether the shop might extend its hours."
tasks.solution_overview:
Inverted who-should and bare might-yes/no fail. Surviving rhetorical inversion, was-to-have, and would + next-morning time shifts are acceptable.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Negative inversion can survive inside a reported clause after said when pronouns and tenses already match. Was to have + past participle (unfulfilled plan) typically remains. Embedded object questions need statement order: who we should notify. Will → would with tomorrow morning → the next morning. Yes/no might needs if/whether + subject + might.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow rare rhetorical inversion and frozen was-to-have; still force statement order on ordinary who/might questions. Mark false on who should we and bare might the shop.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that."
Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed."
Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast."
Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called."
Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that.".**

Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts. "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that" does not force past perfect inside the rather-clause. Preferential rather-clauses are not automatically deepened further.

Keep this: she'd rather I didn't spoil that keeps the preference clause intact.
**B) Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed.".**

Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect for a prior failure. "He asked how come the cake had collapsed" keeps how come and deepens the collapse. Pattern: asked how come + subject + (had) + past participle.

That informal report works — how come the cake had collapsed is valid.
**C) Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast.".**

"Used not to" (or didn't use to) for past habit can remain used not to. Habitual used-to patterns are already past-oriented, so further backshift is unnecessary. "They said they used not to skip breakfast" keeps the old habit meaning.

Accept the line: used not to can stay as-is under past said.
**D) Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called.".**

Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the time-clause present→past. "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called" shifts both the main future perfect and the by-the-time clause. Both layers move together under past asked.

**Tip:** will you have… by the time I…? → if + would have… by the time + past.

This double backshift is sound — would have finished and she called move together.
**E) Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers.".**

Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base (or past) form in formal reports. "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers" is exam-friendly for "Suppose we freeze…" Mandative or tentative freeze after suggested that is acceptable.

Keep this: suggested that we freeze correctly maps the suppose-idea.
highlights: how come the cake had collapsed
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are advanced but valid: rather + past clause, how come, used not to, nested would-have with by-the-time, and suggested that.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts. Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect. Used not to for past habit can remain. Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the by-the-time clause present→past. Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Retain already-past preference and habit patterns; still shift futures and demonstratives; allow suggested that for suppose. Every line passes — treat the set as a finishing model.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce."
Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper."
Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit."
Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade."
Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then."
tactical_explanations:
**A) Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce.".**

Correlative not only…but also can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past. "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce" is optional but grammatical when pronouns and tenses align. Reporting flashy inversion is allowed if the rest of the clause matches the past frame.

Accept the optional inversion: not-only may survive when tenses already fit.
**B) Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper.".**

Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have. Perfect absence-of-need does not become hadn't need under said. "He said he needn't have packed every jumper" keeps the "did it but didn't need to" meaning.

**Tip:** Needn't have stays; do not invent hadn't need.

Keep this: needn't have for unused past necessity remains unchanged.
**C) Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit.".**

Statement order is required — "where the chairs should sit," not "where should the chairs sit." Modal should follows the subject in embedded wh-questions. Repair: She asked where the chairs should sit.

**Trap:** Where + should still needs subject-before-modal after asked.

Mark it wrong and prefer "She asked where the chairs should sit."
**D) Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade.".**

Next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade" changes only will→would in the long stack. Long future-perfect-continuous stacks shift the will piece and the next calendar word.

That long-stack report works — the following March and would have been leasing both shifted.
**E) Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then.".**

Yes/no past continuous needs if or whether + statement order — "whether anyone was monitoring…" — never bare "was anyone…" after asked. Leaving then unchanged does not excuse the missing if/whether frame. Repair: She asked whether anyone was monitoring the feed then.

**Trap:** A matching then can hide bare was-anyone inversion after asked.

Reject bare was-anyone inversion; rewrite as "She asked whether anyone was monitoring the feed then."
tasks.solution_overview:
Two order failures remain: should after where, and bare was-anyone after asked. Inverted not only, needn't have, and future perfect continuous reports are fine.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Correlative not only…but can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past. Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have. Embedded wh + modal needs statement order: where the chairs should sit. Next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing. Yes/no past continuous needs if/whether + statement order.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow rhetorical not-only inversion and frozen needn't have; still refuse bare inversion after asked on ordinary questions. Mark false on where should and asked was anyone.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.
He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.
We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.
The coach approved an plan for the relay team.
Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.**

"Apple" begins with a vowel sound, so the indefinite article must be "an," not "a." The lunchbox and hike wording are fine; only the article before apple is wrong. Matching a/an to the letter you see instead of the sound you hear is what breaks this line.

Mark it wrong and prefer "an apple" — vowel sound after the article wants an.
**B) He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.**

"Umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so "an umbrella" is the correct first-mention form. The sentence introduces one countable item before the concert, which is exactly where a/an belongs. Nothing else in the line needs fixing.

That works: "an" correctly matches the vowel onset of umbrella.
**C) We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.**

"New" begins with a consonant sound (/n/), so English needs "a new bicycle," not "an new bicycle." An adjective between the article and the noun does not change the rule — you still listen to the sound right after a/an. Repair only the article before new; the weekend-trip frame can stay.

**Tip:** Adjectives do not change a/an — listen to the sound that follows.

Reject this article swap; rewrite as "a new bicycle" so a/an follows the /n/ sound.
**D) The coach approved an plan for the relay team.**

"Plan" begins with a consonant sound, so the form must be "a plan," not "an plan." The coach, the approval, and the relay team can stay exactly as written. Only the article immediately before plan is the fault.

That article choice fails — go with "a plan" before the consonant onset.
**E) Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.**

"Email" begins with a vowel sound (/iː/), so "an email" is correct. Saying the next word aloud confirms the vowel onset immediately. This is a clean, standard first-mention pattern.

Keep this: "an email" matches the spoken vowel onset.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are packing lunch, shopping for outdoor gear, and emailing rehearsal times — everyday scenes where a and an sit right before a singular countable noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is only about matching a versus an to the sound that follows, not to the first letter on the page. An adjective between the article and the noun still counts: listen to the first sound of that adjective. First-mention countable nouns take a/an; the wrong shape of that article is what makes a line fail.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Say the word right after a/an aloud. If it starts with a vowel sound, choose an; if it starts with a consonant sound, choose a. Spelling alone (apple, umbrella, email, new, plan) can mislead you — sound wins every time.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.
They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.
She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.
We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.
He is an university student in biology.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.**

"Honest" starts with a silent h, so the spoken form begins with a vowel sound and takes "an." The spelling still shows h, which is why the choice can feel surprising until you hear it. Silent letters decide a/an by sound, not by the letters on the page.

Accept the line — silent-h "honest" correctly takes "an."
**B) They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.**

"European" begins with a /j/ sound (like "you"), which counts as a consonant sound, so "a European" is correct. The eu- spelling looks vowel-first, but the glide at the start blocks an. Treat that "y" onset like any other consonant sound.

**Tip:** Eu- and u- words often take a when they sound like they start with "y."

This is sound: the /j/ glide in European takes "a," not "an."
**C) She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.**

"MBA" is normally read letter by letter, starting with /em/, a vowel sound, so it needs "an MBA." Repair "a MBA" to "an MBA"; the volunteering clause can stay. With abbreviations, base a/an on how you pronounce the first letter name.

Trap: Spelling starts with M, so "a MBA" looks plausible until you say the letter name aloud.

Mark it wrong and prefer "an MBA," matching the spoken letter name /em/.
**D) We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.**

In standard modern pronunciation, "hotel" keeps the /h/, so "a hotel" is the usual form, not "an hotel." Prefer a before clearly sounded h-words in contemporary English. Older "an hotel" usage is not the safe exam default here.

Trap: "An hotel" survives in older or emphatic speech, so it looks like a near-miss on the page.

That fails on modern pronunciation — rewrite as "a hotel."
**E) He is an university student in biology.**

"University" starts with a /j/ sound, so the correct form is "a university student." If you can hear a "y" glide at the start, choose a — the written u does not unlock an. Repair only the article before university.

Trap: The written u makes "an university" look vowel-led until you hear the glide.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "a university student."
tasks.solution_overview:
Trail talk, a French exchange tutor, an MBA, a hotel near the festival, and a biology student: the same a/an choice, but sound and spelling pull in different directions.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

These lines turn on pronunciation traps — silent h, the "y" glide in European and university, letter-name openings in abbreviations, and whether hotel keeps a sounded /h/. Spelling is only a hint; the spoken onset decides a versus an.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Say the next word (or abbreviation) the way you would in careful speech. Silent letters, initialisms starting with vowel-letter names, and /j/-glides are the three places people guess wrong — check those first on every line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.
Please close a window; it is freezing in here.
She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.
Could you pass me a salt from the tray?
They opened an café on the corner last spring.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.**

First mention uses "a novel"; the second mention switches to "the novel" because the same book is now identified. That a → the handoff is exactly how English tracks reference across two clauses. Nothing in the chain is accidental.

**Tip:** a/an introduces; the points back to something already specified.

Keep this handoff: a introduces the book, then the points back to it.
**B) Please close a window; it is freezing in here.**

In this situation the window is a specific one in the room, so English expects "the window," not "a window." When both speakers can identify the thing from context, prefer the. The freezing-room cue makes that shared reference obvious.

Trap: "A window" still looks grammatical in isolation, which is why the situational the is easy to miss.

Call it wrong and prefer "Please close the window" for the shared room referent.
**C) She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.**

Roles after "as" commonly take a/an for one role among many: "as a junior soprano." The choir is already definite with the, and the role is introduced as a class member with a. Occupations and voice parts follow this pattern cleanly.

That role pattern is right — "as a junior soprano" fits cleanly.
**D) Could you pass me a salt from the tray?**

At the table, "salt" is a specific shared item, so "the salt" is the natural choice. Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the, not a. The tray phrase only locates that shared item.

**Tip:** Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the.

Mark it wrong; at the table rewrite as "pass me the salt from the tray."
**E) They opened an café on the corner last spring.**

"Café" begins with a consonant sound (/k/), so use "a café," not "an café." A vowel letter in the spelling does not override a consonant sound. Repair only the article before café.

That article fails the sound test — prefer "a café."
tasks.solution_overview:
A novel at midnight, a freezing room, a choir role, salt on the tray, and a corner café — these lines mix first mention, shared objects, roles, and one a/an sound trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on whether the noun is newly introduced or already clear to both speakers. First mention often takes a/an; a second mention of the same thing switches to the. Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting also prefer the, while roles after "as" commonly keep a/an.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask: Can both people already point to this exact thing? If yes, lean toward the. If the noun is one of a class being introduced — including a role among many — lean toward a/an. Then double-check café-type sound matches so a misspelled an does not sneak through.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sun was still low when the runners started.
Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.
She is only person who finished the crossword.
This is same recipe we used last winter.
He is the tallest player on the school team.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The sun was still low when the runners started.**

Unique celestial bodies take "the": "the sun." The runners are also definite in this race context, so the before runners fits as well. One-of-a-kind natural referents almost always need the.

Accept the line: "the sun" is the required unique form.
**B) Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.**

"Moon" in this sense needs "the moon"; leaving it bare is not standard. Pair the with unique natural landmarks and celestial objects the same way you do with the sun. The harbour line only sets the scene.

Reject the bare noun; rewrite as "The moon looks unusually bright…" with the.
**C) She is only person who finished the crossword.**

"Only" before a singular noun requires "the only person." Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the locked in before the noun. The crossword clause can stay once the is in place.

**Tip:** Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the.

That misses the determiner slot — prefer "the only person who finished the crossword."
**D) This is same recipe we used last winter.**

The fixed pattern is "the same recipe," not bare "same recipe." "Same" almost never stands without the in this comparative use. Insert the before same and the relative clause can stay.

**Tip:** "Same" almost never stands without the in this use.

Mark it wrong and lock in "the same recipe."
**E) He is the tallest player on the school team.**

Superlative forms take "the": "the tallest player." If you see -est (or most + adjective) for a unique ranking in a set, expect the. The school-team frame makes that unique ranking clear.

This is sound — the superlative correctly takes "the."
tasks.solution_overview:
Sunrise races, a bright harbour moon, a crossword finisher, a winter recipe, and a school-team ranking — these lines hunt for the with unique, exclusive, or superlative reference.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unique things (the sun, the moon), superlatives (the tallest), and words like only and same strongly prefer the. The noun must point to one identifiable item in the world or in a set; if that exclusivity marker is missing the, the line fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for uniqueness markers first: celestial one-offs, only, same, and -est / most rankings. If you see one of those, expect the before the noun. Bare Moon, only person, or same recipe without the is almost always the error.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.
She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.
We still need more informations before we choose a route.
The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.
They bought an furniture for the guest room.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.**

"Advice" is uncountable, so it appears with zero article here and is modified by "useful," not by a/an. Uncountable abstract nouns often take zero article when used in a general sense. The line models the pattern you want to protect.

Keep this: bare "useful advice" is the right general mass form.
**B) She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.**

"Advice" cannot take "an"; say "some advice" or "a piece of advice." If you need a countable unit, use a piece/bit/item of + the uncountable noun. Specific packing tips still do not unlock an advice.

Trap: "An advice" looks like ordinary first-mention a/an until you recall advice is a mass noun.

That fails — rewrite as "some advice" or "a piece of advice."
**C) We still need more informations before we choose a route.**

"Information" has no plural form in standard English; use "more information," not "informations." Watch for false plurals on uncountable nouns — the -s ending is the whole problem here. Keep more and drop the illegal plural.

Trap: The -s ending makes "informations" look like a normal plural countable.

Reject the false plural; prefer "more information."
**D) The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.**

"Equipment" is uncountable and correctly appears without a/an; "new" simply describes the mass noun. Zero article + adjective + uncountable noun is a common correct pattern. The science-fair purpose does not suddenly make equipment countable.

That works: "new equipment" needs no a/an.
**E) They bought an furniture for the guest room.**

"Furniture" is uncountable, so "an furniture" is impossible; use "furniture" or "a piece of furniture." Do not place a/an directly before classic uncountables like furniture, equipment, or advice. Strip an, or quantify with a piece of.

Mark it wrong and prefer "furniture" or "a piece of furniture."
tasks.solution_overview:
Ranger tips, packing advice, route information, science-fair equipment, and guest-room furniture — classic uncountable nouns that push back against a/an and false plurals.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Uncountable nouns reject a/an and usually reject plural -s. General reference prefers zero article (useful advice, new equipment), while a quantifying phrase such as a piece of is the way to carve out a unit when you need one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the noun is a mass/abstract (advice, information, equipment, furniture). If yes, ban a/an directly before it and check plural endings too. Prefer zero article for general talk, or a piece/bit/item of when you need a countable unit.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.
The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.
Research shows that morning light can improve mood.
We lack an evidence to support that claim.
Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.**

"Progress" is uncountable and correctly used with zero article for a general process underway. Zero article is normal with progress, research, and similar abstracts. The mural phrase narrows topic without forcing a/an.

Accept bare "Progress" — it fits the uncountable process reading.
**B) The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.**

"News" is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "The news was surprising." The determiner "the" can stay; the verb must agree. "News" looks plural but behaves as singular — that mismatch is the whole problem.

Trap: The -s ending pushes writers toward were, which is the classic agreement trap.

That agreement fails; rewrite as "The news was surprising…"
**C) Research shows that morning light can improve mood.**

General research findings use zero article: "Research shows…" When you mean research as a field or body of work in general, omit a/the. The that-clause content does not change the bare subject pattern.

Keep this: bare "Research" correctly names the field in general.
**D) We lack an evidence to support that claim.**

"Evidence" is uncountable, so "an evidence" is wrong; use "evidence" or "a piece of evidence." Specificity about a claim does not make evidence countable with a/an. Drop an, or quantify with a piece of.

Trap: Specific claims often tempt writers into "an evidence," as if first-mention a/an still applied.

Reject "an evidence"; prefer "evidence" or "a piece of evidence."
**E) Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.**

"Traffic" is uncountable and takes zero article in this general statement about conditions. Mass nouns for weather, traffic, and similar conditions usually need no a/an. The airport trip supplies setting, not a countable unit.

This is sound: bare "Traffic" is the standard mass-noun form.
tasks.solution_overview:
A mural's progress, neighbourhood news, mood research, courtroom-style evidence, and airport traffic — everyday mass nouns that look countable until agreement or a/an goes wrong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Several everyday nouns are uncountable even when they end in -s or feel countable. Keep zero article for general reference and avoid a/an before evidence, progress, and traffic. News takes singular agreement despite its plural look.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Test number first: news/progress/research/evidence/traffic usually refuse plural verbs and refuse a/an as a direct determiner. Prefer zero article for general statements; allow the when a specific body of news is framed, but still keep singular was, not were.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**A) Children need clear routines at home.**

Plural nouns in a general sense take zero article: "Children need…" General plurals usually omit the because no definite set of kids has been named. The home setting stays general too.

Keep this genericity: bare "Children" correctly means children in general.
**B) The neighbours expect quieter evenings during exam week.**

Here "the neighbours" can refer to the known people next door, so the is acceptable and natural. The + plural is fine when the group is definite in context. Exam week just supplies the time frame.

That definite plural works — "the neighbours" names a known local group.
**C) Water is still scarce after the long drought.**

Uncountable "water" used generically takes zero article. Materials and substances in general statements often need no determiner. The drought explains why, without turning water into a definite bottle or tap.

Accept bare "Water" for the generic substance reading.
**D) She drinks the coffee every morning before class.**

Habitual general coffee-drinking uses zero article: "She drinks coffee every morning," not "the coffee," unless a specific coffee is meant. Do not force the onto uncountables used in a general habitual sense. Drop the before coffee and keep the morning routine.

Trap: "The coffee" sounds fine for a known cup, so it is an easy false friend in a habit line.

Mark the habit line wrong and prefer "She drinks coffee every morning…"
**E) Teachers should explain key ideas carefully.**

Plural "Teachers" in a general professional statement correctly takes zero article. Job-title plurals meaning "teachers in general" stay bare. The advice is about the profession as a class, not one named staff list.

That professional plural is right — bare "Teachers" means the field in general.
tasks.solution_overview:
Kids' routines, quieter exam-week evenings, scarce water, morning coffee, and careful teachers — general plurals and general uncountables versus a forced the.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

General plurals and general uncountables prefer zero article. Use the only when the group or substance is already limited to a known set. Habitual coffee as a substance is bare; the coffee usually means a specific brew already identified.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each plural or mass noun, ask whether the speaker means "in general" or "this known set." General → usually zero (Children, Water, Teachers). Known neighbours next door → the neighbours is fine. Habitual substance use → drop the unless a specific serving is meant.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.

**A) He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.**

Fixed patterns "go to work" and "by bus" both use zero article. Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks. The weekday habit fits the institutional-purpose reading perfectly.

**Tip:** Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks.

Leave this standing: both "to work" and "by bus" are bare fixed frames.
**B) She travelled to Lisbon by a train last Friday.**

That transport frame fails — rewrite as "by train."
**C) They sent the parcels by courier overnight.**

Keep this: "by courier" correctly stays bare.
**D) I usually go to the home after the evening class.**

Reject the detour; prefer "go home after the evening class."
**E) We went to school together in the same district.**

"Go to school" with zero article means attendance as a student, which fits this sentence. Purpose-of-institution uses often drop the. The same district just locates that shared schooling.

tasks.solution_overview:
Commuting by bus, a Friday train to Lisbon, overnight courier parcels, going home after class, and schooling in the same district — frozen chunks where articles do not follow ordinary logic.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Several high-frequency chunks freeze the determiner choice: by bus/train, go to work/school, and go home. Treat them as fixed patterns rather than building them word by word with "logical" a/the.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Whenever you see by + transport or go to work/school/home, recall the memorised frame first. by train stays bare; go home drops both to and the in this meaning; go to school (attendance) stays bare. If someone inserted a or the inside those frames, that is usually the fault.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

This patient reading is sound — bare "in hospital" fits the purpose idiom.
**B) We drove past the hospital on our way to the lake.**

**Tip:** Switch to the when you mean the building, not the institutional purpose.

Keep the landmark reading: "the hospital" correctly means the building.

**E) She stayed in bed until noon because of a migraine.**

tasks.solution_overview:
Post-operation recovery, driving past a hospital, activists and a hillside prison, and a migraine day in bed — institution nouns flipping between purpose and building.

Institution nouns flip between zero article (purpose: patient, prisoner) and the (the building as a place). British in hospital / in prison for purpose contrasts with the hospital / the prison as landmarks. In bed for resting follows the same purpose logic.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read each line for purpose versus physical location. Patient/inmate/resting readings → usually zero (in hospital, in prison, in bed). Landmark or building description → the. If activists are "in" as inmates, strip the; if the prison sits on a hill as a place, keep the.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**A) She plays the piano at family gatherings.**

Musical instruments take "the" in this general ability/habit pattern: "play the piano." play + the + instrument is the default for named instruments. Family gatherings only set the scene.

Keep this instrument rule: "play the piano" is the expected frame.
**B) He plays the football for the local amateur side.**

Sports use zero article: "play football," not "play the football." Contrast instruments (the) with sports and games (zero). Drop the before football; the club name can stay definite.

That sports article fails — rewrite as "play football."
**C) They listen to the radio during the morning walk.**

"Listen to the radio" is the standard pattern for the medium. the radio / the news are common fixed media patterns. The morning walk is just when they listen.

Accept the media frame: "the radio" is fixed and natural here.
**D) I watched a television until midnight after the film.**

Habitual or general TV watching is "watch television," not "watch a television," unless you mean one physical set. Medium versus device: the medium often takes zero; a specific device can take a/the. Here the medium reading is intended, so drop a.

**E) She is learning the violin with a private tutor.**

"Learn the violin" follows the same instrument rule as play the piano. Keep the with named instruments after play/learn. The private tutor is a separate countable first mention with a.

tasks.solution_overview:
Family piano nights, an amateur football side, morning radio walks, late TV after a film, and violin lessons — instruments, sports, and media each freeze different articles.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Instruments prefer the (play/learn the piano, the violin); sports prefer zero (play football). Media words like radio and television also have preferred patterns — do not invent a/an forms where the medium itself is meant.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Sort the noun: instrument → expect the; sport/game → expect zero; medium (the radio, watch television) → use the set media pattern. If the line forces the onto a sport or a onto TV-as-medium, that is usually wrong.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Most students supported the later start time.
The most of guests opposed the outdoor seating plan.
Half of the cake has already been eaten.
Both finalists gave a strong closing speech.
All of luggage must be labelled before check-in.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Most students supported the later start time.**

"Most" + plural noun takes zero article when speaking generally about the majority: "Most students…" most + noun (no the) is the frame for general majorities. The later start time is the definite proposal they supported.

Keep bare "Most students" for a general-majority claim.
**B) The most of guests opposed the outdoor seating plan.**

Do not say "the most of guests"; use "most of the guests" or "most guests." After most of, you normally need the + definite noun phrase. Rebuild the whole quantifier frame rather than leaving the most of.

Trap: "The most" from superlatives blends into "the most of," a hybrid exam writers often invent.

That quantifier hybrid fails — prefer "most of the guests" or "most guests."
**C) Half of the cake has already been eaten.**

"Half of the cake" correctly combines the quantifier with a definite noun phrase. half/most/some of + the + specific noun is a safe pattern. Singular agreement with cake is also consistent.

Accept "Half of the cake": the safe of-the frame is in place.
**D) Both finalists gave a strong closing speech.**

"Both finalists" needs no article before both; "a strong closing speech" correctly introduces one speech each. both/all/each have their own determiner rules — do not stack the before both. The countable speech still needs a.

That determiner pairing works — bare "Both finalists" plus "a … speech" are both right.
**E) All of luggage must be labelled before check-in.**

"All of luggage" is incomplete; write "all of the luggage" or "all luggage." all of must be followed by a determined noun phrase (often with the). Either add the after of, or drop of and keep all luggage.

Trap: "All of" feels complete on its own, so writers often forget the after of.

Mark it wrong and prefer "all of the luggage" or "all luggage."
tasks.solution_overview:
Start-time votes, outdoor seating guests, leftover cake, finalists' speeches, and labelled luggage — quantifiers that demand exact determiner frames.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Quantifier patterns interact with determiners: most + noun, most of the + noun, half of the +, and all of the +. Avoid blending those frames into hybrids like the most of guests or all of luggage.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the quantifier is bare most/both/all before a general plural, usually no the right after it. If you use most of / half of / all of, expect a determined noun phrase (often the + noun). Spot illegal blends and rebuild the whole frame, not just one word.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**C) They offer a course in photography this term.**

**Tip:** Count the course, not the subject noun itself.

That structure is sound: bare "photography" sits inside countable "a course."
**D) The mathematics in this puzzle is unexpectedly elegant.**

Here "the mathematics" refers to the specific maths in this puzzle, so the is justified. The + subject is fine when limited by a postmodifier or clear context. Unexpected elegance is about that defined slice of maths.

**Tip:** The + subject is fine when limited by a postmodifier or clear context.

Accept the licensed definite: the postmodifier justifies "the mathematics."
**E) She teaches the English at a private college.**

Language subjects in general take zero article: "teaches English," not "teaches the English." Language names as school subjects are usually bare. Drop the before English; keep a private college as written.

Mark it wrong and prefer "teaches English" with zero article.
tasks.solution_overview:
Economics degrees, museum history, photography courses, elegant puzzle maths, and English teaching — subject and language names that stay bare until narrowed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Subject and language names are bare in general academic use, but the appears when the noun is limited to a specific body of material. Separate the countable "course" from the subject label itself.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the noun names a field or language in general study/teaching, prefer zero (economics, history, English, photography as subject). If a postmodifier or clear context picks out a specific slice (the mathematics in this puzzle), the is licensed. Count a course; do not article the subject name needlessly.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The Netherlands remains a popular cycling destination.

**A) The Netherlands remains a popular cycling destination.**

Country names that are plural or include a common noun often take "the": "the Netherlands." the with Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States, Philippines, and similar names is the regular pattern. The cycling frame does not change the country article.

**Tip:** the with Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States, Philippines, etc.

Keep "The Netherlands" — plural-looking country names take the.
**B) She moved to United Kingdom after finishing her degree.**

The standard form is "the United Kingdom," not bare "United Kingdom" after to. Full political names with Kingdom/States/Republic usually need the. Insert the before United Kingdom.

Trap: Bare country defaults make writers drop the from Kingdom/States names.

That country name fails without the; rewrite as "moved to the United Kingdom…"
**C) Their hostel is just outside Hague, near the sea.**

Trap: Most cities are bare, so leaving Hague without The looks like the usual zero-article rule.

Reject bare Hague; prefer "outside The Hague."
**D) We spent two weeks in Brazil last summer.**

Most single-name countries take zero article: "in Brazil." Default for country and city names is zero unless the name belongs to a the-group. Last summer only times the trip.

Accept bare "Brazil" — single-name countries stay zero by default.
**E) The Amazon is vital to several rainforest ecosystems.**

Famous rivers take "the": "the Amazon." the with rivers, seas, oceans, and canal names is the safe waterway rule. Ecosystem importance does not license dropping the.

**Tip:** the with rivers, seas, oceans, and canal names.

This river article is right: "The Amazon" correctly takes the.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cycling in the Netherlands, a move to the UK, The Hague by the sea, a Brazil summer, and the Amazon — geography rules for countries, cities, and rivers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Geography has compact rules: most countries and cities are bare, but plural/political names and many waterways take the. A handful of names include The as part of the proper noun (The Hague).

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Default countries and cities to zero (Brazil). Force the with political/plural names (the Netherlands, the United Kingdom) and famous rivers (the Amazon). Watch for names where The is built in (The Hague). Bare United Kingdom or Hague is the usual failure mode.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

Lake Victoria in textbooks, an Atlantic freighter crossing, Mount Everest hikers, a week in the Alps, and the Sahara — natural features that split bare versus the.

Natural features split cleanly: lakes and Mount-names are often bare; oceans, ranges, deserts, and many seas take the. Learn the groups rather than guessing per word.

Classify the feature: Lake/Mount + name → usually zero; ocean/sea/range/desert → usually the. Atlantic without the, Alps without the, or Sahara without the are the common misses. Great Lakes as a group is a separate exception to remember later.

tasks.title: Task 15

Poverty, life, society, honesty, and curiosity — broad abstract nouns that stay bare until a phrase turns them into a specific instance.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**A) The advice she received from her coach was unusually clear.**

Uncountable "advice" can take "the" when a relative clause identifies a specific body of advice. Uncountable + the is fine once the noun is made specific. Clarity is about that identified advice, not advice-in-general.

**Tip:** Uncountable + the is fine once the noun is made specific.

Keep "The advice" — the relative clause licenses the definite mass reading.
**B) Equipment that arrived yesterday is still in the hallway.**

"Equipment" remains uncountable; zero article works even with a defining relative clause when the noun is used as a mass. You may also say "the equipment that arrived…" — both can be acceptable; bare is not wrong here. The hallway only places it.

**Tip:** You may also say "the equipment that arrived…" — both can be acceptable.

That mass reference works: bare "Equipment that arrived…" is acceptable.
**C) An information in the appendix contradicts the summary.**

"Information" cannot take "an"; use "information" or "a piece of information." Specificity does not magically make an uncountable noun countable with a/an. Drop an, or quantify with a piece of, even if the appendix pinpoints the content.

Trap: Appendix pinpointing tempts writers into "an information" as if specificity unlocked a/an.

Mark it wrong and prefer "information" or "a piece of information."
**D) The research published last week challenges our assumptions.**

"The research published last week" correctly uses the because the postmodifier identifies a particular study set. Postmodifiers often licence the with otherwise general uncountables. Assumptions stay ours; the research is the definite challenge.

**Tip:** Postmodifiers often licence the with otherwise general uncountables.

Accept "The research" — the postmodifier makes that body of work definite.
**E) We need a progress before the next rehearsal.**

"Progress" is uncountable, so "a progress" is wrong; say "progress" or "some progress." Never place a/an directly before progress. The next rehearsal only sets the deadline.

Trap: "A progress" looks like ordinary countable first mention before a deadline.

Reject "a progress"; rewrite as "progress" or "some progress."
tasks.solution_overview:
Coach advice that landed, hallway equipment, appendix information, last week's research, and rehearsal progress — uncountables that can take the when narrowed, but never a/an.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Uncountables can take the when narrowed by context, but they still reject a/an. Specificity changes zero versus the, not countability itself. Relative clauses and published-last-week style postmodifiers often licence the.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask two separate questions: Is the mass noun identified enough for the? And is someone illegally using a/an anyway? the advice she received and the research published last week can be fine; an information and a progress never are. Zero-article equipment with a defining clause can also be acceptable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was appointed the captain of the rowing club.

tactical_explanations:
**A) She was appointed the captain of the rowing club.**

After appoint/elect/name, English often uses "the" + unique role: "appointed the captain." Unique office titles after appoint/elect frequently take the. The rowing club makes the post singular and definite.

**Tip:** Unique office titles after appoint/elect frequently take the.

Keep "the captain" — unique office after appoint correctly takes the.
**B) He became a head of the drama department after the reshuffle.**

Prefer "the head of the drama department" for a unique post, or rephrase; "a head of…" sounds like one of several equal heads. Unique organisational roles usually take the, not a. Repair a to the before head.

Trap: "A head of…" looks like ordinary role first-mention, but the post is unique.

That role needs uniqueness marking; prefer "the head of the drama department."
**C) They elected her treasurer of the local book club.**

Zero article is also possible after elect/appoint when the title follows directly: "elected her treasurer." Both "elected her treasurer" and "elected her the treasurer" appear; bare title after the object is standard. The local book club names the organisation.

**Tip:** Both "elected her treasurer" and "elected her the treasurer" appear; bare title after the object is standard.

Accept bare "treasurer" after elect + object — that title frame is standard.
**D) She is a only photographer who stayed until closing.**

"Only" requires "the only photographer," not "a only." Also, "only" begins with a vowel sound, so a would be wrong even without that rule. the only is a fixed determiner pattern — rebuild it as a chunk.

Trap: Writers often keep a from ordinary first mention and bolt only on afterward.

Mark it wrong and lock in "the only photographer."
**E) He remains the unique finalist still active in round three.**

Native wording prefers "the only finalist" (or "the sole finalist"); "the unique finalist" is awkward in this ranking sense. For exclusivity in a set, only/sole beats unique with the. Repair unique to only or sole.

Trap: "Unique" feels synonymous with "only," so the unique finalist can pass as polished until native ranking idiom is checked.

Reject the awkward ranking; rewrite as "the only finalist" (or "the sole finalist").
tasks.solution_overview:
Rowing captains, drama heads, book-club treasurers, the only photographer, and exclusive finalists — titles and exclusivity markers with special determiner habits.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Titles and unique roles have special determiner habits after appoint/elect and with only. Aim for the with unique posts, and keep the only as a locked chunk. Unique can sound awkward where only/sole is the natural exclusivity word.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After appoint/elect/name, prefer the for a unique office, or a bare title after the object (elected her treasurer). Reject a head of… for a one-of-a-kind post, and reject a only… outright. For set exclusivity, prefer the only / the sole over the unique.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of neighbours have requested clearer recycling rules.
The number of open tickets fell after the software update.
She has a knowledge of Portuguese that helps on trips.
He has knowledge of Portuguese from years in Lisbon.
We saw a rise in visitors after the gallery redesign.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A number of neighbours have requested clearer recycling rules.**

"A number of" means "several" and correctly pairs with a plural noun; the determiner pattern itself is standard. a number of + plural is a fixed quantifying frame. Clearer recycling rules are just the request content.

**Tip:** a number of + plural is a fixed quantifying frame.

Keep "A number of neighbours" — it correctly means several.
**B) The number of open tickets fell after the software update.**

"The number of" correctly refers to a specific total; here the noun phrase is fully determined and grammatical. Contrast a number of (several) with the number of (the total count). The software update explains the drop.

**Tip:** Contrast a number of (several) with the number of (the total count).

That count reading is right: "The number of" names the total.
**C) She has a knowledge of Portuguese that helps on trips.**

"A knowledge of" is an accepted pattern when knowledge is limited to a field: "a knowledge of Portuguese." Some abstracts allow a when followed by of + field. The relative clause just confirms usefulness on trips.

**Tip:** Some abstracts allow a when followed by of + field.

Accept "a knowledge of Portuguese" as a recognized field pattern.
**D) He has knowledge of Portuguese from years in Lisbon.**

Zero-article "knowledge of" is equally natural for the same idea. Both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be correct; meaning stays general-competence. Years in Lisbon supply the source.

**Tip:** Both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be correct for general competence.

This bare twin also works — "knowledge of Portuguese" is equally fine.
**E) We saw a rise in visitors after the gallery redesign.**

Countable "rise" correctly takes "a" for a newly mentioned increase: "a rise in visitors." Singular countable nouns need a determiner in this slot. The gallery redesign is the cause clause.

Call this sound: singular countable "rise" correctly takes "a."
tasks.solution_overview:
Recycling petitions, open tickets, Portuguese knowledge, and a rise in gallery visitors — fixed frames where a number of, the number of, and optional a knowledge of all behave differently.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch fixed frames such as a number of versus the number of, and notice when abstracts optionally take a before of-phrases. Singular countables like rise still need a determiner.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read a number of as "several" + plural; read the number of as a specific total. For knowledge of + field, both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be fine. Separately check that countable rise/increase tokens still carry a/the when singular.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Next week we will finalise the festival programme.
The next week we will finalise the festival programme.
In 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
In the 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
On Monday morning the team packs for the match.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Next week we will finalise the festival programme.**

Time expressions like "next week," "last year," and "this morning" take zero article in standard adverbial use. next/last/this + time unit → usually zero. The festival programme stays definite as the thing being finalised.

**Tip:** next/last/this + time unit → usually zero.

Keep bare "Next week" — calendar adverbials stay zero.
**B) The next week we will finalise the festival programme.**

"The next week" is wrong in this future-plan adverbial; keep bare "next week." Save the next for sequenced items inside a known series (the next slide), not for calendar next week. Drop the before next week.

Trap: "The next" from sequenced lists bleeds into calendar "next week," a classic false friend.

That sequenced the does not belong here; rewrite as "Next week we will finalise…"
**C) In 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.**

Decades need "the": "in the 1990s." the + decade/century is the normal historical pattern. Insert the before 1990s.

Trap: Bare years make writers leave decades bare too.

Mark the decade wrong and prefer "In the 1990s…"
**D) In the 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.**

"In the 1990s" correctly includes the. Same pattern for the 1800s, the twentieth century, and similar historical spans. Paper maps are just the technology of that decade.

Accept "In the 1990s" — decades take the.
**E) On Monday morning the team packs for the match.**

Days and parts of days used adverbially are often bare: "On Monday morning…" on Monday / in summer / at night frequently take zero article. The team and the match can still be definite.

That day adverbial is right: bare "On Monday morning" is the usual form.
tasks.solution_overview:
Festival programmes next week, the 1990s on paper maps, and Monday morning match packing — calendar adverbials with rigid article habits.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Time phrases are highly patterned: next/last week stay bare, while decades and centuries take the. Do not import the into calendar adverbials where English expects zero.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For next/last/this + time unit as an adverbial, keep zero. For in + decade/century, require the (in the 1990s). Days and parts of days like On Monday morning are often bare. the next week as a future-plan adverbial is the classic false friend.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is in charge of costumes for the school play.
He was hit on head during the basketball practice.
They shook hands after settling the argument.
Please write the essay from beginning to the end carefully.
We need to keep the garden under control this summer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She is in charge of costumes for the school play.**

"In charge of costumes" uses zero article before the functional area in this common pattern. Many be/in + noun phrases freeze without a/the (in charge, in debt, in trouble). The school play stays definite as the production.

**Tip:** Many be/in + noun phrases freeze without a/the (in charge, in debt, in trouble).

Keep bare "in charge of" — the frozen idiom wants zero article.
**B) He was hit on head during the basketball practice.**

Body-contact idioms take possessive or the: "on the head" / "on his head," not bare "on head." on the + body part is the usual set phrase after verbs like hit/pat. Use "on the head" (or "on his head") during practice.

Trap: Bare body-part objects look parallel to other bare-noun idioms until you recall the set frame.

That body-part idiom fails bare; rewrite as "on the head" (or "on his head").
**C) They shook hands after settling the argument.**

"Shake hands" is a fixed zero-article idiom. Learn hands/arms/legs idioms as chunks; do not insert the automatically. Settling the argument is just the moment of reconciliation.

Accept bare "shook hands" as the fixed reconciliation idiom.
**D) Please write the essay from beginning to the end carefully.**

The paired idiom is "from beginning to end" (both bare) or "from the beginning to the end"; mixing bare beginning with "the end" is inconsistent. Keep both sides of a fixed pair parallel in determiner choice. Match bare–bare or the–the on both sides.

Trap: Mixing one bare side with one the-side looks half-fixed and often slips past casual reading.

Reject the mismatched pair; prefer "from beginning to end" or "from the beginning to the end."
**E) We need to keep the garden under control this summer.**

"Under control" is a zero-article prepositional idiom. under control / in progress / on schedule are typically bare. The garden stays definite; this summer sets the season.

This prepositional freeze is sound — bare "under control" is the idiom.
tasks.solution_overview:
Costumes for the play, a basketball head bump, a handshake after an argument, beginning-to-end essay care, and a garden under control — idioms where determiner choice is frozen.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Advanced accuracy often means recognising idioms where determiner choice is frozen. Prefer the set phrase over building articles logically word by word. Body-part contact and paired from…to… frames are especially strict.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When you spot in charge, on the head, shake hands, from beginning to end, or under control, recall the chunk. Do not bare on head, and do not mix bare beginning with the end inside one pair. Parallel determiner choice on both sides of a fixed pair is the repair check.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Many hikers reached the ridge before sunset.
There is much enthusiasm for the weekend pottery class.
Much tourists queued outside the museum.
Few of the recipes needed special equipment.
We received little praise after the choir rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Many hikers reached the ridge before sunset.**

"Hikers" is a plural noun you can count one by one, and "many" is the quantifier that fits that pattern. The sentence is clean on both the noun and the determiner. Read it as a model of many + countable plural in an everyday outdoor scene.

Keep this: "many" is the right partner for countable plural "hikers."
**B) There is much enthusiasm for the weekend pottery class.**

"Enthusiasm" is a mass feeling, not a set of separate units, so "much" is the right partner. Singular "is" also agrees with that uncountable subject idea. Treat this as the textbook contrast to "many."

That pairing is sound — "much" fits the mass feeling "enthusiasm."
**C) Much tourists queued outside the museum.**

"Tourists" is a countable plural you could number, so "much" is the wrong tool. Prefer "many tourists." Once you notice you could answer "how many?" with a number, drop much and little for that noun.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Many tourists queued outside the museum."
**D) Few of the recipes needed special equipment.**

"Recipes" is countable plural, and "few of" correctly limits that set. The of-phrase still depends on a plural countable after of, which you have here. Tone is mildly negative (not many), but the grammar is fine.

**Tip:** few/a few with countables; little/a little with uncountables.

Accept the line: "few of" correctly limits the countable recipes.
**E) We received little praise after the choir rehearsal.**

"Praise" behaves as an uncountable mass, so "little" is the matching quantifier. You are saying "not much praise," not "not many praises." Keep this as the uncountable twin of "few."

This is sound — "little" matches uncountable "praise" after the rehearsal.
tasks.solution_overview:
You are warming up on the countable split with hiking, pottery, museums, recipes, and choir praise — everyday scenes that still follow exam grammar.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The core pairing is many/few with countables and much/little with uncountables. Plurals you can number want many or few; mass nouns like enthusiasm and praise want much or little. Of-phrases such as few of still follow the noun after of.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the head noun first and ask whether you could count separate units. If yes, reject much and little; if no, reject many and few. Then confirm the quantifier matches that class before you tick true or false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The amount of litter on the beach has fallen since spring.
The number of cyclists has risen sharply.
The amount of cyclists has decreased this month.
A large number of neighbours joined the street clean-up.
There was a large amount of fog over the harbour.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The amount of litter on the beach has fallen since spring.**

"Litter" is a mass of rubbish, not a countable row of items, so "amount of" is the right frame. Singular "has fallen" agrees with that mass reading. Use this as the clean beachside model for amount + uncountable.

Accept the beach line: "amount of" correctly frames mass "litter."
**B) The number of cyclists has risen sharply.**

"Cyclists" are countable people, so "number of" is required. The phrase "the number of…" is grammatically singular, which is why "has" is correct even though cyclists is plural. Lock verb agreement to number, not to the people inside the of-phrase.

**Tip:** the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

Keep this: "the number of cyclists has" locks singular agreement to number.
**C) The amount of cyclists has decreased this month.**

Cyclists are countable people you can headcount, so measuring them with amount is the classic mix-up. Prefer "the number of cyclists." Amount stays with masses you measure; number stays with units you count.

That fails — rewrite as "The number of cyclists has decreased this month."
**D) A large number of neighbours joined the street clean-up.**

"A large number of" correctly introduces plural countable neighbours for the street clean-up. This construction roughly means "many neighbours," so a plural verb like "joined" is natural. Contrast it mentally with singular "the number of."

**Tip:** a number of + plural usually takes a plural verb.

This works: "a large number of neighbours" naturally takes plural "joined."
**E) There was a large amount of fog over the harbour.**

"Fog" is weather-as-mass, so "amount of fog" and singular "was" both fit. You would not say "many fogs" in this harbour scene. Keep amount + uncountable as your default for fog, traffic, and similar masses.

That harbour measure is sound — "amount of fog" treats weather as mass.
tasks.solution_overview:
This card is all beach litter, cyclists, neighbours, and harbour fog — still the same amount-versus-number decision underneath.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If the units are discrete (cyclists, neighbours), choose number. If you are measuring a mass (litter, fog), choose amount. "The number of" then pulls a singular verb even when the noun after of is plural.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the noun after of or after amount/number. Ask whether you would answer with a headcount or with a mass measure. Pick the matching noun phrase, then check that the verb follows the head of the quantifier phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: All of the equipment is new.
The equipments in the lab need updating.
We bought three new pieces of equipment.
There are many evidences against the claim.
The evidence supports the detective's conclusion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) All of the equipment is new.**

"Equipment" stays uncountable even when you mean several machines, so the verb is singular "is." "All of the equipment" therefore behaves like a single mass subject. This is the safe lab pattern exams love to test.

Keep this lab pattern: uncountable "equipment" correctly takes singular "is."
**B) The equipments in the lab need updating.**

"Equipments" is not standard English — keep the bare mass form "equipment." If you must count, write "pieces of equipment." The plural -s here is the whole error; the lab scene does not license a countable plural form.

**Trap:** Learners often add -s because they picture several machines — exams still reject "equipments."

Reject this pluralisation; the clean version is "The equipment in the lab needs updating" (or "pieces of equipment… need").
**C) We bought three new pieces of equipment.**

"Pieces of equipment" is the approved counting scaffold: piece unlocks a number while equipment itself stays uncountable. Three pieces is therefore grammatical buying language. Memorise piece/item of for any mass noun you need to count.

**Tip:** piece/item of + uncountable lets you count units.

That buying line is sound — "pieces of equipment" correctly unlocks countable units.
**D) There are many evidences against the claim.**

"Evidence" is uncountable, so "many evidences" fails on both the pluralisation and the countable quantifier. Prefer "much evidence" or "several pieces of evidence," and drop the -s on evidence. Exams treat evidence like information: mass form only.

**Trap:** "Many evidences" looks plausible if you are used to countable plurals, but standard exam English bans it.

Mark it wrong and prefer "There is much evidence against the claim" (or "several pieces of evidence").
**E) The evidence supports the detective's conclusion.**

Uncountable "evidence" takes a singular verb, here "supports." Even if the detective weighs several facts, the noun still behaves as one mass. Keep information, research, and evidence in the same singular-mass family.

Accept the detective line: singular "supports" matches mass "evidence."
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab kit and detective evidence dominate this set — classic uncountable nouns that learners over-pluralise.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Equipment and evidence do not take a plural -s in exam English. Count them only with piece/item of, and keep the verb singular when the bare noun is the subject. "Many evidences" and "equipments" are near-automatic false marks.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see -s on equipment or evidence, reject it. If the sentence already uses pieces of…, accept the count scaffold. Otherwise demand singular agreement with the mass noun itself.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Less information was available than we expected.
Fewer matches were cancelled this week.
Less noise was reported after the new windows arrived.
There is little doubt about the team's formation.
There is little doubt about the festival schedule.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Less information was available than we expected.**

"Information" is uncountable, so "less" is the precise comparative. Singular "was" matches that mass subject. Keep this as your clean less + uncountable baseline.

This comparative is sound — "less information" correctly measures a mass.
**B) Fewer matches were cancelled this week.**

"Matches" is a countable plural, so "fewer" is the form exams prefer. You could answer "how many matches?" with a number, which locks the choice. Treat fewer as the default for cancelled fixtures, tickets, and similar plurals.

**Tip:** if the noun is plural and countable, prefer fewer.

Keep this: "fewer matches" is the exam-safe choice for a countable plural.
**C) Less noise was reported after the new windows arrived.**

"Noise" is a mass, so "less noise" is correct after the new windows. You are reducing volume of sound, not counting separate noises. Mass nouns like noise, traffic, and waste almost always take less, not fewer.

That window fix works: "less noise" matches the uncountable mass noun.
**D) There is little doubt about the team's formation.**

"Doubt" here is uncountable, and "there is little…" is the matching pattern with singular "is." The sports formation topic does not change the grammar. Remember little = not much of a mass.

Accept the sports line: "there is little doubt" correctly frames uncountable doubt.
**E) There is little doubt about the festival schedule.**

Same grammatical frame again: uncountable "doubt" with "little" and singular "is." Repeating the pattern with a festival schedule helps you feel how stable the rule is. Use there is/are only after you know the noun's count class.

That festival rewrite still holds — little + uncountable "doubt" again takes singular "is."
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are intentionally clean — information, cancelled matches, window noise, team formation, and festival schedules — so you can lock less/little versus fewer before the later traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less and little partner with uncountables (information, noise, doubt). Fewer partners with countable plurals (matches). Singular there is fits little + uncountable.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each sentence, classify the noun, then choose less/little or fewer accordingly. Because this card has no planted errors, use it as a positive model rather than hunting for damage.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We still need much more data before we publish the survey.
How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
How much volunteers attended the beach clean-up?
Only a few bakers entered the pie contest.
Only a little bakers entered the pie contest.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We still need much more data before we publish the survey.**

In careful exam English, "data" is treated as uncountable, so "much more data" is acceptable. The survey-publishing context does not turn data into a countable plural here. Keep much/little as your default with data on this paper.

**Tip:** in exams, treat data as uncountable with much/little.

Keep this survey wording: "much more data" fits the exam mass reading of data.
**B) How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?**

Volunteers are people you can number, so "how many" is the correct question frame. The beach clean-up theme still obeys the countable rule. If the answer could be "twelve people," you needed many, not much.

That question is sound — "how many volunteers" correctly asks for a headcount.
**C) How much volunteers attended the beach clean-up?**

"Volunteers" are countable people, so "how much volunteers" is wrong. Prefer "how many volunteers." How much asks about mass or quantity of an uncountable, not a headcount of people.

Mark it wrong and prefer "How many volunteers attended the beach clean-up?"
**D) Only a few bakers entered the pie contest.**

"A few" correctly quantifies plural countable bakers and carries a neutral or mildly positive "some" feel. The pie contest remains a countable scene. Contrast a few (some) with bare few (almost none) later, but grammar here is solid.

**Tip:** a few = some (positive); few = not many (negative tone).

Accept the contest line: "a few bakers" correctly quantifies a countable plural.
**E) Only a little bakers entered the pie contest.**

"A little" belongs with uncountables, but "bakers" is plural countable. Prefer "a few bakers." Think "a little flour" versus "a few bakers" and the mix-up becomes obvious.

That mix-up fails — rewrite as "Only a few bakers entered the pie contest."
tasks.solution_overview:
Survey data, beach volunteers, and a pie contest bake the how much/how many and a few/a little contrasts into one card.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

How many asks about countable sets of people or items; how much asks about masses. A few partners with countables; a little partners with uncountables. Exam English often treats data as a mass noun with much.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For questions, imagine the answer type: a headcount needs many, a mass needs much. For a few/a little, check whether the noun can take a plural -s as separate units. Reject any cross-pairing before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of the novel was unfinished.
Much of the novels was unfinished.
Many of the novels were unfinished.
Several of the chapters were cut.
A great deal of research has been published on sleep.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Much of the novel was unfinished.**

"Much of" plus a singular unit ("the novel") is natural and takes singular "was." You are talking about a large part of one book, not counting books. Treat much of + singular/mass as a stock pattern.

Keep this: "much of the novel was" correctly covers part of one singular noun.
**B) Much of the novels was unfinished.**

After plural "novels," you need "many of the novels were," not "much of… was." Much of wants a singular or mass noun; the plural forces many of and a plural verb. The of-phrase noun decides both the quantifier and the agreement.

**Trap:** "Much of the novels" looks like a small tweak from A, which makes it a classic near-miss.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "Many of the novels were unfinished."
