**C) Many of the novels were unfinished.**

This is the repaired plural version: many of + plural countable + plural "were." Of-phrases still demand agreement with the counted noun's number. Use it as the contrast twin of A.

That plural twin is sound — "many of the novels were" matches countable plurals.
**D) Several of the chapters were cut.**

"Several" always implies more than two countable units, here chapters, with plural "were." The editing scene does not change the rule. If you cannot pluralise the noun, several cannot apply.

Accept the editing line: "several of the chapters were" correctly frames countable units.
**E) A great deal of research has been published on sleep.**

"A great deal of" behaves like much and pairs with uncountable "research" plus singular "has." Sleep research stays a mass topic in exam English. Prefer studies only when you need an explicit countable plural.

**Tip:** a great deal of ≈ much; use with uncountables.

This is sound — "a great deal of research has" keeps the mass reading.
tasks.solution_overview:
Novels, chapters, and sleep research put the of-phrase rules under the spotlight: much of, many of, several of, and a great deal of.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Look at the noun after of. Singular or mass nouns take much of / a great deal of with singular verbs. Plural countables take many of / several of with plural verbs. Mixing much of with a bare plural is the planted trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the noun after of, classify it, then choose the quantifier and verb together. Do not let the word much distract you when the noun is already plural — switch to many and plural agreement.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She gave me some useful advice on the audition.
She gave me some useful advices on the audition.
We need more detailed information from the guide.
We need more detailed informations from the guide.
The news was announced after the match ended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She gave me some useful advice on the audition.**

"Advice" is uncountable, so "some useful advice" is the natural audition tip. You never add -s for ordinary exam English. If you must count, switch to "a piece of advice."

Accept the audition tip: bare mass "advice" is the correct uncountable form.
**B) She gave me some useful advices on the audition.**

"Advices" is the classic over-pluralisation — keep "advice" or count with "pieces of advice." The audition context cannot rescue the -s ending. Learner languages that pluralise advice often create this exact false.

**Trap:** "Advices" is a high-frequency near-miss copied from languages that count advice as plural.

Mark it wrong and prefer "She gave me some useful advice on the audition."
**C) We need more detailed information from the guide.**

"Information" likewise stays uncountable and takes no plural -s. "More detailed information" is exactly how a guide briefing should read. Treat information like advice: mass form only.

Keep this guide briefing: uncountable "information" takes no plural -s.
**D) We need more detailed informations from the guide.**

"Informations" is ungrammatical — keep "information," or say "bits/pieces of information" if you need a count. The false plural is the whole story here. Exams mark the -s form false immediately.

**Trap:** "Informations" parallels the advices trap and is equally non-standard in exam English.

That pluralisation fails — rewrite as "We need more detailed information from the guide."
**E) The news was announced after the match ended.**

"News" looks plural but is uncountable and takes singular "was." After the match, the announcement is still "the news is/was," never "are/were" in careful use. Remember the -s is spelling, not a plural marker.

**Tip:** the news is … (not are).

This is sound — deceptive plural-looking "news" correctly takes singular "was."
tasks.solution_overview:
Audition advice, guide information, and post-match news are high-frequency uncountables that learners love to pluralise wrongly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Advice, information, and news stay singular as masses. Reject -s forms and keep singular verbs with news. Piece/bit of is the only clean counting route.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Spot any -s on advice or information and mark false. For news, ignore the deceptive spelling and demand a singular verb. Accept the unmarked mass forms as true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is too much homework in this module.
There are too many homeworks in this module.
We have made little progress on the mural.
We have made few progress on the mural.
Only a little time remains before the concert starts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There is too much homework in this module.**

"Homework" is a mass of study work, so "too much" plus singular "is" is correct. Modules feel heavy in volume, not in countable "homeworks." Keep much/little with this school mass noun.

Keep this module complaint: "too much homework" correctly measures uncountable study work.
**B) There are too many homeworks in this module.**

"Homeworks" is not standard — keep "homework" uncountable with much/is. If it feels like a pile of study work, treat it as a mass, not a countable set. The plural -s is the planted error.

Reject the plural -s; prefer "There is too much homework in this module."
**C) We have made little progress on the mural.**

"Progress" is uncountable, so "little progress" correctly reports a small amount of mural advancement. You would not say "few progresses" in this sense. Little keeps the slightly negative "not much" tone.

That mural update is sound — "little progress" matches the uncountable mass noun.
**D) We have made few progress on the mural.**

"Few" needs a plural countable, but "progress" is uncountable. Prefer "little progress." The mural topic does not turn progress into a countable noun.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We have made little progress on the mural."
**E) Only a little time remains before the concert starts.**

"Time" as remaining duration is uncountable, so "a little time" is right before the concert. A little is the positive "some" twin of bare little. Duration questions almost always want much/little, not many/few.

**Tip:** a little = some (positive); little = not much (negative).

Accept the countdown: "a little time" correctly quantifies remaining duration.
tasks.solution_overview:
Module homework, mural progress, and concert countdown time are everyday mass nouns that take much/little, not many/few.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Homework, progress, and time (duration) stay uncountable. Reject homeworks and few progress. Notice the tone split between little and a little, but do not let tone override countability.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the noun names a pile, process, or duration rather than separate countable units. If it does, choose much/little and singular agreement; reject many/few immediately.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon.
Less runners than expected finished the half marathon.
The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer.
The café used fewer sugar in the lemonade this summer.
There were fewer typos in the revised draft.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon.**

"Runners" is countable plural, so "fewer" is the precise comparative for the half marathon. Exams still reward fewer with people and other countable plurals. Read this as the gold-standard less-versus-fewer line.

Keep this half-marathon line: "fewer runners" correctly compares a countable plural.
**B) Less runners than expected finished the half marathon.**

Plural people take "fewer," not "less." Prefer "fewer runners." Informal speech sometimes blurs the line, but exam marking stays strict here.

**Trap:** "Less runners" is a common spoken near-miss that still fails careful exam English.

That spoken near-miss fails — rewrite as "Fewer runners than expected finished the half marathon."
**C) The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer.**

"Sugar" is a mass ingredient in the lemonade, so "less sugar" is correct. You are reducing quantity of a substance, not counting sugar crystals as units. Switch to fewer only if you count spoons or bags.

This café measure is sound — "less sugar" correctly reduces an uncountable mass.
**D) The café used fewer sugar in the lemonade this summer.**

Mass "sugar" takes "less," not "fewer." Fewer only works when the noun is plural and countable, which sugar is not in this café scene. Strip the lemonade context and the countability error is obvious.

**Trap:** "Fewer sugar" mirrors the runners trap in reverse — a classic exam swap.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The café used less sugar in the lemonade this summer."
**E) There were fewer typos in the revised draft.**

"Typos" are countable errors, so "fewer typos" is exact. If you can put a number in front (ten typos), use fewer. Draft-editing language is a reliable countable domain.

Accept the draft fix: "fewer typos" correctly quantifies countable errors.
tasks.solution_overview:
Half-marathon runners, café lemonade sugar, and draft typos are the classic less-versus-fewer battlefield.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Plural countables (runners, typos) want fewer. Mass quantities (sugar) want less. Informal "less people" is still a trap on this exam track.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip the scene down to the noun and ask "can I count these as separate units?" Yes → fewer; no → less. Apply that same test to both the race lines and the café lines.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A large amount of evidence was presented in court.
A large number of evidence was presented in court.
Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.
The equipment have already been installed.
Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A large amount of evidence was presented in court.**

"Evidence" is uncountable, so "amount of evidence" with singular "was" is courtroom-safe. You measure the mass of evidence, not a number of evidences. Keep amount for evidence, equipment, and furniture.

Keep this courtroom frame: "amount of evidence was" correctly measures a mass noun.
**B) A large number of evidence was presented in court.**

"Number of" needs a plural countable, but "evidence" is not one. Prefer "amount of evidence" or "a large number of pieces of evidence." Never write number of evidence.

**Trap:** "A large number of evidence" looks formal and almost right — a real exam near-miss.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "A large amount of evidence was presented in court."
**C) Several pieces of evidence were disclosed yesterday.**

"Pieces of evidence" correctly builds countable units, so plural "were" follows. This is how you count when the base noun must stay uncountable. Piece of is your courtroom unlock key.

**Tip:** piece of unlocks counting for uncountables.

That unlock works: "pieces of evidence were" correctly creates countable units.
**D) The equipment have already been installed.**

Uncountable "equipment" needs singular "has," not "have." Say "the equipment has already been installed" even if many devices were fitted. Agreement tracks the mass noun, not the imagined items.

**Trap:** Plural "have" feels natural if you picture several devices — exams still lock to singular.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The equipment has already been installed."
**E) Most of the furniture was damaged in transit.**

"Furniture" is uncountable and takes singular "was" when damaged in transit. Luggage and equipment share the same pattern. Do not invent "furnitures" or force a plural verb.

This transit line is sound — mass "furniture" correctly takes singular "was."
tasks.solution_overview:
Court evidence, installed equipment, and damaged furniture stay uncountable even when you mean several items.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Use amount or pieces of with evidence; keep singular verbs with equipment and furniture. Number of + evidence is an automatic fail unless you insert pieces.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First decide whether the head noun is a mass. If yes, ban bare number of and plural verbs. Only accept plural agreement when piece/item creates real countable units.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There is not much time left to revise the essay.
There are not many times left to revise the essay.
We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic.
We have plenty of chancs to reschedule the picnic.
Hardly any of the guests supported the playlist change.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There is not much time left to revise the essay.**

Here "time" means remaining duration, which is uncountable, so "much" and singular "is" are correct. Essay revision left on the clock is a mass, not a countable set. Read not much time as little time remaining.

Accept the essay countdown: "not much time" correctly measures remaining duration.
**B) There are not many times left to revise the essay.**

"Many times" usually means frequency ("often"), which twists the intended remaining-duration meaning. Prefer "much time." For countdown-to-deadline language, stay with uncountable time.

**Trap:** "Not many times left" sounds almost fluent, but it smuggles a frequency reading into a duration context.

That frequency reading fails — rewrite as "There is not much time left to revise the essay."
**C) We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic.**

"Chances" is a countable plural, and "plenty of" works happily with countables. Picnic rescheduling options can be numbered. Plenty of also works with uncountables, but here the plural noun already fits.

**Tip:** plenty of works with both countables and uncountables.

Keep this picnic option: "plenty of chances" correctly quantifies countable opportunities.
**D) We have plenty of chancs to reschedule the picnic.**

The plural spelling must be "chances," not "chancs." Even though plenty of is fine, the misshapen countable plural sinks the sentence. Watch silent-e plurals on countables.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We have plenty of chances to reschedule the picnic."
**E) Hardly any of the guests supported the playlist change.**

"Hardly any of" plus plural countable guests is a natural negative quantifier pattern. It means almost none of the guests liked the playlist change. Negative quantifiers still require the right noun type underneath.

This playlist vote is sound — "hardly any of the guests" correctly limits a countable plural.
tasks.solution_overview:
Essay-revision time, picnic chances, and playlist guests mix duration, countable opportunities, and negative quantifiers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Time as duration is uncountable (much time), while chances and guests are countable. Hardly any still needs a compatible noun after of. Spelling errors on countable plurals count as false.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate duration from frequency when you see time/times. Confirm countable plurals are spelled correctly after plenty of. Then check that negative of-phrases sit on the right noun class.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A few of the students raised lighting concerns.
Few of the students raised lighting concerns, which surprised the tutor.
Little of the flour remains for the final batch.
A little of the flour remains for the final batch.
Few of the flour remains for the final batch.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A few of the students raised lighting concerns.**

"A few of" plus plural countable students correctly signals a small but real number. The lighting-concern scene stays countable throughout. Tone is neutral or positive: some students spoke up.

Keep this lighting note: "a few of the students" correctly frames countable people.
**B) Few of the students raised lighting concerns, which surprised the tutor.**

Bare "few of" is also grammatical; it stresses scarcity and a more negative tone. The tutor's surprise fits "almost none," but the countable requirement is unchanged. Few versus a few is tone, not a grammar fork, when the noun is countable.

**Tip:** few vs a few is tone, not grammar — both need countables.

That scarcer tone still works — bare "few of the students" is grammatical with negative feel.
**C) Little of the flour remains for the final batch.**

"Little of" plus uncountable "flour" correctly stresses that almost none remains for the batch. Baking language is a natural mass domain. Little of the + uncountable is the mirror of few of the + plural.

Accept the baking line: "little of the flour" correctly stresses scarcity of a mass.
**D) A little of the flour remains for the final batch.**

"A little of" is equally grammatical and more positive: some flour remains. Again the noun is uncountable flour, so a little is licensed. Tone shifts; count class does not.

**Tip:** a little = some; little = not much.

This remaining-flour reading is sound — "a little of the flour" marks a small mass left.
**E) Few of the flour remains for the final batch.**

"Few of" demands a countable plural, but "flour" is a mass. Prefer "little of the flour" (or "few of the bags/cups"). Crossing the countable line with food masses is the exact trap this card is built to catch.

**Trap:** "Few of the flour" looks parallel to "few of the students," which is why it fools people.

Reject the countable swap; prefer "Little of the flour remains for the final batch."
tasks.solution_overview:
Classroom lighting feedback and bakery flour show that a few/few and a little/little are all fine — until you swap them across the countable line.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A few/few need plural countables (students). A little/little need uncountables (flour). Tone differences are real, but they do not excuse mixing few with a mass noun.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Classify the noun after of first. If it is a plural countable, accept few/a few; if it is a mass, accept little/a little. Reject the crossed pairing even when the rest of the sentence looks fluent.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The number of remote learners is increasing every year.
The number of remote learners are increasing every year.
A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes.
A number of remote learners is requesting evening classes.
The amount of remote learners is increasing every year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of remote learners is increasing every year.**

"The number of" makes a singular subject even though learners is plural, so "is" is correct. Remote-learning growth is still about one rising figure. Lock the verb to number, not to learners.

**Tip:** the number of + plural noun → singular verb.

Keep this growth line: singular "is" agrees with "the number," not with "learners."
**B) The number of remote learners are increasing every year.**

Plural "are" after "the number of" is wrong — keep singular "is." Do not let the nearby plural noun steal the agreement. The grammatical head is number, not learners.

**Trap:** The plural noun right after of is the classic distractor that pulls agreement off "number."

That agreement miss fails — rewrite as "The number of remote learners is increasing every year."
**C) A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes.**

"A number of" means several and normally takes a plural verb, here "are requesting." Evening-class demand from several learners fits that plural reading. Contrast a number (plural) with the number (singular).

**Tip:** a number of ≈ some/several → plural verb.

Accept the request line: "a number of … are" correctly reads as plural "several."
**D) A number of remote learners is requesting evening classes.**

With "a number of learners," prefer plural "are," not singular "is." The article a versus the flips the agreement rule, and this line gets that flip wrong. Treat a number of as meaning some/several.

**Trap:** Singular "is" after "a number of" feels matching to A, but the article change flips the rule.

Mark it wrong and prefer "A number of remote learners are requesting evening classes."
**E) The amount of remote learners is increasing every year.**

Learners are countable people, so use "number of," not "amount of." Amount of work would be fine; amount of learners is not. People and other countable units always want number.

**Trap:** "Amount of remote learners" looks measuring and formal, but amount stays with masses.

Reject amount for people; prefer "The number of remote learners is increasing every year."
highlights: A number of remote learners are
A number of remote learners is
tasks.solution_overview:
Remote learners requesting evening classes stack two traps at once: the number versus a number, and amount versus number.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"The number of" is singular; "a number of" is plural in sense. People must be counted with number, not amount. Verb agreement follows the determiner before number.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the word before number first (the/a), choose the verb, then check whether people should be under number at all. Reject amount of + people immediately.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
Many of what the coach recommended has already been tried.
None of the evidence points to intentional foul play.
None of the evidences point to intentional foul play.
Both of the equipment need replacing before the trip.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried.**

"Much of what…" treats the coach's advice-content as an uncountable mass and takes singular "has." You are not counting separate tips in this wording. Much of what / much of the advice is a reliable singular pattern.

Keep this coaching line: "much of what … has" correctly frames mass content.
**B) Many of what the coach recommended has already been tried.**

"What the coach recommended" is not framed as a plural countable set, so "many of what" is unnatural. Prefer "many of those drills" or "many of the tips." Keep many of for explicit plurals.

**Trap:** "Many of what" looks parallel to "much of what," which makes the swap a near-miss.

That parallel swap fails — rewrite as "Much of what the coach recommended has already been tried" (or "Many of those drills…").
**C) None of the evidence points to intentional foul play.**

With uncountable evidence, "none of the evidence" commonly takes singular "points" in careful formal English. The foul-play sports frame does not change the mass noun. Prefer singular agreement here on exam papers.

**Tip:** none of + uncountable → singular verb in careful formal English.

Accept the foul-play note: "none of the evidence points" keeps singular mass agreement.
**D) None of the evidences point to intentional foul play.**

"Evidences" is wrong; keep evidence uncountable. Write "none of the evidence" or "none of the pieces of evidence" if you insist on counting units. The plural -s is the planted error.

**Trap:** "None of the evidences" recycles the classic evidence-plural trap under a new quantifier.

Mark it wrong and prefer "None of the evidence points to intentional foul play."
**E) Both of the equipment need replacing before the trip.**

"Both" needs two countable units, but "equipment" is uncountable. Prefer "both pieces of equipment need replacing." Before the trip, count with piece/item or name two devices.

**Trap:** "Both of the equipment" sounds tidy until you notice both cannot attach to a mass noun.

Reject both + mass; the clean version is "Both pieces of the equipment need replacing before the trip."
tasks.solution_overview:
Coach recommendations, foul-play evidence, and trip equipment push of-phrases into advanced territory: much of what, none of, and both.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Much of what… works as a mass; many of what does not. None of the evidence stays singular and uncountable. Both only attaches to countable pairs, never to bare equipment.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask what kind of noun the quantifier expects, then inspect the material after of. If the quantifier demands count units and the noun is a mass, insert piece/item or reject the line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We have received a great deal of positive feedback.
We have received a great number of positive feedback.
There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
There were a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.
Only a small proportion of listeners chose the jazz option.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We have received a great deal of positive feedback.**

"A great deal of" means roughly much and correctly quantifies uncountable "feedback." Survey or performance feedback stays a mass on this paper. Keep deal for uncountables and number for plural countables.

This feedback line is sound — "a great deal of positive feedback" correctly measures a mass.
**B) We have received a great number of positive feedback.**

Feedback is uncountable, so "a great number of feedback" fails. Prefer "a great deal of feedback" or "a great number of comments/emails." Number wants things you can pluralise.

**Trap:** "A great number of feedback" echoes A with the wrong head — a polished near-miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We have received a great deal of positive feedback."
**C) There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.**

"Quantity of" with mass "rainwater" and singular "was" is correct for the tank. Quantity and amount often take singular agreement with mass nouns. The weather-collection scene is pure uncountable measuring.

Keep the tank reading: "there was a large quantity of rainwater" matches mass measuring.
**D) There were a large quantity of rainwater in the tank.**

Singular "quantity" as the grammatical subject needs "was," not "were." There was a large quantity of… is the fixed frame here. Do not let the of-phrase noun steal plural agreement.

**Trap:** Plural "were" is pulled by rainwater’s physical mass feeling, but the head is singular quantity.

That agreement miss fails — rewrite as "There was a large quantity of rainwater in the tank."
**E) Only a small proportion of listeners chose the jazz option.**

"Proportion of" plus plural countable listeners is standard survey language, and "chose" fits the plural sense. Jazz-option polling is a natural home for proportion/percentage of. Reports use this pattern constantly.

Accept the poll line: "a small proportion of listeners chose" correctly frames countable voters.
tasks.solution_overview:
Feedback, rainwater tanks, and jazz-poll listeners look similar under deal/number/quantity/proportion — but each head selects a different noun type and verb.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Deal pairs with uncountables like feedback; number needs plural countables. Quantity with a mass often takes singular there was. Proportion of listeners is fine with a plural countable.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the quantifier to countability first, then force the verb to agree with the real head of the phrase. Reject number of + feedback and plural were with singular quantity.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Research shows that morning light can improve alertness.
Researches show that morning light can improve alertness.
Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.
Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.
A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Research shows that morning light can improve alertness.**

Uncountable "research" correctly takes singular "shows." Morning-light alertness is presented as a body of research, not as counted papers. Keep research is / research shows as your default.

Keep this alertness claim: mass "research" correctly takes singular "shows."
**B) Researches show that morning light can improve alertness.**

Do not pluralise academic "research" as "researches" in this sense. Switch to studies or projects when you need a countable plural. The -es form is the error.

**Trap:** "Researches show" feels like ordinary subject–verb plural, but exam research stays mass.

Reject the false plural; prefer "Research shows that morning light can improve alertness."
**C) Several researches have confirmed the same pattern.**

"Several" needs a countable plural, and "researches" is unidiomatic. Prefer "several studies" or "several research projects." Several cannot rescue a bad mass pluralisation.

**Trap:** "Several researches" compounds the researches trap with a quantifier that demands count units.

That fails — rewrite as "Several studies have confirmed the same pattern."
**D) Several studies have confirmed the same pattern.**

"Studies" is the countable counterpart that "several" was looking for. This is the clean repair of the researches lines. Distinguish research (mass) from studies (count).

**Tip:** research (mass) vs studies (count).

Accept the clean counterpart: "several studies have" correctly counts research units.
**E) A piece of research published last year challenged the consensus.**

"A piece of research" is an acceptable formal count expression for one study. Piece of again unlocks counting without pluralising research itself. Last year's challenge to the consensus fits that single-unit frame.

This formal count is sound — "a piece of research" correctly names one unit.
tasks.solution_overview:
Morning-light research behaves like evidence: keep the mass form, switch to studies for several, or use a piece of research for one unit.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Reject researches and several researches. Accept research shows, several studies, and a piece of research. Several always signals that you need a true countable plural.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the sentence needs one mass claim, keep research singular. If it needs multiple units, replace research with studies or add piece of. Never invent a plural -es on research for this exam sense.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Far less runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.
Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean.
Considerably fewer clutter is left after the spring clean.
There has been far too much gossip and far too few facts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.**

"Far" merely intensifies "fewer," and runners remain countable. Qualifying-time athletics still wants fewer for people. Intensifiers never switch the countable rule.

Keep this qualifier line: "far fewer runners" correctly intensifies fewer + countable.
**B) Far less runners than last year cleared the qualifying time.**

Plural countable runners still need "fewer," even after "far." Prefer "far fewer runners." Far less interest would be fine; far less runners is not.

**Trap:** The intensifier "far" distracts from the less/fewer choice — a classic hard-card near-miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Far fewer runners than last year cleared the qualifying time."
**C) Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean.**

"Clutter" is uncountable, so "considerably less clutter" is correct after the spring clean. Considerably is only an intensifier sitting on less. Boxes would take fewer; clutter takes less.

That spring-clean measure is sound — "considerably less clutter" intensifies less + mass.
**D) Considerably fewer clutter is left after the spring clean.**

Uncountable clutter cannot take "fewer." Prefer "less clutter." Strip considerably and the error is obvious.

**Trap:** "Considerably fewer clutter" looks intensified and careful, but fewer still needs a countable plural.

Reject fewer with clutter; rewrite as "Considerably less clutter is left after the spring clean."
**E) There has been far too much gossip and far too few facts.**

The parallel contrast is deliberate: much + uncountable gossip, few + countable facts. Mixed quantifiers in one sentence still obey each noun's type. Too and far only strengthen the same choices.

**Tip:** mixed quantifiers in one sentence still obey each noun's type.

Accept the contrast: much gossip and few facts each match their noun class.
tasks.solution_overview:
Qualifying-time runners, spring-clean clutter, gossip, and facts show that intensifiers (far, considerably, too) only dress up the same less/fewer and much/few choices.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Strip the adverb and decide from the noun alone. Countable plurals keep fewer/few; uncountables keep less/much. Parallel sentences can mix quantifiers safely when each half matches its noun.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mentally delete far/considerably/too, classify the noun, then put the intensifier back on the correct base quantifier. Reject any line where the intensifier is sitting on the wrong partner.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike.
Each equipment must be labelled before the hike.
No further evidence is required at this stage.
No further evidences are required at this stage.
A substantial amount of sunlight has already flooded the atrium.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike.**

"Each" needs a singular countable noun, and "item of equipment" supplies that unit before the hike. Equipment itself stays uncountable underneath the counting scaffold. This is the model repair for each + mass nouns.

Keep this hike checklist: "each item of equipment" correctly supplies a countable unit.
**B) Each equipment must be labelled before the hike.**

"Each equipment" fails because equipment is uncountable. Prefer "each piece/item of equipment." The hike labelling task cannot license bare each + mass.

**Trap:** "Each equipment" looks like tidy inventory language, but each cannot attach to a mass noun.

That inventory shortcut fails — rewrite as "Each item of equipment must be labelled before the hike."
**C) No further evidence is required at this stage.**

"Evidence" stays uncountable with singular "is." "No further evidence is…" is standard formal English at this stage of a case. Do not pluralise evidence to force a plural verb.

Accept the case stage: "no further evidence is" keeps the mass singular.
**D) No further evidences are required at this stage.**

Avoid plural "evidences" and the plural verb that follows — keep "evidence is," or say "further pieces of evidence" if you must count. The -s and are travel together as one error bundle.

**Trap:** "No further evidences are" looks formally pluralised, but exam evidence stays mass.

Mark it wrong and prefer "No further evidence is required at this stage."
**E) A substantial amount of sunlight has already flooded the atrium.**

"Amount of sunlight" treats sunlight as an uncountable mass with singular "has." Atrium flooding by light is measured, not counted as separate sunlights. Rainwater and fog often behave the same way.

This atrium measure is sound — "amount of sunlight has" correctly measures uncountable light.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pre-hike labelling, case evidence, and atrium sunlight show how determiners like each and no further expose uncountable nouns immediately.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Each demands a countable unit, so insert item/piece of before equipment. Evidence stays uncountable under no further. Amount of sunlight is a clean mass measure.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check whether the determiner presupposes countable units. If it does and the noun is a mass, require piece/item of or reject the sentence. Otherwise keep singular mass agreement.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.
Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.
A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.
Too little attention has been paid to hydration on long walks.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay.**

"Luggage" is uncountable, so "scarcely any of the luggage was" is correct after the delay. Like furniture and baggage, it rejects a plural -s. Singular agreement follows the mass noun.

Keep this delay line: uncountable "luggage" correctly takes singular "was."
**B) Scarcely any of the luggages were recovered after the delay.**

"Luggages" is non-standard — keep luggage uncountable with singular agreement, or say "pieces of luggage." The travel-delay story does not create a countable plural form.

**Trap:** "Luggages were" feels parallel to bags/suitcases, but the exam noun stays mass.

Reject the false plural; prefer "Scarcely any of the luggage was recovered after the delay."
**C) A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.**

"Criteria" is already plural, so "a surprising number of the criteria were" matches countability and plural verb. Remember criterion (singular) versus criteria (plural). Inconsistent standards are counted, not measured as a mass.

**Tip:** criterion (singular) / criteria (plural).

Accept the standards note: "number of the criteria were" treats criteria as plural countable.
**D) A surprising amount of the criteria were mutually inconsistent.**

Prefer "number of the criteria"; amount is for mass nouns, not plural criteria. You might say amount of inconsistency, but criteria themselves take number. Plural learned nouns still want number, not amount.

**Trap:** "Amount of the criteria" looks measuring and academic, but amount cannot take plural countables.

That measuring swap fails — rewrite as "A surprising number of the criteria were mutually inconsistent."
**E) Too little attention has been paid to hydration on long walks.**

"Attention" is uncountable, so "too little attention" with singular "has" is correct for hydration advice on long walks. Little attention / much attention; few comments if you switch to a countable. Hydration is the topic, but attention is the mass noun that drives the grammar.

This walk advice is sound — "too little attention has" correctly quantifies an uncountable mass.
tasks.solution_overview:
Delayed luggage, inconsistent criteria, and walk hydration mix an uncountable, a plural countable learned noun, and another uncountable in one card.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Luggage stays mass and singular. Criteria are plural countable and want number of, not amount of. Attention takes little/much. Identify each head noun's class before choosing any/number/amount/little.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label luggage, criteria, and attention independently, then pick the quantifier that matches that label. Reject luggages and amount of criteria on sight.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The jury found insufficient evidence to convict.
The jury found insufficient evidences to convict.
There remains a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter.
There remains a large amount of unresolved questions in the chapter.
Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The jury found insufficient evidence to convict.**

"Insufficient evidence" correctly keeps evidence uncountable in the courtroom sense. Sufficient/insufficient naturally partner with mass nouns like evidence and information. This is the lone fully clean line on the hardest card.

Keep the lone clean courtroom line: "insufficient evidence" correctly keeps the mass form.
**B) The jury found insufficient evidences to convict.**

"Evidences" is wrong in this legal/academic sense — keep "evidence," or use "insufficient pieces of evidence" if counting is required. The jury scene does not license the plural.

**Trap:** "Insufficient evidences" recycles the courtroom plural trap one last time.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The jury found insufficient evidence to convict."
**C) There remains a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter.**

"A large number of unresolved questions" is plural in sense, so prefer "there remain," not singular "remains." There remain + plural; there remains + singular/mass. The chapter's open questions need plural agreement.

**Trap:** Singular "there remains" feels formal, but "a large number of questions" still wants plural remain.

That agreement miss fails — rewrite as "There remain a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter."
**D) There remains a large amount of unresolved questions in the chapter.**

Questions are countable, so "amount of unresolved questions" is off, and singular "remains" still clashes. Prefer "a large number of unresolved questions remain" or "an amount of uncertainty remains." This line stacks two errors: wrong quantifier plus wrong agreement.

**Trap:** Amount + countable questions plus singular remains is a double near-miss that still fails.

Reject the double near-miss; prefer "There remain a large number of unresolved questions in the chapter."
**E) Fewer than ten percent of the equipment have been calibrated.**

Equipment is uncountable, so "fewer… have" is wrong on both fronts. Prefer "less than ten percent of the equipment has been calibrated" or "fewer than ten pieces of equipment have…." Percent of + uncountable takes singular; fewer needs countable units.

**Trap:** "Fewer than ten percent … have" looks statistical and careful, but equipment is still a mass.

That calibration line fails — rewrite as "Less than ten percent of the equipment has been calibrated."
tasks.solution_overview:
The final card mixes courtroom evidence, chapter questions with there remain(s), and percent-of agreement with equipment — only one sentence survives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Evidence stays uncountable. Number of questions wants plural remain, not remains, and never amount of questions. Percent of equipment is singular mass agreement; fewer needs countable pieces.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Resolve countability first, then force verb agreement to follow that decision. When two errors stack (wrong quantifier plus wrong verb), mark false even if one half almost looks repairable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.**

"Heavier" already carries the comparative ending -er, so adding "more" marks the degree twice. A two-suitcase contrast needs only one comparative marker before than. Drop "more" and keep the short -er form against last summer's suitcase.

Mark it wrong and prefer "This suitcase is heavier than the one I packed last summer."
**B) My sister's flat is larger than mine.**

One-syllable "large" correctly becomes "larger" before than. That is the standard short-adjective pattern for comparing two flats. Nothing extra is needed beyond the -er form.

Keep this: larger than is the clean short-adjective comparative for two flats.
**C) Of the three trails, this path is the worse.**

"Of the three trails" ranks a group of three, but "the worse" is only the comparative. Among three or more options you need the superlative. Swap to "the worst" so the grade of comparison matches the set size.

That grade fails among three trails — rewrite as "Of the three trails, this path is the worst."
**D) The new bus stop is closer than the old one.**

"Close" is short, so "closer than" correctly compares the new stop with the old one. Two named places call for a comparative, not a superlative. The ending and the than-clause both fit.

Accept the line: closer than rightly contrasts the new stop with the old one.
**E) She sings more better than she did at the school concert.**

"Better" is already the irregular comparative of well/good, so "more better" stacks a second marker. Irregular comparatives never take an extra more. Keep only better before the than-clause about the school concert.

Reject the double marker; the clean version is "She sings better than she did at the school concert."
tasks.solution_overview:
Suitcases, flats, trails, bus stops, and a school concert — everyday scenes asking whether each comparison is marked correctly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This opener targets double marking and the two-versus-many rule. Short adjectives usually take -er / -est; irregulars like better and worse already carry the comparative meaning, so stacking "more" on top is always wrong.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask two questions: Is the adjective already comparative or superlative? And does the sentence compare two things or rank a whole group? Mark true only when both the form and the grade of comparison fit.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
The evening train was quieter than the morning service.
This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.
It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.**

Five bakeries on the high street form a clear group, and Miller's is ranked inside that set. "The freshest" is the right -est form for one-syllable fresh. No most is required when -est already carries the superlative.

That works — the freshest correctly ranks Miller's bread among five bakeries.
**B) That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.**

English never forms "gooder." The irregular chain is good → better → best. Invented -er endings on irregular adjectives fail in careful and exam English. Rebuild the contrast with better than yesterday's soup.

Mark it wrong and prefer "That soup tastes better than the one from yesterday."
**C) The evening train was quieter than the morning service.**

Two-syllable "quiet" commonly takes -er in everyday English. "Quieter than the morning service" cleanly contrasts two trains. There is no need to stretch the line into more quiet here.

Keep this: quieter than is a natural -er contrast between the two train services.
**D) This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.**

Multi-syllable "interesting" correctly takes more … than when the novel is set against the film. Longer adjectives almost never add -er. The more + base + than frame is exactly what this contrast wants.

Accept the line: more interesting than fits the long adjective against the film.
**E) It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.**

"Coldest" is already the superlative, so "most coldest" doubles the grade. Pair most only with the base adjective, never with an -est form. Strip most and leave the coldest winter walk.

That stacking fails — rewrite as "It was the coldest winter walk we have ever taken."
tasks.solution_overview:
Bakeries, soup, trains, a novel-versus-film pair, and a winter walk — check that each adjective picks the right comparative system.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You are sorting -er/-est against more/most, spotting mangled irregulars such as "gooder," and catching double superlatives like "most coldest." Longer adjectives prefer more/most; short ones usually take the ending.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the adjective, count its syllables, and ask whether the sentence ranks inside a group. If you see "most" glued to an -est form, or a homemade -er on an irregular, mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more taller than his twin brother.
Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.
Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.
The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.
My laptop runs gooder after the software update.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is more taller than his twin brother.**

"Taller" already carries -er, so "more taller" is double marking. Delete more whenever the comparative ending is already present. The twin-brother contrast then runs on a single clean comparative.

Reject this double mark; prefer "He is taller than his twin brother."
**B) Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.**

"Of all the desserts" ranks a whole set, so the grade must be superlative. "The less sweet" is only comparative and undershoots the group ranking. Less compares two; least ranks many.

That undershoots the dessert set — rewrite as "Of all the desserts, this tart is the least sweet."
**C) Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.**

Two-syllable "clear" commonly forms "clearer than" for a textbook contrast. The comparative ending is natural here and needs no repair. The explanation-versus-chapter pair sits cleanly under than.

This is sound: clearer than is a natural comparative for the explanation–chapter pair.
**D) The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.**

"Worse" is already comparative, and "worser" is nonstandard — "more worser" piles both errors. The fixed chain is bad → worse → worst with no extras. After noon the weather simply turned worse.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The weekend weather turned worse after noon."
**E) My laptop runs gooder after the software update.**

"Gooder" is not English; the fixed chain stays good / better / best. Homemade -er forms on irregulars always fail. After the software update the laptop runs better.

That invented form fails — rewrite as "My laptop runs better after the software update."
tasks.solution_overview:
Twins, desserts, a textbook chapter, worsening weather, and a laptop update — a dense run of beginner comparison traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set stacks double marking ("more taller," "more worser"), less versus least, and broken irregulars ("gooder"). Fix the comparison word itself before you worry about style.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First strip any stacked "more" or invented -er. Then check whether "of all" demands a superlative (least, not less). Irregulars bad/good have fixed shapes — do not reinvent them.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.
She chose the most cheap ticket available online.
Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.
This playlist is the best of the three we built.
The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.**

"Easy" correctly changes y to i and adds -er: easier than Monday's. That spelling shift is standard for consonant + y adjectives. The two-quiz contrast needs nothing beyond the -er form.

Keep this: easier than uses the standard y → i spelling for the two quizzes.
**B) She chose the most cheap ticket available online.**

One-syllable "cheap" wants the -est ending, not most + base. "The most cheap ticket" reaches for the wrong comparative system. Prefer the ending on short adjectives unless the -est form sounds awkward.

Reject most + short base; prefer "She chose the cheapest ticket available online."
**C) Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.**

"Small" simply adds -er: smaller than the neighbour's is the standard comparative. No consonant doubling is required here (unlike big → bigger). The garden pairing sits cleanly under than.

That works — smaller than cleanly compares the two gardens.
**D) This playlist is the best of the three we built.**

"The best of the three" correctly uses the irregular superlative inside a set of three playlists. Good → better → best fits group ranking without an extra most. Of the three cues the highest grade.

Accept the line: the best of the three is the right irregular superlative for the playlists.
**E) The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.**

"Farther/further" is already comparative, so "more farther" doubles the mark. Irregular distance forms never take an extra more. Keep farther or further alone before from the hotel.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The museum was farther from the hotel than we expected."
tasks.solution_overview:
A quiz, online tickets, neighbouring gardens, playlists, and a museum walk — spelling and irregular distance forms come into play.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm -er spelling (easy → easier), avoid "most" on short adjectives that want -est, and leave irregulars like best and farther alone. They do not need an extra "more."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the ending first, then the intensifier or "most." If the adjective is already comparative or irregular, strip any stacked marker before you tick true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.
Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.
She felt worse after skipping breakfast.
Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.
His second attempt was better than the first.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.**

"Spicy" forms "spicier" for a clean two-item food contrast with the mild menu option. The -y → -ier change is standard and needs no more. Heat level is compared between two versions, so comparative is enough.

Keep this: spicier than correctly contrasts the two curry versions.
**B) Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.**

Only two coats are in play, so the superlative the warmest overshoots. Between two items English wants a comparative, not the highest grade. Among many would unlock warmest; a pair keeps warmer.

**Trap:** Between the two + -est looks polished but is the wrong grade.

That overshoots a pair — rewrite as "Between the two coats, the wool one is warmer."
**C) She felt worse after skipping breakfast.**

"Worse" is the correct irregular comparative of bad/ill after skipping breakfast. No more and no worser — the form stands alone. The line simply reports feeling worse than before.

Accept the line: worse stands alone as the irregular comparative after breakfast.
**D) Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.**

Four rooms need a superlative, but the more quiet is only comparative. Groups of three or more take the highest grade. Repair to the quietest (or the most quiet) so the attic tops the set.

**Trap:** Of the four + more + adjective looks comparative-ready but the set size demands -est/most.

Reject comparative grade for four rooms; prefer "Of the four rooms, the attic is the quietest."
**E) His second attempt was better than the first.**

"Better than the first" correctly compares two attempts with the irregular comparative. Two items → better; a whole group → best. The second-versus-first frame is a pure pair.

This is sound: better than rightly compares the second attempt with the first.
tasks.solution_overview:
Curry heat, two coats, skipped breakfast, four rooms, and two exam attempts — the two-versus-many rule is the headline.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on whether the cue phrase compares a pair or ranks a group. "Between the two" almost always wants a comparative; "of the four" wants a superlative. Keep irregular worse/better clean.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the quantity words (between two, of four, than the first). Match comparative to pairs and superlative to groups of three or more, then confirm irregular spelling.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.
This café is more popular than the one by the river.
My phone battery lasts longer than yours.
She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.
He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.**

"Tidy" correctly becomes "tidier" after clearing the counter. Consonant + y → -ier is the expected spelling for this short adjective. The line reports a before-and-after look, not a group ranking.

That works — tidier uses the expected -ier spelling after the clear-up.
**B) This café is more popular than the one by the river.**

Three-syllable "popular" correctly takes more … than against the riverside café. Long adjectives almost always use more/most rather than -er/-est. The café-versus-café contrast sits cleanly in that frame.

Keep this: more popular than fits the longer adjective against the riverside café.
**C) My phone battery lasts longer than yours.**

"Longer than yours" cleanly compares battery life for two phones. Duration often rides on long / longer / longest without needing more. One -er marker is enough for the two-phone contrast.

Accept the line: longer than cleanly compares the two phone batteries.
**D) She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.**

"The least expensive bike in the shop" correctly ranks cost among many options. Least + adjective is the standard superlative of inferiority. The shop is a set bigger than a simple pair, so least is right.

This is sound: least expensive correctly ranks cost across the shop's bikes.
**E) He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.**

"Faster" already marks the comparative, so "more faster" doubles it. -er adverbs reject an extra more just as adjectives do. Keep only faster for the evening-versus-morning contrast.

**Trap:** Intensifying more + -er adverb looks emphatic but is double marking.

Mark it wrong and prefer "He runs faster in the evenings than in the mornings."
tasks.solution_overview:
A tidier kitchen, café popularity, phone batteries, bike prices, and evening runs — mostly clean models with one stacked adverb trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Most lines show healthy -ier, more + long adjective, -er for duration, and least + adjective for ranking cost. The clear fault is stacking "more" on an -er adverb such as "faster."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat the first four as reference forms. On the last, strip the extra "more" so only one comparative marker remains before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The river is deeper here than near the bridge.
Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.
Their dog is friendlier than ours.
She felt more happier after the phone call.
This is the worst film I have seen all year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The river is deeper here than near the bridge.**

"Deeper than near the bridge" correctly compares two stretches of the same river. One-syllable adjectives take -er for two-item contrasts. Here versus the bridge is a simple pair, not a group ranking.

Keep this: deeper than correctly compares the two stretches of river.
**B) Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.**

Only two recipes are named, so the simplest is the wrong grade. Of/between two demands a comparative, not a superlative. Simpler keeps the ranking inside a pair.

**Trap:** Of the two + -est is a common overshoot when the set size is only a pair.

That pair wants comparative grade — rewrite as "Of the two recipes, this one is simpler."
**C) Their dog is friendlier than ours.**

"Friendly" correctly forms "friendlier" (more friendly is also acceptable). The -y → -ier pattern is natural for this personality comparison. Their dog versus ours is a clean two-item contrast.

Accept the line: friendlier than is a natural -ier contrast between the dogs.
**D) She felt more happier after the phone call.**

"Happier" already includes the comparative, so "more happier" doubles the mark. Remember happy → happier → happiest with no stacked more. After the phone call she simply felt happier.

Reject the stacked more; prefer "She felt happier after the phone call."
**E) This is the worst film I have seen all year.**

"The worst film I have seen all year" correctly uses the irregular superlative for a broad ranking. Bad → worse → worst needs no extras. All year cues a wide set, so the highest grade fits.

That works — the worst rightly ranks the film across the whole year.
tasks.solution_overview:
River depth, two recipes, friendly dogs, a happy phone call, and a miserable film — watch "of the two" especially.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Of the two" almost always blocks a superlative. Keep -ier spelling tidy on friendlier/happier, and leave irregular worst alone once the grade of comparison is right.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the cue says two, demand a comparative. If the cue ranks a year of films or a clear group, allow the superlative. Then check for stacked "more" on -ier forms.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.
He is the elder of the two cousins.
This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.
Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.
We walked further than planned before turning back.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.**

"Less exciting than the pilot" correctly softens a longer adjective across two episodes. Less + adjective + than is the comparative of inferiority. The second episode versus the pilot is a pair, so comparative is enough.

Keep this: less exciting than is a valid inferiority comparative for the two episodes.
**B) He is the elder of the two cousins.**

"The elder of the two cousins" is a traditional family comparative for people in a pair. Elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age — both patterns appear in exams. Of the two locks the grade to a two-person contrast.

**Tip:** elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age.

Accept the line: the elder of the two is an accepted family comparative.
**C) This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.**

Spelling and grade both fail — "bigest than" should be "bigger than." Double the g and use comparative with than: big → bigger → biggest. A than-clause wants comparative, not a mangled -est form.

Mark it wrong and prefer "This rucksack is bigger than I need for a day hike."
**D) Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.**

"The most relaxing" correctly ranks pottery among several hobbies. -ing adjectives of three syllables take most, not -est. Among her hobbies cues a group ranking.

This is sound: the most relaxing correctly ranks pottery among her hobbies.
**E) We walked further than planned before turning back.**

"Further than planned" is a standard irregular comparative of distance or extent. Farther and further both work for physical distance in modern English. The walk versus the plan is a clean than-contrast.

That works — further than is a valid irregular distance comparative for the walk.
tasks.solution_overview:
TV episodes, cousins, a day-hike rucksack, hobbies, and an overlong walk — less + adjective, family elder, and the big/bigger spelling trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set adds comparative of inferiority (less + adjective), the family form elder, and the spelling trap big → bigger (not "bigest"). Read than-clauses carefully: they want a comparative, not a mangled superlative.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the preposition and ending on each line. Than + misspelled -est is an automatic false; less + long adjective + than is usually fine.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.
Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.
The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.
He is not as tall as his older sister.
The sequel was as good than the original.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.**

"As strong as the one from the market stall" correctly states equal strength. As … as compares sameness, not ranking, and both markers are present. The tea and the stall brew sit in a true equality frame.

Keep this: as strong as correctly marks equal strength between the two brews.
**B) Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.**

After "as neat" you need a second as, not than. Than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality. Mixing the two systems is a classic exam slip.

**Trap:** as + adjective + than looks almost right but swaps the closing marker.

That mixes systems — rewrite as "Her handwriting is as neat as her brother's."
**C) The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.**

"As peaceful as it did in spring" correctly keeps both as-markers for equal calm. Dropping the second as would break the equality pattern. The park now versus spring uses a full as … as frame.

Accept the line: both as-markers keep the park's equality frame intact.
**D) He is not as tall as his older sister.**

"Not as tall as his older sister" is the standard negative equality pattern. In everyday meaning it is close to less tall than, but the frame stays as … as. The negative sits on the first as without changing the closing as.

**Tip:** not as … as ≈ less … than in everyday meaning, but keep the as … as frame.

This is sound: not as tall as correctly marks negative equality with his sister.
**E) The sequel was as good than the original.**

"As good than" mixes equality with a comparative closer. Never write as … than; rebuild with a second as. The sequel-versus-original idea still wants sameness, not ranking.

**Trap:** as … than is a polished-looking hybrid that is always wrong.

Reject as … than; prefer "The sequel was as good as the original."
tasks.solution_overview:
Tea strength, handwriting, a peaceful park, height in the family, and a film sequel — equality lives in the as … as frame.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Equality comparisons use as + adjective + as. If than sneaks in after as + adjective, the sentence is wrong — swap than for the second as. Negative equality (not as … as) is still the same frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for both as-markers. A lone as before the adjective with than after it is the classic trap; rebuild as … as before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She drives much more carefully than she did last year.
This bag is far heavier than it looks.
The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.
He speaks English better than I expected.
They arrived slightly earlier than the others.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She drives much more carefully than she did last year.**

"Much more carefully" correctly strengthens the comparative of a -ly adverb. Much / far / a lot can boost a single comparative without changing its form. Last year's driving is the than-anchor for one clean more + adverb.

That works — much intensifies one comparative in much more carefully.
**B) This bag is far heavier than it looks.**

"Far heavier" correctly intensifies a short -er comparative. Far + -er is natural and strong for surprise weight. The bag versus how it looks still uses a single comparative form.

Keep this: far heavier boosts a single -er form without stacking markers.
**C) The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.**

"A lot more harder" doubles the comparative by stacking more with -er. Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two. Keep a lot harder or much harder — never both more and -er.

**Trap:** a lot more + -er feels emphatic but is classic double marking.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The climb was a lot harder than the map suggested."
**D) He speaks English better than I expected.**

"Better than I expected" correctly compares performance with the irregular comparative. The clause after than is fine, and better needs no more. Irregular better stands alone under the intensifier-free than-clause.

Accept the line: better than needs no stacked more against the expectation.
**E) They arrived slightly earlier than the others.**

"Slightly earlier" correctly softens the comparative of early. Slightly / a bit / rather can modify comparatives without adding a second marker. Arrival versus the others keeps one -er form.

This is sound: slightly earlier softens one comparative of arrival time.
tasks.solution_overview:
Careful driving, a deceptively heavy bag, a hard climb, better English, and an early arrival — intensifiers meet single comparative forms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Intensifiers such as much, far, a lot, and slightly are fine before one comparative. They become wrong the moment they sit beside a second marker such as more + -er.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow the booster only if exactly one comparative remains. If you see "a lot more harder," strip either "more" or the -er ending — never keep both.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.
She is one of the smarter students in the class.
This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.
He is one of the tallest player on the team.
That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.**

"One of the most beautiful cities I have visited" hits all three slots: superlative, plural cities, and the frame. This is the model pattern for ranking within a visited set. One of the always packages with a superlative plus a plural noun.

**Tip:** one of the + superlative + plural noun.

Keep this: one of the + most beautiful + plural cities hits the full package.
**B) She is one of the smarter students in the class.**

After "one of the" you need a superlative, not comparative smarter. The frame blocks ordinary -er forms even when students are plural. Smartest restores the highest grade inside the class set.

**Trap:** one of the + comparative -er looks almost grammatical but the frame demands -est/most.

That grade is too low for the frame — rewrite as "She is one of the smartest students in the class."
**C) This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.**

"One of the best meals" correctly pairs the irregular superlative with a plural noun. Best / worst fit the same frame as most + adjective. Home-cooked meals form the plural set behind one of the.

Accept the line: one of the best meals pairs irregular superlative with a plural noun.
**D) He is one of the tallest player on the team.**

"One of" requires a plural noun, but "player" is singular. Always use a plural after one of, even when the superlative tallest is already right. Players restores the missing plural slot.

**Trap:** tallest looks finished, but the singular noun after one of still fails.

Reject the singular after one of; prefer "He is one of the tallest players on the team."
**E) That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.**

"Funnier" is comparative, but the frame wants a superlative. Comparative -er forms do not follow one of the. Funniest ranks the joke inside the show's set.

**Trap:** one of the + -er is the twin of the smarter trap — wrong grade inside the frame.

That comparative fails inside the frame — rewrite as "That was one of the funniest jokes in the show."
highlights: one of the most beautiful cities
tasks.solution_overview:
Cities, classmates, home-cooked meals, teammates, and jokes — the fixed frame one of the + superlative + plural noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember the package: one of the + superlative + plural noun. Ordinary comparatives and singular nouns after "one of" are the usual exam traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check three slots every time: "one of the," a true superlative (not -er), and a plural noun. Fail any slot and mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more she practised, the more confident she became.
The harder he trained, the better his times got.
More she waited, more anxious she felt.
The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.
The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The more she practised, the more confident she became.**

"The more she practised, the more confident she became" correctly links two parallel comparatives. Keep "the" before each comparative in this correlative pattern. Practice and confidence rise together under matching articles.

That works — both halves keep the + comparative as confidence rises.
**B) The harder he trained, the better his times got.**

"The harder he trained, the better his times got" shows that -er and irregular comparatives both fit. The pairing is grammatical and natural. Training effort and race times move in opposite useful directions under the same frame.

Keep this: harder and better both sit cleanly under the correlative the.
**C) More she waited, more anxious she felt.**

Both articles are missing from the correlative comparative. Dropping "the" breaks the "the + comparative … the + comparative" pattern. Restore "the" before more in each half.

**Trap:** bare More … more … looks parallel but lacks the required articles.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The more she waited, the more anxious she felt."
**D) The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.**

"The less we argued, the happier the evening felt" is a valid inferiority pair. Less / fewer can lead the first half without trouble. Fewer arguments line up with a happier evening under matching the-markers.

Accept the line: the less … the happier is a sound correlative pair for the evening.
**E) The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.**

"The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be" is a classic time-and-cost pairing. Both halves keep the + comparative. Early booking maps onto lower prices in the fixed double-comparative frame.

This is sound: sooner and cheaper keep the correlative articles for booking.
tasks.solution_overview:
Practice and confidence, training and times, waiting and anxiety, fewer arguments, early booking — correlative the … the … pairs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Correlative comparatives need "the + comparative" in both halves. Mixed shapes (harder / better, less / happier, sooner / cheaper) are fine; missing "the" is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read left and right of the comma. If either article "the" disappears before a comparative, rebuild the correlative before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.
He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.
Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.
The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.
They danced more graceful than the other couple.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.**

"More skilfully" correctly forms the comparative of a -ly adverb for how she paints. Long adverbs take more/most, not -er. Anyone else in the club is the than-anchor for manner, not a person-quality adjective.

Keep this: more skilfully compares manner with a long -ly adverb.
**B) He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.**

"Quicker" (or more quickly) is acceptable in modern usage for manner here. Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English when finishing a puzzle. Either form marks how fast he finished against I did.

**Tip:** Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English.

Accept the line: quicker than is an accepted short-adverb comparative for finishing the puzzle.
**C) Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.**

"More slow" uses the adjective where the verb speak needs an adverb. Adjective slow is not the same as adverb slowly. Recipe instructions need manner after speak, so the -ly form is required.

**Trap:** more + adjective after a verb of manner looks comparative but misses the adverb ending.

That adjective fails after speak — rewrite as "Please speak more slowly so I can follow the recipe."
**D) The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.**

"Better" correctly compares how the choir sang on two occasions. The adverb chain is well → better → best. Last night versus the rehearsal is a clean manner contrast.

This is sound: better correctly compares how the choir sang on the two nights.
**E) They danced more graceful than the other couple.**

Manner after danced needs more gracefully, not the adjective graceful. After danced / spoke / sang, prefer adverb forms. The other couple is the than-anchor for how they danced.

**Trap:** more + bare adjective after a dance/speak/sing verb is a near-miss manner error.

Mark it wrong and prefer "They danced more gracefully than the other couple."
tasks.solution_overview:
Painting, puzzles, recipe instructions, choir night, and a dance floor — separate adjective comparison from adverb comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When the word modifies a verb (speak, dance, sing), you usually need an adverb comparative — more slowly / more gracefully / better — not a bare adjective. Long -ly adverbs take more/most.

**Part 2: How to decide.**
