Ask what is being compared: a person/thing or a manner of action. Manner after a verb almost always wants an adverb form; mark false when an adjective leaks into that slot.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.
Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.
Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.
The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.
His answer was different from mine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.**

Latinate "superior" pairs with to, not than. Superior / inferior / preferable lock to to as a fixed preposition. Last winter's jacket is the comparison target under to.

**Trap:** superior than borrows ordinary comparative than but these Latinate adjectives refuse it.

Reject than after superior; prefer "This jacket is superior to the one I bought last winter."
**B) Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.**

"Inferior to the earlier sketch" is the correct fixed comparative-like pattern. Do not rewrite these with homemade -er forms. The design-versus-sketch contrast rides on to, not than.

Keep this: inferior to uses the fixed Latinate preposition against the sketch.
**C) Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.**

"Preferable to the dried kind" correctly states a preference between two pasta options. Preferable to ≈ better as a choice than, but the preposition stays to. Fresh versus dried stays inside that locked pattern.

Accept the line: preferable to correctly states the fresh-versus-dried pasta choice.
**D) The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.**

Preferable never takes than. Swap than for to and keep the coastal-versus-inland contrast. The meaning is preference, but the grammar is the Latinate to-frame.

**Trap:** preferable than is the twin of superior than — wrong preposition on a fixed adjective.

That preposition fails — rewrite as "The coastal path is preferable to the inland route."
**E) His answer was different from mine.**

"Different from mine" is the standard British exam form. Treat different from as the safe choice in tested writing. His answer versus mine sits under from without needing than.

**Tip:** Treat different from as safe in exams.

This is sound: different from is the standard exam pairing for the two answers.
tasks.solution_overview:
Jackets, sketches, pasta, coastal paths, and different answers — Latinate comparison words that lock to fixed prepositions.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Some comparison words never take than. Superior, inferior, and preferable lock to "to." Learn those fixed prepositions separately from ordinary -er / more patterns. Different from is the safe exam form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When you see superior/inferior/preferable, demand "to." Than after those adjectives is an automatic false; ordinary -er comparatives still use than as usual.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.
We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.
She made less mistakes on the second draft.
He drinks less coffee than he used to.
There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.**

"Fewer people" correctly uses fewer with a countable plural at the market. Fewer + countable; less + uncountable is the core split. People can be counted one by one, so fewer fits.

Keep this: fewer people matches the countable plural at the market.
**B) We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.**

"Less time" correctly pairs with uncountable time before the ferry. Time, money, traffic, and advice usually take less. The amount of time cannot be counted as separate people-like units here.

That works — less time matches the uncountable mass before the ferry.
**C) She made less mistakes on the second draft.**

"Mistakes" is countable, so "less mistakes" is wrong in careful English. If you can count them, prefer fewer. The second-draft contrast still wants a quantity comparative, just the countable one.

**Trap:** less + countable plural is common in speech but fails careful/exam English.

Mark it wrong and prefer "She made fewer mistakes on the second draft."
**D) He drinks less coffee than he used to.**

"Less coffee" correctly treats coffee as an uncountable amount. Less + mass noun is the natural pairing for drinks measured as volume. He used to drink more; the reducing amount stays under less.

Accept the line: less coffee correctly treats the drink as a mass amount.
**E) There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.**

"Traffic" is uncountable, so "fewer traffic" fails. Fewer needs a plural countable noun. After nine the road has less traffic, not fewer traffic.

**Trap:** fewer + mass noun echoes the countable rule but picks the wrong noun type.

Reject fewer with a mass noun — rewrite as "There is less traffic on this road after nine."
tasks.solution_overview:
Market crowds, ferry clocks, draft mistakes, coffee habits, and road traffic — less versus fewer by noun type.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less and fewer are comparative quantity words. Decide first whether the noun is countable plural or an uncountable mass, then pick fewer or less.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can count separate units (people, mistakes), prefer fewer. If you measure a mass (time, coffee, traffic), use less. That single test decides most of A–E.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.
The music grew more and more louder near the stage.
The waves became higher and higher before the storm.
She felt worse and worse during the long flight.
The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.
tactical_explanations:
**A) My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.**

"Busier and busier" correctly shows gradual increase with a repeated comparative as the festival nears. Adj-er and adj-er means steadily more. The week intensifies in one comparative system only.

Keep this: busier and busier marks the week's steady increase toward the festival.
**B) The music grew more and more louder near the stage.**

"More and more louder" doubles the marking by mixing systems. Pick either louder and louder or more and more loud. Near the stage the volume rises, but only under one comparative pattern.

**Trap:** more and more + -er feels gradual but stacks two comparative systems.

That stacks systems — rewrite as "The music grew louder and louder near the stage."
**C) The waves became higher and higher before the storm.**

"Higher and higher" correctly intensifies a short comparative as the waves build. Repeat the -er form for gradual change. Before the storm the height climbs under a single repeated comparative.

Accept the line: higher and higher is the right repeated -er pattern for the waves.
**D) She felt worse and worse during the long flight.**

"Worse and worse" correctly repeats the irregular comparative on the long flight. Irregulars can double the same way: better and better, worse and worse. How she felt declines under one irregular form repeated.

This is sound: worse and worse is a valid irregular gradual pair on the flight.
**E) The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.**

"Increasingly" already means more and more, so "increasingly more difficult" is redundant. Do not stack increasingly with more. Toward the end the puzzle simply grew increasingly difficult — or more and more difficult.

**Trap:** increasingly more looks emphatic but restates the same booster twice.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The puzzle grew increasingly difficult toward the end."
tasks.solution_overview:
A busy festival week, stage volume, rising waves, a long flight, and a toughening puzzle — gradual-change patterns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Gradual change either repeats one comparative (louder and louder) or uses more and more + base adjective. Mixing systems — or adding increasingly to more — creates double marking.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pick one system and stick to it. If you see "more and more" beside an -er form, or "increasingly more," strip the redundancy before marking true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.
This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.
She is taller than any girl in her class.
This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.
He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.**

"No other beach on the island is as clean as this one" correctly sets up a unique equality comparison. No other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest. The island's beaches are excluded one by one so this beach stands alone.

**Tip:** no other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest.

Keep this: no other + as … as marks this beach as uniquely clean on the island.
**B) This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.**

"Cheaper than any other place we checked" correctly excludes the rest of the set. Any other keeps the compared hostel outside the group. Without other, the hostel could oddly sit inside the places being beaten.

**Tip:** any other keeps the compared item outside the group.

Accept the line: any other correctly keeps the hostel outside the places it beats.
**C) She is taller than any girl in her class.**

Without other/else, she remains inside "any girl in her class." Exclusion words prevent logical self-comparison. Taller than any other girl — or anyone else — keeps her outside the set she beats.

**Trap:** taller than any girl sounds absolute but compares her with a set that still includes her.

That self-includes her in the set — rewrite as "She is taller than any other girl in her class."
**D) This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.**

Do not mix "the shortest" with "of any other." Superlative and any other usually fight each other. Choose either the shortest path or shorter than any other path to the lake.

**Trap:** the shortest of any other glues two competing exclusion systems into one broken phrase.

Reject the mixed systems; prefer "This route is shorter than any other path to the lake."
**E) He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.**

"Better than anyone else in the family" correctly uses else to exclude him from the comparison group. Else / other prevents logical self-comparison. Family piano skill is ranked with him left safely outside the beaten set.

That works — anyone else correctly excludes him from the family piano set.
tasks.solution_overview:
Island beaches, hostels, classroom height, lake paths, and family piano — advanced comparison hinges on exclusion words.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Other and else keep the compared person or thing outside the group. Without them, someone can be compared with a set that still includes that person — a classic logic trap. Superlative plus "any other" usually fights itself.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check whether the compared item is excluded. Add other/else when needed, and do not glue "the shortest" to "of any other" in the same breath.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.
She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.
They would rather stay in than go out tonight.
He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.
We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.**

"Prefer walking to cycling" is the standard comparative preference pattern with parallel gerunds. Prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund. Mild weather only sets the scene; the grammar lives in prefer … to ….

**Tip:** prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund.

Keep this: prefer … to … correctly contrasts walking with cycling.
**B) She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.**

Prefer takes to, not than. Prefer … than is almost always wrong in exam English. Morning tea versus coffee still wants the locked to-frame.

**Trap:** prefers … than borrows comparative than but prefer refuses that preposition.

Mark it wrong and prefer "She prefers tea to coffee in the morning."
**C) They would rather stay in than go out tonight.**

"Would rather stay in than go out tonight" correctly contrasts two base-verb options. Would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive. Stay and go are parallel bare verbs under rather … than.

Accept the line: would rather … than … pairs two bare infinitives for tonight's choice.
**D) He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.**

After "would rather" use the bare infinitive, not to leave. Delete to after would rather. Leaving early versus missing the last train stays under rather … than with base verbs.

**Trap:** would rather to + verb looks infinitive-careful but the structure bans to.

Reject to after would rather — rewrite as "He would rather leave early than miss the last train."
**E) We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.**

"Prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway" is an accepted alternative with parallel -ing forms. Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering). Home cooking versus takeaway stays balanced under prefer … rather than ….

**Tip:** Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering).

This is sound: prefer … rather than … with parallel -ing forms is accepted here.
tasks.solution_overview:
Walking versus cycling, tea versus coffee, stay-in versus go-out, early trains, and home cooking — preference structures as cousins of comparatives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preference patterns are prefer A to B, and would rather A than B. Watch the preposition (to, not than after prefer) and the bare infinitive after would rather (no "to").

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the structure first. Prefer wants to; would rather wants than plus a base verb. Parallel -ing forms keep prefer … rather than … tidy.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.
This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.
Her second cake was twice as large as the first.
The second half was half as long than the opening act.
Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.**

"Nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be" correctly intensifies a negative equality comparison. Nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as. The new café versus the old one's busyness still closes with as.

**Tip:** nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as.

Keep this: nowhere near as … as keeps the full scaled-equality frame for the café.
**B) This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.**

Keep the as … as frame — not nearly as steep as the guidebook claimed, not than. Intensifiers do not cancel the need for a second as. The trail versus the guidebook claim is still equality, only scaled down.

**Trap:** not nearly as … than keeps the intensifier but swaps the closing as for than.

That swaps the closer — rewrite as "This trail is not nearly as steep as the guidebook claimed."
**C) Her second cake was twice as large as the first.**

"Twice as large as the first" correctly multiplies an equality comparison. Twice / three times + as + adjective + as is the fixed scale pattern. Cake size versus the first bake still needs both as-markers.

Accept the line: twice as large as uses the fixed multiplier frame for the cakes.
**D) The second half was half as long than the opening act.**

Write "half as long as," not "half as long than." Multipliers still need as … as even when the idea is reduction. The second half versus the opening act is scaled equality, not a plain comparative.

**Trap:** half as … than is the reduction twin of as … than — wrong closer after a multiplier.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The second half was half as long as the opening act."
**E) Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.**

"Slightly less humid than yesterday" correctly softens a comparative of inferiority. Less + adjective + than remains available beside as … as patterns. Today versus yesterday is a true comparative, so than is right here.

That works — less … than correctly softens today's humidity against yesterday.
tasks.solution_overview:
Busy cafés, steep trails, oversized cakes, show lengths, and humidity — scaled equality still needs a closing as.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Scaled equality (twice as, half as, not nearly as, nowhere near as) still needs a closing as. Than only returns when you switch to a true comparative such as less … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the line opens with twice/half/not nearly/nowhere near + as, demand a matching as later. Replace any than in that slot before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.
She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.
This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.
He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.
That was by far a better concert than the one in March.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.**

"Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit" correctly pairs a group phrase with a superlative. Of all / among all → superlative. The market set is larger than a pair, so freshest fits.

Keep this: of all + the freshest matches group ranking across the local markets.
**B) She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.**

"By far the most organised person in our flatshare" correctly intensifies a superlative. By far / easily / much the + superlative is the usual package. The flatshare set is ranked with an intensified highest grade.

**Tip:** by far / easily / much the + superlative.

Accept the line: by far locks onto the most organised superlative in the flatshare.
**C) This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.**

With "much the," use a superlative — much the hardest, not much the harder. Much the pairs with -est / most, not a comparative. This month's crossword set wants the highest grade under the booster.

**Trap:** much the + comparative looks intensified but the booster demands superlative grade.

That booster wants superlative grade — rewrite as "This crossword is much the hardest I have tried this month."
**D) He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.**

"Easily the funniest host on the late-night shows" correctly strengthens a superlative ranking. Easily the + superlative is common in speech and exams. The late-night host field is a group, so funniest is the right grade.

This is sound: easily the funniest intensifies a true superlative among late-night hosts.
**E) That was by far a better concert than the one in March.**

"By far a better concert than the one in March" can intensify a comparative when exactly two concerts are compared. By far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives. March versus that night is a pair, so better after by far is allowed.

**Tip:** by far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives.

That works — by far a better … than correctly intensifies a clear two-concert comparative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Local markets, organised flatmates, tough crosswords, late-night hosts, and concerts — intensifiers locked onto the right grade of comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Final polish: intensifiers like by far, easily, and much the usually lock onto superlatives. If the sentence clearly compares only two items, a comparative after by far can still work — but "much the harder" is the wrong grade.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the booster to the comparison grade. Of all / among → superlative; a clear pair after by far may keep a comparative. Reject "much the" + comparative.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Despite of the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Although the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.
Because the delay, the museum tour started twenty minutes late.
The picnic was cancelled owing a sudden thunderstorm.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Despite the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.**

Despite takes a noun phrase straight away, and "the heavy rain" is exactly that. The main clause then follows cleanly, so the concessive opener is well formed. You do not need of after despite, and you do not need a finite verb inside the despite chunk.

Keep this: despite correctly takes the noun phrase "the heavy rain."
**B) Despite of the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.**

The word of after despite is never standard English. The noun phrase itself is fine — only the extra preposition breaks the linker. Delete of and write "Despite the heavy rain," or switch to "in spite of the heavy rain."

**Trap:** "Despite of" is a high-frequency exam near-miss because in spite of does need of.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Despite the heavy rain," or "In spite of the heavy rain."
**C) Although the heavy rain, we finished the outdoor photography session.**

Although must introduce a clause with a finite verb, not a bare noun phrase. Here "the heavy rain" leaves although hanging without a subject–verb frame. Repair as "Although it rained heavily," or move to despite / in spite of if you want to keep the noun.

**Trap:** Swap despite's noun pattern onto although and the sentence looks almost right — until you hunt for a verb.

That fails — rewrite as "Although it rained heavily," or switch to despite + noun.
**D) Because the delay, the museum tour started twenty minutes late.**

Because introduces a clause, so "Because the delay" leaves you hanging with only a noun. Write "because of the delay" or "Because there was a delay." Cause linkers split into because (clause) versus because of (noun).

**Tip:** Because + noun is almost always wrong — insert of or rebuild as a full clause.

Reject this; use "Because of the delay" or "Because there was a delay."
**E) The picnic was cancelled owing a sudden thunderstorm.**

The fixed causal unit is owing to + noun. Here to is missing, so "owing a sudden thunderstorm" fails even though the meaning is clear. Restore "owing to a sudden thunderstorm" and the cause phrase works again.

**Tip:** Treat "owing to" as one linker; if to is gone, mark false.

Mark it wrong and prefer "owing to a sudden thunderstorm."
tasks.solution_overview:
You are checking linking-word grammar on wet outdoor plans: rain, delays, and a cancelled picnic.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is about matching the linker to the grammar that follows. Despite and owing to want a noun idea; although and because want a full clause with a verb. The classic exam traps are despite of, although + noun, because + noun, and owing without to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each sentence, name the linker, then ask what comes next: noun phrase or finite clause? If those two do not match, mark false. Keep everyday meanings intact — only the connector shape decides the truth value.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.
Although the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.
The trail was icy; however, the hikers still reached the summit café.
The trail was icy, however the hikers still reached the summit café without stronger punctuation.
The concert started late owing technical problems with the sound desk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.**

In spite of correctly takes the noun phrase "the crowded platform," and the main clause about Maya finding a seat follows. This is the standard concessive noun pattern, interchangeable in shape with despite. A crowded platform is a noun idea, so in spite of is the right family of linker.

That works: in spite of correctly frames the noun concession.
**B) Although the crowded platform, Maya found a seat on the morning train.**

Although cannot sit in front of a bare noun phrase such as "the crowded platform." Rewrite as "Although the platform was crowded…" or switch to in spite of / despite. The missing finite verb is what makes although illegal here.

**Trap:** A noun after although is usually a despite transplant that still looks plausible at speed.

Reject this near-miss; rewrite as "Although the platform was crowded…" or keep in spite of + noun.
**C) The trail was icy; however, the hikers still reached the summit café.**

However is working as a conjunctive adverb between two independent clauses. The semicolon before it supplies the strong break formal writing wants. The contrast between the icy trail and reaching the café is clearly marked.

**Tip:** Semicolon (or period) + however + comma is the clean formal pattern.

Accept the line: semicolon + however joins the contrasting clauses cleanly.
**D) The trail was icy, however the hikers still reached the summit café without stronger punctuation.**

A lone comma before clause-joining however is weak or wrong in careful exam English. Prefer a semicolon or a new sentence so however does not create a comma splice. If however could open a fresh sentence, do not glue it with a comma alone.

**Trap:** Comma + however between full clauses is a classic splice that still looks almost formal.

That punctuation fails — give however a semicolon or period, not only a comma.
**E) The concert started late owing technical problems with the sound desk.**

Owing is incomplete without to. The cause meaning is right — the concert is late for technical problems — but the preposition string is not. Restore "owing to technical problems with the sound desk."

Mark it wrong and prefer "owing to technical problems with the sound desk."
tasks.solution_overview:
Maya's crowded platform, an icy trail, and a late concert put contrast and cause linkers under pressure.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You are sorting two families: in spite of / despite before nouns versus although before clauses, then checking however between full sentences. A second cause trap appears when owing loses its to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the connector first. After in spite of, expect a noun; after although, expect subject + verb; after however, expect strong punctuation (semicolon or full stop) before it joins another independent clause.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of the closed bridge, cyclists took the riverside path instead.
Because the bridge was closed, cyclists took the riverside path instead.
Even though the recipe looked complicated, Leo baked the cake successfully.
Even though the complicated recipe, Leo baked the cake successfully.
Whereas the first half was quiet, the second half of the match was frantic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Because of the closed bridge, cyclists took the riverside path instead.**

Because of + "the closed bridge" correctly names the reason, and the main clause about the riverside path follows. The noun form of the cause linker is exactly what this sentence needs. A closed bridge is a noun idea, so of belongs with because here.

Keep this: because of correctly takes the noun cause.
**B) Because the bridge was closed, cyclists took the riverside path instead.**

Because introduces the full clause "the bridge was closed," which supplies subject and verb. That is the matching clause pattern for the same idea as A, just shaped differently. Do not insert of when a finite clause already follows because.

This is sound — because introduces the finite cause clause.
**C) Even though the recipe looked complicated, Leo baked the cake successfully.**

Even though takes a finite clause, and "the recipe looked complicated" gives you one. The concession with Leo's successful bake is therefore grammatical and natural. Even though works like although: both want a subject and a tensed verb.

Accept the line: even though correctly governs a finite clause.
**D) Even though the complicated recipe, Leo baked the cake successfully.**

Even though cannot govern a bare noun phrase such as "the complicated recipe." Restore a verb — "even though the recipe looked complicated" — or move to despite + noun. Same baking story, wrong linker grammar after even though.

**Trap:** Learners often park despite's noun under even though; the sentence still sounds concessive.

That linker fails — prefer "even though the recipe looked complicated" or despite + noun.
**E) Whereas the first half was quiet, the second half of the match was frantic.**

Whereas cleanly contrasts two finite clauses: a quiet first half against a frantic second half. Both sides have verbs, which is what whereas requires for a balanced contrast. Use whereas for side-by-side contrasts, not as a simple cause linker.

That pairing is sound — whereas contrasts two complete clauses.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cyclists, a cake bake, and a frantic second half of a match all hinge on cause and concession linkers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Cause offers because of (noun) and because (clause); concession offers even though (clause) and, nearby, whereas for clause-to-clause contrast. The trap in this set is even though attached to a noun alone.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, identify the linker and test its partner. Noun phrases belong with because of; finite clauses belong with because, even though, and whereas. One mismatched partner is enough for false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite of repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.
In spite the repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.
Although Nina forgot to water the plants, they somehow survived the weekend.
The library was quiet because of a school holiday in the neighbourhood.
Tickets sold out early; however, a few returns appeared at the box office.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Despite of repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.**

Despite never partners with of. The noun phrase "repeated reminders" is fine; the extra preposition is the only error. Drop of and write "Despite repeated reminders…"

**Trap:** Despite of looks parallel to in spite of, which is why this trap catches so many learners.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Despite repeated reminders…"
**B) In spite the repeated reminders, Nina forgot to water the balcony plants.**

The full phrase is in spite of, not in spite alone. Insert of before "the repeated reminders." Learn the trio as fixed spelling: despite (no of) / in spite of / although (clause).

**Tip:** If you see bare "in spite," restore of before you move on.

That fails — rewrite as "In spite of the repeated reminders…"
**C) Although Nina forgot to water the plants, they somehow survived the weekend.**

Although + "Nina forgot to water the plants" correctly opens a concessive clause. The survival of the plants follows as the main result. When the concessive idea already has its own verb, although is a safe choice.

Keep this: although correctly introduces a finite concessive clause.
**D) The library was quiet because of a school holiday in the neighbourhood.**

Because of + "a school holiday in the neighbourhood" correctly states the cause of the quiet library. A school holiday is a noun idea, so the of-form is required rather than bare because. The reason linker and its partner match.

Accept the line: because of correctly frames the noun cause.
**E) Tickets sold out early; however, a few returns appeared at the box office.**

Semicolon + however correctly joins two contrasting independent clauses about sold-out tickets and late returns. Read however as a sentence adverb that likes a strong break before it. A comma after however completes the usual formal pattern.

This is sound: semicolon + however marks the contrast cleanly.
tasks.solution_overview:
Nina's forgotten watering, a quiet library, and sold-out tickets spotlight spelling pairs and punctuation around contrast.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch the fixed pairs despite (no of) versus in spite of (of required). Then confirm although is carrying a real clause and however is sitting after strong punctuation between independent clauses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan of after despite or a missing of after in spite first — those are instant false markers. Next check whether although has a verb and whether however has a semicolon or period in front of it.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.
Because of thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.
Despite the fog lingering all morning, several walkers still set out.
Although the fog lingered all morning, several walkers still set out.
However, the coastal path remained closed for safety checks.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Owing to thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.**

Owing to + "thick fog" correctly states the cause of the postponed crossing. Formal notices often prefer this linker before abstract nouns such as fog. Before a noun, owing to behaves like because of.

Keep this: owing to correctly takes the noun cause.
**B) Because of thick fog, the ferry crossing was postponed until noon.**

Because of + the same noun phrase is an equally correct causal pattern. The ferry postponement is explained without forcing a full clause after the linker. Grammar after the cause word decides whether you need of.

That works: because of correctly names the thick-fog cause.
**C) Despite the fog lingering all morning, several walkers still set out.**

Despite can take a gerund-style noun phrase such as "the fog lingering all morning." That -ing phrase behaves like a noun object, so the concession before the walkers set out is grammatical. Despite + -ing is fine; despite + finite clause usually is not.

**Tip:** Despite + -ing phrase is legal; save although for a tensed clause.

Accept the line: despite correctly hosts the -ing noun phrase.
**D) Although the fog lingered all morning, several walkers still set out.**

Although + "the fog lingered all morning" supplies a finite verb, which is exactly what although wants. The same story as C, but in clause form rather than an -ing phrase. Lingered is the tensed verb that licenses although here.

This is sound — although correctly governs the finite fog clause.
**E) However, the coastal path remained closed for safety checks.**

Sentence-initial However, with a following comma, cleanly opens a contrast about the closed coastal path. Starting with However is fine in formal writing. The punctuation problem appears when however joins mid-paragraph clauses with only a weak comma before it — not when it opens a new sentence.

Keep the opener: sentence-initial However + comma is well formed.
tasks.solution_overview:
Thick coastal fog postpones a ferry and still tempts walkers — every linker in this set is actually well formed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You are confirming legal pairings: owing to / because of + noun, despite + -ing noun phrase, although + finite clause, and sentence-initial However with a comma. The "traps" are lessons in what good versions look like, not errors to catch.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Still apply the same test: name the linker, name what follows. Here every partner matches, so every statement is true — use that as a calibration set for fog-themed cause and concession.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rehearsal stopped because of a broken stage light.
The rehearsal stopped because a stage light was broken.
The rehearsal stopped because of a stage light was broken.
In spite of the broken light, the cast finished Act Two.
Whereas the lighting failed, the orchestra kept perfect timing.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rehearsal stopped because of a broken stage light.**

Because of + "a broken stage light" correctly explains the stoppage. A broken light is a noun idea, so the of-form fits without forcing a clause. The rehearsal stops for a concrete thing, not for a whole finite clause after of.

That works: because of correctly takes the noun cause.
**B) The rehearsal stopped because a stage light was broken.**

Because + "a stage light was broken" is the matching clause form of the same reason. Both A and B can be right; the grammar after the linker decides which shape you need. Subject + verb after because means leave of out.

Keep this: because correctly introduces the finite cause clause.
**C) The rehearsal stopped because of a stage light was broken.**

Do not stack because of onto a full clause with was. Either drop of ("because a stage light was broken") or compress the idea into a noun after because of. The hybrid "because of + subject + verb" mixes two patterns that must stay separate.

**Trap:** Because of + tensed verb looks smooth if you have just seen both legal shapes side by side.

Reject this hybrid — drop of, or rewrite the clause as a noun after because of.
**D) In spite of the broken light, the cast finished Act Two.**

In spite of + "the broken light" correctly frames the concession while the cast finishes Act Two. The broken light remains a noun idea, so in spite of / despite both work. Concession here is about enduring a thing, not introducing a new finite clause under the linker.

Accept the line: in spite of correctly takes the noun concession.
**E) Whereas the lighting failed, the orchestra kept perfect timing.**

Whereas contrasts two complete clauses — lighting failed versus the orchestra kept timing. Use whereas for side-by-side contrasts, not as a simple cause linker. Both halves here carry real verbs, so the contrast is balanced.

This contrast is sound — whereas pairs two finite clauses.
highlights: because of a stage light was
tasks.solution_overview:
A broken stage light stops a rehearsal, and the cast and orchestra show how cause and contrast linkers should (and should not) be stacked.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The key trap is gluing because of onto a full clause. Legitimate patterns stay clean: because of + noun, because + clause, in spite of + noun, and whereas + clause + clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find a tensed verb after because of and you have a false hybrid. Elsewhere, check that noun and clause partners still match their linkers.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Despite the fact that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
Despite that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
Although the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.
The kitchen was tiny. However, the dinner still felt generous.
Space was limited however the hosts somehow seated twelve guests comfortably.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Despite the fact that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.**

Despite the fact that + clause is an accepted formal workaround when you truly need a clause idea after despite. The tiny kitchen and the lively dinner contrast cleanly, even if the phrasing is heavier than plain although. Prefer although when you can, but this longer shape is still grammatical.

**Tip:** Prefer although when you can; despite the fact that is wordy but legal.

Keep this: despite the fact that correctly licenses the following clause.
**B) Despite that the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.**

"Despite that" + clause is non-standard in careful exam English. Switch to although, or to despite the fact that. Do not force despite to swallow a bare that-clause.

**Trap:** Despite that sounds like a neat shortcut beside despite the fact that — and that is the near-miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Although the kitchen was tiny" or "Despite the fact that the kitchen was tiny."
**C) Although the kitchen was tiny, they hosted a lively dinner.**

Although + "the kitchen was tiny" is the cleanest concessive choice here. Same meaning as A, with less padding and a perfect clause partner. When the concessive half already has subject and verb, although is the natural pick.

That works: although cleanly introduces the tiny-kitchen clause.
**D) The kitchen was tiny. However, the dinner still felt generous.**

A full stop before However correctly separates the contrasting sentences about the tiny kitchen and the generous feeling of the dinner. Period + However + comma is as strong as semicolon + however. Treat starting However like a new sentence adverb.

Accept the line: period + However correctly opens the contrast.
**E) Space was limited however the hosts somehow seated twelve guests comfortably.**

Running however between clauses with no strong punctuation is incorrect in formal writing. Insert a semicolon or period, and usually a comma after however. Never leave however floating between clauses with zero stops.

**Trap:** Floating mid-sentence however without punctuation still looks fluent in drafty prose.

That fails — give however a semicolon or period before it joins the next clause.
tasks.solution_overview:
A tiny kitchen and a lively dinner test how despite, although, and however handle clause-level contrast.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Despite normally wants nouns; the workaround despite the fact that + clause is wordy but accepted, while bare despite that + clause is not. Although wants a plain clause; however wants sentence-level punctuation.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you need a clause after a concessive idea, prefer although, or the longer despite the fact that — not despite that. For however, insist on a period/semicolon (or parenthetical commas), never a free float between clauses.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
Because of a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
Although the power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.
In spite of the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.
Whereas the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Owing to a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.**

Owing to + "a power cut" correctly marks the cause of the earlier screening. Before a noun, owing to behaves like because of. The cinema switches screening time for that noun cause.

Keep this: owing to correctly takes the power-cut noun.
**B) Because of a power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.**

Because of + the same noun is equally correct in the same slot. Do not mix this noun pattern with although's clause rule when you paraphrase. Either causal noun linker works; the follow-on grammar must still match.

This is sound — because of names the same noun cause.
**C) Although the power cut, the cinema switched to an earlier screening.**

Although needs something like "Although there was a power cut," not a bare noun. A power cut is a noun idea — feed it to despite / because of / owing to, or rebuild a full clause after although. Without a verb after although, the linker and its follow-on disagree.

**Trap:** Although + noun borrows the power-cut idea from the legal owing to / because of lines and looks half-right.

Reject this; rewrite as "Although there was a power cut," or switch to despite / owing to + noun.
**D) In spite of the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.**

In spite of + "the power cut" correctly frames the concession while the audience stays seated. Staying put despite a power cut is a classic noun-concession pattern. In spite of / despite + noun fits this story cleanly.

That works: in spite of correctly takes the power-cut concession.
**E) Whereas the power cut, the audience stayed in their seats.**

Whereas requires a full clause, not a noun phrase. Rewrite as "Whereas the power failed…" or switch to despite / in spite of. Contrast linkers are not interchangeable without rewriting what follows.

**Trap:** Whereas + the same noun that works after in spite of is a neat swap trap.

Mark it wrong — rebuild a finite clause after whereas, or use despite / in spite of + noun.
tasks.solution_overview:
A cinema power cut forces the same noun idea through five different linkers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The power cut can follow owing to, because of, or in spite of, because those linkers take nouns. It cannot follow although or whereas, which demand finite clauses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep the noun "the power cut" fixed in your mind, then ask whether the linker on that line accepts a noun. If it wants a clause instead, mark false and picture the repaired verb phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment succeeded despite early doubts from the lab team.
The experiment succeeded in spite of early doubts from the lab team.
The experiment succeeded although early doubts from the lab team.
Early doubts were widespread; however, the results still matched the prediction.
Early doubts were widespread, the results however still matched the prediction with no change in word order.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The experiment succeeded despite early doubts from the lab team.**

Despite + "early doubts from the lab team" correctly expresses concession after the main clause about success. Mid- or end-sentence despite is fine when a noun follows. The experiment succeeds against a noun idea, which is despite's usual job.

Accept the line: despite correctly takes the noun concession after the main clause.
**B) The experiment succeeded in spite of early doubts from the lab team.**

In spite of mirrors despite before the same noun phrase. Prefer one style consistently in a report; both forms are grammatical here. Despite and in spite of share the noun-object pattern.

Keep this: in spite of correctly frames the same noun concession.
**C) The experiment succeeded although early doubts from the lab team.**

Although cannot take "early doubts…" without a verb. Repair as "Although the team had early doubts…" Same concession, different grammar after the linker.

**Trap:** Although + noun looks like a quick rewrite of the despite line and is a mid-level transplant trap.

That fails — prefer "Although the team had early doubts…" or keep despite + noun.
**D) Early doubts were widespread; however, the results still matched the prediction.**

Semicolon + however correctly contrasts widespread doubts with results that still matched the prediction. Keep a comma after however in this formal pattern. Strong punctuation marks however as a clause-level contrast adverb.

This is sound: semicolon + however joins the contrasting clauses correctly.
**E) Early doubts were widespread, the results however still matched the prediction with no change in word order.**

Dropping however into the middle without proper clause punctuation makes the sentence clumsy and formally wrong here. Park however at a clause edge with a semicolon or period, or set it off as a true parenthetical. Do not leave it as a loose insert between two clauses glued by a comma.

**Trap:** Loose mid-clause however with weak punctuation is a polished-looking splice at this difficulty.

Reject the loose join — give however a semicolon/period edge or proper parenthetical commas.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab doubts and a still-successful experiment put post-clause concession and however punctuation on display.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After a success statement, despite / in spite of + noun is the natural concessive shape. Although still needs a verb, and however needs clear sentence boundaries — burying it mid-clause without proper punctuation fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the material after despite / in spite of / although first. Then read the however lines as punctuation problems: semicolon pattern good, loose mid-clause insert bad.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of rising pollen levels, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Because pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Because of pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.
Even though pollen levels were high, a few athletes still trained outdoors.
Even though high pollen levels, a few athletes still trained outdoors.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Because of rising pollen levels, many runners skipped the morning jog.**

Because of + "rising pollen levels" correctly states the reason runners skipped the jog. Rising pollen levels behaves as a noun idea after because of. Noun cause → because of; clause cause → bare because.

Keep this: because of correctly takes the noun pollen cause.
**B) Because pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.**

Because + "pollen levels were rising" is the matching clause form. Keep because of and because as a clean pair: noun versus clause for the same real-world cause. A tensed verb after because means of should stay out.

That works: because correctly introduces the rising-pollen clause.
**C) Because of pollen levels were rising, many runners skipped the morning jog.**

Because of must not introduce a full clause with were. Drop of, or rewrite the clause as a noun phrase. A tensed verb sitting after because of is your cue to rewrite at once.

**Trap:** The hybrid mixes the legal because-of noun line with the legal because clause and feels almost right.

Mark it wrong — drop of, or compress the clause into a noun after because of.
**D) Even though pollen levels were high, a few athletes still trained outdoors.**

Even though + "pollen levels were high" correctly marks concession while a few athletes still train outdoors. Even though and although share the same clause requirement. Subject + tensed verb after even though licenses the linker.

Accept the line: even though correctly governs a finite concession clause.
**E) Even though high pollen levels, a few athletes still trained outdoors.**

Even though cannot take a bare noun phrase such as "high pollen levels." Switch to despite high pollen levels, or add a verb after even though. Same outdoor-training idea, wrong follow-on.

**Trap:** Even though + noun is the sister trap to although + noun — plausible if you just saw despite + noun.

That linker fails — rewrite as "even though pollen levels were high" or use despite + noun.
tasks.solution_overview:
Rising pollen levels and outdoor training bring the because / because of and even though / despite swaps into one story.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Cause and concession each swap partners: because of and despite take nouns; because and even though take clauses. Spot the hybrid "because of + were" and the bare noun after even though.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the linker, then look for a tensed verb. A verb after because of or a noun-only stretch after even though means false; matched pairs mean true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She kept painting, although her wrist ached after every session.
She kept painting despite her wrist ached after every session.
She kept painting in spite of her aching wrist.
Her wrist ached; she continued, however, with shorter sessions.
Her wrist ached, however she continued with shorter sessions using only a comma.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She kept painting, although her wrist ached after every session.**

Although + "her wrist ached after every session" correctly softens the contrast with continued painting. Pain plus persistence is a natural although pattern because the concessive half already has a verb. Finite verb after although usually means the pattern is right.

This is sound — although correctly introduces the aching-wrist clause.
**B) She kept painting despite her wrist ached after every session.**

Despite cannot take the finite clause "her wrist ached." Use although, or rewrite as "despite her aching wrist." Do not feed a tensed clause directly to despite.

**Trap:** Despite + subject + verb is a mid/hard near-miss when the meaning is clearly concessive.

Mark it wrong and prefer "although her wrist ached" or "despite her aching wrist."
**C) She kept painting in spite of her aching wrist.**

In spite of + "her aching wrist" is the correct concessive noun form of the same idea. Convert the clause into a noun, and in spite of / despite become available. Aching wrist packs the pain idea into a noun object.

Keep this: in spite of correctly takes the noun concession.
**D) Her wrist ached; she continued, however, with shorter sessions.**

Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts the ache with continuing in shorter sessions. Mid-clause however with commas on both sides is allowed when it is truly parenthetical. That pattern is different from splice-joining two full clauses with only a comma before however.

**Tip:** Commas both sides = parenthetical however, not a splice.

That works: parenthetical however is correctly set off with commas.
**E) Her wrist ached, however she continued with shorter sessions using only a comma.**

However joining two clauses with only a preceding comma is a classic splice error. Use a semicolon or period before however when it links full clauses. Same word as D, different punctuation job — and this one fails.

**Trap:** The lone-comma join looks almost like the legal parenthetical pattern if you read too fast.

Reject the splice — give clause-joining however a semicolon or period.
tasks.solution_overview:
An aching wrist and shorter painting sessions contrast clause linkers with noun linkers, then test two however patterns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Although takes a finite clause; despite does not. In spite of wants the noun form of the same idea. For however, parenthetical commas are legal, but a comma splice between full clauses is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Convert mentally between "her wrist ached" and "her aching wrist" to see which linker fits. Then separate legal parenthetical however from illegal clause-joining with only a preceding comma.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Owing to roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.
Owing roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.
Despite roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.
Although roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.
Whereas the outbound coach was late, the return journey ran on time.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Owing to roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.**

Owing to + "roadworks on the ring road" correctly explains the late arrival. Travel notices often open with owing to + cause. Keep to attached to owing in this pattern.

Keep this: owing to correctly frames the roadworks cause.
**B) Owing roadworks on the ring road, the coach arrived forty minutes late.**

To is missing — write "owing to roadworks." End- or start-of-sentence owing still needs its full linker. An orphan owing is an instant fail even when the cause noun is clear.

**Trap:** Dropping to from owing to is a short, high-yield exam trap.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Owing to roadworks on the ring road…"
**C) Despite roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.**

Despite + the -ing phrase "roadworks slowing traffic" is grammatical. Despite + noun/-ing lines up with although + clause for the same concessive idea. Several passengers still making connections is the main clause that follows.

Accept the line: despite correctly hosts the -ing concession phrase.
**D) Although roadworks slowing traffic, several passengers still made their connections.**

Although needs a finite verb — "Although roadworks slowed traffic…" Bare "Although roadworks slowing traffic" is a common transfer error from the despite pattern. Add a tensed verb or switch linker.

**Trap:** Although + -ing transplants the legal despite line and looks nearly grammatical.

That fails — rewrite as "Although roadworks slowed traffic…" or keep despite + -ing.
**E) Whereas the outbound coach was late, the return journey ran on time.**

Whereas contrasts two complete clauses about the outbound coach versus the return journey. Whereas likes balanced clause pairs, not noun fragments. Both halves here have real verbs, so the contrast lands cleanly.

This is sound — whereas contrasts two finite travel clauses.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ring-road roadworks delay a coach and still let some passengers make their connections.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Check that owing to is complete, then decide whether an -ing phrase belongs after despite (yes) or after although (usually no). Whereas still demands two full clauses about outbound versus return.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for orphan "owing" without to first. Then test -ing phrases: legal after despite, illegal after although unless you rebuild a finite verb. Finish by confirming whereas has verbs on both sides.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The choir performed well despite having had only two rehearsals that week.
The choir performed well although having had only two rehearsals that week.
Because of having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.
Because having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.
Having had only two rehearsals; however, the choir still sounded confident.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The choir performed well despite having had only two rehearsals that week.**

Despite + the perfect gerund phrase "having had only two rehearsals that week" correctly marks concession. Despite + having (had) … is a polished formal pattern before the choir still performs well. The -ing stretch behaves as a noun object of despite.

**Tip:** Despite + having… is a reliable advanced concession shape.

Keep this: despite correctly takes the perfect gerund concession.
**B) The choir performed well although having had only two rehearsals that week.**

Although needs a finite clause — "Although the choir had had only two rehearsals…" Do not transplant a despite -ing phrase under although. Same meaning, wrong linker partner.

**Trap:** Although + having had… looks sophisticated because it borrows despite's advanced shape.

Reject this transplant; prefer "Although the choir had had only two rehearsals…" or keep despite + having…
**C) Because of having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.**

Because of + "having only two rehearsals" correctly states the cause of the shortened programme. Because of can take -ing phrases that act like nouns. The conductor shortens the programme for that noun-like cause.

That works: because of correctly takes the -ing cause phrase.
**D) Because having only two rehearsals, the conductor shortened the programme.**

Bare because needs subject + verb, not a hanging -ing phrase. Add of, or rewrite "Because they had only two rehearsals…" A solitary -ing after because leaves the clause unfinished.

**Trap:** Because + -ing is the ugly twin of legal because of + -ing — easy to miss at speed.

Mark it wrong — add of, or rebuild as "Because they had only two rehearsals…"
**E) Having had only two rehearsals; however, the choir still sounded confident.**

A dangling -ing opener cannot be glued to however with only a semicolon in this broken shape. Rebuild as two full independent clauses before and after however. The contrast word cannot repair missing clause structure on its own.

**Trap:** Semicolon + however looks formally right until you notice the first half is not an independent clause.

That fails — rebuild independent clauses on both sides of however.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two short choir rehearsals push advanced -ing constructions under despite, although, because of, because, and however.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Gerund phrases fit after despite / because of, but not after bare although / because. A dangling -ing opener also cannot rescue a malformed however pairing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the -ing stretch is acting as a noun object of despite / because of. If it hangs after although / because, or props up a broken however frame, mark false and rebuild with full clauses where needed.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
Despite what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
Although what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.
The guidebook was outdated; the gallery, however, posted clear opening hours online.
The guidebook was outdated however the gallery posted clear opening hours online.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.**

In spite of + the free relative "what the guidebook claimed" works because the what-clause acts as a noun. The gallery still being closed on Mondays follows as the main clause. What/how clauses can follow in spite of / despite / because of as noun objects.

Accept the line: in spite of correctly takes the what-clause as a noun object.
**B) Despite what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.**

Despite + the same what-clause is equally correct. Despite and in spite of share this noun-like object pattern before the main clause about Monday closure. Despite what… and in spite of what… are parallel formal options.

Keep this: despite correctly takes the same what-clause object.
**C) Although what the guidebook claimed, the gallery was still closed on Mondays.**

Although needs an ordinary clause, not "although what…" without a verb frame that makes sense as although's partner. Prefer "Although the guidebook claimed otherwise…" Rebuild rather than forcing the what-clause under although.

**Trap:** Although what… looks parallel to despite what… and is a hard near-miss.

That linker fails — rewrite as "Although the guidebook claimed otherwise…" or keep despite / in spite of what…
**D) The guidebook was outdated; the gallery, however, posted clear opening hours online.**

Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts outdated print with clear opening hours online. Commas on both sides signal parenthetical however, not a splice between bare clauses. The gallery posted hours while the guidebook lagged.

This is sound: mid-clause however is correctly parenthetical.
**E) The guidebook was outdated however the gallery posted clear opening hours online.**

No strong punctuation appears before however between two clauses. Insert a semicolon or start a new sentence. The contrast meaning is fine; the join is not.

**Trap:** Floating however between clauses without a break is the usual hard punctuation trap.

Mark it wrong — insert a semicolon or period before however.
tasks.solution_overview:
An outdated guidebook and Monday gallery hours test what-clauses after noun linkers and however punctuation.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wh-clauses behave like nouns after despite / in spite of, but although still wants a normal subject–verb clause. Pair that insight with a careful however check: parenthetical commas good, no strong break bad.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If what/how follows despite or in spite of, treat it as a noun object. If although what… lacks a normal clause frame, mark false. Then score however on punctuation alone.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whereas most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
Despite most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
In spite of most guests preferring the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.
Because of most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.
Although most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Whereas most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.**

Whereas + "most guests preferred the terrace" correctly opens a balanced contrast with guests who stayed indoors. Whereas needs a tensed verb in each half of the contrast. Preferred and stayed both supply that finite marking.

That works: whereas contrasts two finite guest clauses.
**B) Despite most guests preferred the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.**

Despite cannot take "most guests preferred…" as a finite clause. Switch to although, or to "despite most guests preferring…" Keep the idea; change either the linker or the verb shape.

**Trap:** Despite + preferred is a hard transplant from the legal whereas / although finite pattern.

Reject this — use although + preferred, or despite / in spite of + preferring.
**C) In spite of most guests preferring the terrace, a few stayed indoors near the fireplace.**

In spite of + "most guests preferring the terrace" correctly compresses the same idea into a noun-like -ing phrase. Preferring turns the clause into a legal object for in spite of. A few guests still staying indoors is the contrasting main clause.

**Tip:** -ing compression unlocks in spite of / despite for this story.

Keep this: in spite of correctly takes the preferring phrase.
**D) Because of most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.**

Because of + the same -ing phrase correctly marks cause when the hosts move the buffet outside. The identical -ing stretch can serve cause (because of) or concession (in spite of). Noun-like -ing after because of is the legal cause shape here.

Accept the line: because of correctly takes the -ing cause phrase.
**E) Although most guests preferring the terrace, the hosts moved the buffet outside.**

Although still needs "Although most guests preferred…" with a finite verb. Preferring alone after although is not enough. Final check on every although: find the tensed verb or mark false.

**Trap:** Although + preferring steals the legal -ing shape from in spite of / because of.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Although most guests preferred…" or keep because of / in spite of + preferring.
highlights: In spite of most guests preferring
tasks.solution_overview:
Terrace guests versus fireplace stay-ins reshape one party detail under five different linkers.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Whereas and although want finite verbs; despite does not take "preferred" as a finite clause; in spite of / because of can take the compressed -ing form preferring. One party fact, five grammar shapes.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the linker, then name what follows it. Preferred (finite) versus preferring (-ing) is the fork that separates true from false in this set.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Despite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Although having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Although he had little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.
Free time was scarce; however, the club rides still felt restorative.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.**

In spite of + "having little free time" correctly frames concession with a gerund before Sam joins the club. Having + noun after in spite of / despite is a reliable pattern. The scarce free time is packed into a noun-like -ing object.

Keep this: in spite of correctly takes the having… gerund concession.
**B) Despite of having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.**

Remove of — "Despite having little free time…" Despite + -ing is fine; despite of + -ing is not. One illegal of ruins an otherwise good gerund concession.

**Trap:** Despite of before -ing still looks parallel to in spite of having…

That fails — rewrite as "Despite having little free time…"
**C) Although having little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.**

Although does not take a bare -ing phrase in careful formal English. Add a subject + finite verb, as in D. "Although having…" is a common transfer error from the despite pattern.

**Trap:** Although having… looks advanced because it copies the legal gerund after in spite of / despite.

Reject this; rebuild with "Although he had little free time…"
**D) Although he had little free time, Sam joined the weekend cycling club.**

Although + "he had little free time" repairs the previous pattern with a clear subject and finite verb. When in doubt after although, insert an explicit subject (he / Sam). Although + full clause is the safe rewrite of although -ing.

This is sound — although correctly introduces the finite free-time clause.
**E) Free time was scarce; however, the club rides still felt restorative.**

Semicolon + however correctly contrasts scarce free time with rides that still felt restorative. Keep the comma after however in this formal join. Strong punctuation marks however as a clause-level contrast adverb.

Accept the line: semicolon + however joins the contrast correctly.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sam's scarce free time and a weekend cycling club highlight gerund concessions and their fake twins.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Gerund concessions after in spite of / despite are elegant, but although still wants a full clause. Watch the fake "despite of" and the fake "although -ing" patterns that borrow illegally from the despite family.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see having after in spite of / despite, celebrate — then check that of is not stuck on despite, and that although has a real subject + verb, not a bare -ing transplant.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The match resumed, owing to a brief break in the storm clouds.
The match resumed owing a brief break in the storm clouds.
A break in the clouds arrived; the pitch, however, remained too wet for play.
A break in the clouds arrived, however the pitch remained too wet for play with only a comma before however.
Despite a break in the clouds arriving, several seats in the stand stayed empty.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The match resumed, owing to a brief break in the storm clouds.**

Mid-sentence owing to + "a brief break in the storm clouds" correctly states the cause of the resumed match. A comma before owing to is common when the cause follows the result. Result first, then owing to + noun, is a natural order.

That works: owing to correctly explains why the match resumed.
**B) The match resumed owing a brief break in the storm clouds.**

To is missing — write "owing to a brief break." End-of-sentence or mid-sentence owing still needs its full linker. Meaning is clear; form is not.

**Trap:** Orphan owing without to remains a high-yield trap even in denser storm sentences.

Mark it wrong and prefer "owing to a brief break in the storm clouds."
**C) A break in the clouds arrived; the pitch, however, remained too wet for play.**

Parenthetical however between commas correctly contrasts the break in the clouds with a pitch that remained too wet. Mid-clause however with commas is allowed when it does not join two bare clauses with a weak comma alone. Commas both sides mark the parenthetical use.

Keep this: parenthetical however is correctly punctuated.
**D) A break in the clouds arrived, however the pitch remained too wet for play with only a comma before however.**

Using however as a coordinator with only a preceding comma remains poor formal style. Distinguish parenthetical however (commas both sides) from clause-joining however (semicolon/period). This line is the splice version of the legal parenthetical pattern in C.

**Trap:** Lone comma before however is the hardest twin of legal mid-clause however.

That punctuation fails — use a semicolon or period before clause-joining however.
**E) Despite a break in the clouds arriving, several seats in the stand stayed empty.**

Despite + "a break in the clouds arriving" correctly marks concession while seats stay empty. "Despite X arriving" lines up with "although X arrived" for the same idea. Despite + -ing phrase remains a solid concession tool at this level.

Accept the line: despite correctly hosts the arriving phrase.
highlights: Despite a break in the clouds arriving
tasks.solution_overview:
A storm-interrupted match forces you to separate legal mid-clause however from illegal comma splices, while owing to and despite -ing stay in view.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Harder however items distinguish parenthetical mid-clause use (commas both sides) from illegal comma-only joins between clauses. Pair that with a clean owing to check and a despite + -ing concession.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each however line, ask: parenthetical or clause-joiner? Parenthetical needs commas both sides; clause-joiner needs a semicolon or period. Separately, confirm owing still has to, and despite can host the -ing phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Because of how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.
Because how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.
Although how abruptly the trail narrowed surprised the guides, nobody turned back.
In spite of how abruptly the trail narrowed, nobody turned back.
The trail narrowed abruptly. Owing to that change, the group slowed to single file.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Because of how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.**

Because of + the free relative "how abruptly the trail narrowed" is grammatical because the how-clause acts as a noun. The group slowing to single file follows naturally. Wh-clauses can act as nouns after because of / despite / in spite of.

Keep this: because of correctly takes the how-clause as a noun object.
**B) Because how abruptly the trail narrowed, the group slowed to single file.**

Bare because needs a normal clause, not "because how…" without of. If a how/what clause follows, you usually need because of, not bare because. Restore of or rebuild an ordinary subject–verb clause.

**Trap:** Because how… without of looks almost parallel to because of how… — a sharp advanced miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Because of how abruptly the trail narrowed…"
**C) Although how abruptly the trail narrowed surprised the guides, nobody turned back.**

Although + a clause in which "how abruptly the trail narrowed surprised the guides" is fine. The how-clause sits inside a larger finite clause, so although is satisfied. Nobody turning back follows as the main outcome.

**Tip:** Here the how-clause is inside although's finite clause, not a bare noun substitute.

This is sound — although governs a full finite clause containing the how-idea.
**D) In spite of how abruptly the trail narrowed, nobody turned back.**

In spite of + "how abruptly the trail narrowed" correctly marks concession. In spite of how / despite what are polished formal patterns before the decision not to turn back. The how-clause is treated as a noun object of in spite of.

That works: in spite of correctly takes the how-clause concession.
**E) The trail narrowed abruptly. Owing to that change, the group slowed to single file.**

Sentence-initial Owing to + "that change" correctly links back to the prior narrowing. Pointing with that change keeps owing to attached to a clear noun rather than to a dangling clause. Owing to + noun (including a pointing noun) stays clean across sentence boundaries.

Accept the line: owing to correctly takes the pointing noun that change.
tasks.solution_overview:
An abruptly narrowing trail slows hikers to single file and tests how-clauses as noun objects.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Advanced items use how-clauses as noun objects of because of / in spite of. Bare because still wants an ordinary subject–verb clause — do not drop of before how. Although can host a how-clause only when it sits inside a larger finite clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If how follows because of or in spite of, treat it as a noun. If how follows bare because, expect false. Then check that although's how-stretch still leaves a finite verb for although itself.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Notwithstanding the delayed train, the friends still made the exhibition opening — and despite the same delay, they refused to skip the café stop.
Despite delayed trains, they reached the gallery; however, several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Although delayed trains, they reached the gallery, however several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Owing to the delayed train, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
Because of delayed trains were overcrowded, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
tactical_explanations:
