**C) No sooner had the oven preheated than the dough was ready.**

No sooner had the oven preheated places had before the subject. Than matches no sooner as the correlative linker. Past-perfect inversion and than are both right.

Accept the line: no sooner + had + than is already complete.
**D) At no point did the guide admit that the path was closed.**

At no point behaves like at no time for fronting. Did the guide admit supplies do-support and parks the auxiliary before the subject. The path-closure admission is inverted correctly.

Keep this: at no point did + subject already places the auxiliary first.
**E) Rarely a quiet carriage stays quiet for the whole journey.**

Rarely opens a present-simple claim with no auxiliary moved or invented. A quiet carriage stays quiet keeps everyday order after the frequency negative. Add does: Rarely does a quiet carriage stay quiet for the whole journey.

Reject this; rewrite as "Rarely does a quiet carriage stay quiet for the whole journey."
tasks.solution_overview:
Most lines invert cleanly (under no circumstances, no sooner, at no point). The traps are not until without main-clause inversion and rarely without do-support - both classic exam misses in sports and travel wording.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not until + time clause → invert the main clause only. Be-verb inversion after under no circumstances needs no extra do. No sooner + had + than. At no point + did. Rarely + present simple → does/do.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate time-clause order from main-clause order for not until. For be, invert be itself; for present simple after rarely, invent does. Mark TRUE when the auxiliary already sits before the subject.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only by booking early can we secure seats near the stage.
No sooner had the parcel arrived when the courier rang again.

Never before has the festival sold out in a single morning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only by booking early can we secure seats near the stage.**

Only by booking early is a restrictive front with an -ing phrase. The main clause still must invert: can we secure shows that modal swap. Only by / only with / only through all behave this way.

That works: only by… can + subject correctly inverts the following clause.
**B) No sooner had the parcel arrived when the courier rang again.**

Had the parcel arrived looks perfect after no sooner, so the order scan can fool you. The linker is when, but no sooner always pairs with than. When belongs with hardly/scarcely/barely — swap it here.

Trap: correct had-inversion with the wrong correlative is a classic near-miss on mid-level papers.

Mark it wrong and prefer "No sooner had the parcel arrived than the courier rang again."
**C) Not only did traffic jam the bridge, but the tunnel closed as well.**

Not only did traffic jam the bridge already inverts with did. But… as well finishes the contrast in an acceptable parallel second half. Keep verb ideas balanced once the first half has inverted.

Accept the line: not only did… but… as well is inverted and complete.
**D) Under no circumstances should raw chicken sit on the worktop.**

Under no circumstances should raw chicken sit places the modal before the subject. Food-safety tone does not change the rule: expect should/must/will next after this opener. The inversion is already done.

Keep this: under no circumstances + should + subject already shows the modal swap.
**E) Never before has the festival sold out in a single morning.**

Never before behaves like never for present-perfect fronting. Has the festival sold out parks has before the subject and keeps the participle after it. Never before / never again follow that same perfect swap.

tasks.solution_overview:
Inversion is mostly done right across booking, traffic, food safety, and festival sell-outs. The subtle miss is the correlative after no sooner: word order can look perfect and still fail if than/when is swapped.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only by + phrase still forces main-clause inversion. No sooner pairs with than, not when. Not only + did + but… as well. Under no circumstances + modal. Never before behaves like never for present-perfect inversion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First confirm the auxiliary sits after the front. Then, for no sooner lines, check the linking word even if had is correctly placed. A wrong correlative alone is enough to mark FALSE.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly had the teacher finished speaking than phones started buzzing.

tactical_explanations:
**A) Hardly had the teacher finished speaking than phones started buzzing.**

Hardly had the teacher finished speaking already inverts past perfect correctly. The fail is the linker than — hardly takes when (or before), not than. Than is reserved for no sooner; swap it here even though word order looks polished.

Trap: perfect inversion with a borrowed no-sooner correlative is a high-yield exam miss.

That fails — rewrite as "Hardly had the teacher finished speaking when phones started buzzing."
**B) Not until the keys were found did the family leave the flat.**

Not until the keys were found leaves the time clause in normal order. Did the family leave supplies the main-clause inversion that follows. That split is the whole not-until rule.

Keep this: not until… did… inverts only the main clause, as taught.
**C) Seldom do neighbourhood shops stay open past midnight.**

Seldom do neighbourhood shops stay invents do-support for present simple. Frequency negatives need do/does/did when no other auxiliary exists, and do is already here. The midnight-opening claim is therefore clean.

Accept the line: seldom do + subject + base verb is already present-simple inversion.
**D) On no account the intern may unlock the storeroom alone.**

On no account fronts a prohibition, so the modal should come next. The intern may still keeps subject before may. Move the modal: On no account may the intern unlock the storeroom alone.

Trap: on no account looks formal enough that subject-modal order can feel "written," but it fails the inversion test.

Reject this near-miss; prefer "On no account may the intern unlock the storeroom alone."
**E) Little did the runners know a shortcut waited behind the hill.**

Little did the runners know is the stock restrictive template. Little meaning "not at all" fronts like a negative and takes did + subject + base verb. The shortcut line matches that pattern exactly.

That pairing is sound — little did + subject + base verb is the restrictive pattern.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two errors mix correlative choice (hardly… than) with missing modal inversion (on no account). Everyday classroom, keys, shops, storerooms, and runners - judge both word order and the linking word after the fronted phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hardly pairs with when, not than - even when had is correctly inverted. Not until + clause → did in the main clause. Seldom + do. On no account requires the modal before the subject. Little did… is the stock restrictive shape.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For hardly lines that already invert, still audit when vs than. For on no account, demand modal-subject swap. Mark TRUE only when both order and correlative (if any) are right.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**C) Scarcely had the guests sat down when dessert appeared.**

**D) Not only did the app crash, it also wiped the draft message.**

That order fails — rewrite as "Under no circumstances will the cleaner mix bleach with ammonia."
tasks.solution_overview:
Only after and under no circumstances still trap people who invert late or not at all. The other three already show the target shapes - nowhere else, scarcely, not only - for laundry, cherries, dessert, apps, and cleaning rules.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only after + time clause → invert the main clause (were/did before subject). Nowhere else + will. Scarcely had… when…. Not only did… with a continuing second clause. Under no circumstances + will before the subject.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**B) Rarely have gardens recovered so quickly after a late frost.**

**C) Not only was the suitcase heavy, but the zip was broken.**

Not only was the suitcase heavy inverts be itself after fronted not only. The but-clause keeps the contrast clear without needing do-support. With was/were, invert be and leave the second half parallel.

That works: not only was… but… is correctly inverted and continued.
**D) At no time were passengers told about the platform change.**

At no time were passengers told inverts be in a passive frame. At no time / at no point / at no stage are equivalent triggers for that swap. Passive voice does not cancel the inversion requirement.

This is sound — at no time + were + subject is clean be-inversion.
**E) Barely had the bakery opened when the first queue formed.**

Barely had the bakery opened when the first queue formed mirrors hardly. Had before the subject and when afterward are both required and both present. Barely equals hardly for inversion purposes.

tasks.solution_overview:
A clean model set: no sooner, rarely, not only, at no time, barely - curtains, gardens, luggage, platform announcements, bakery queues. If your own answers miss any of these shapes, rewrite the wrong ones to match these templates.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

No sooner + had + than. Rarely + present perfect (have/has + subject). Not only + was/were. At no time + were (be-inversion). Barely + had + when.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Every line should already show auxiliary before subject and the right correlative. Treat this task as a checklist: if anything fails that scan, you would mark FALSE - here none do.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only if the weather clears will the outdoor market go ahead.
The notice not only lists opening times but also warns about roadworks.
No sooner had breakfast ended than the day trip coaches arrived.
Hardly the ink had dried on the consent form when surgery was cancelled.
Under no circumstances are personal heaters permitted in the office.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only if the weather clears will the outdoor market go ahead.**

Only if the weather clears leaves the conditional clause in normal order. Will the outdoor market go inverts the main clause after that clause ends. Fronted only if still triggers the same main-clause swap as only when.

Accept the line: only if… will + subject correctly inverts the main clause.
**B) The notice not only lists opening times but also warns about roadworks.**

Here not only sits mid-sentence after the notice, not at the front. Mid-clause not only… but also keeps ordinary subject-verb order; inversion is not required. Lists and warns already show that normal pairing correctly.

**Tip:** Invert only when not only is fronted; mid-clause not only stays uninverted.

That works: mid-sentence not only… but also needs no inversion, and this line is fine.
**C) No sooner had breakfast ended than the day trip coaches arrived.**

No sooner had breakfast ended than the coaches arrived already inverts past perfect. Than is present and correct after no sooner. Confirm that linker every time — it is right here.

Keep this: no sooner + had + than is already complete.
**D) Hardly the ink had dried on the consent form when surgery was cancelled.**

Hardly fronts the consent-form line, but the ink still precedes had. Past perfect after hardly must place had before the subject, then the participle. Repair: Hardly had the ink dried on the consent form when surgery was cancelled.

Trap: when is correct, so the correlative looks fine while the missing had-before-subject is the real fail.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Hardly had the ink dried on the consent form when surgery was cancelled."
**E) Under no circumstances are personal heaters permitted in the office.**

Under no circumstances are personal heaters permitted inverts be after the policy opener. Are precedes the subject; no extra do is needed with a be-main verb. Notices and office rules often use exactly this shape.

This is sound: under no circumstances + are + subject already shows be-inversion.
tasks.solution_overview:
The sophistication here is knowing when not to invert: mid-clause not only… but also is fine without a swap. The only hard fail is hardly without had-before-subject - markets, notices, coaches, consent forms, and office policy mixed together.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only if + clause → invert the main clause. Mid-sentence not only… but also keeps normal order. No sooner… than with had. Hardly needs had before the subject. Under no circumstances + are (be-inversion).

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask first whether not only is fronted or mid-clause. Mid-clause → no inversion required. Fronted negatives → demand the auxiliary. Hardly without had before the subject is an automatic FALSE.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until did the plumber fix the leak the floorboards were dry.
In no circumstances should leftover rice sit out overnight.
Seldom has a village fete drawn such a crowd in midweek.
No longer the tram line serves the old factory estate.
Only after did the museum reopen were tickets put on sale.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Not until did the plumber fix the leak the floorboards were dry.**

Did has been jammed into the not-until clause itself: Not until did the plumber…. The time clause must stay normal; only the following main clause inverts. Repair by restoring normal past in the time clause and inverting the main clause: Not until the plumber fixed the leak were the floorboards dry.

Trap: seeing did anywhere after not until can feel like "inversion done," but the auxiliary must sit in the main clause, not inside the time clause.

That fails — prefer "Not until the plumber fixed the leak were the floorboards dry."
**B) In no circumstances should leftover rice sit out overnight.**

In no circumstances should leftover rice sit pulls should before the subject. In / under no circumstances are interchangeable for this modal swap. The food-safety line already shows question order after the opener.

Accept the line: in no circumstances + should + subject is correctly inverted.
**C) Seldom has a village fete drawn such a crowd in midweek.**

Seldom has a village fete drawn inverts present perfect after a frequency negative. Has precedes the subject; drawn is the past participle that follows. Frequency negative and perfect auxiliary line up.

Keep this: seldom has + subject + past participle already places the auxiliary first.
**D) No longer the tram line serves the old factory estate.**

No longer opens the tram line claim, but the subject still comes next with no do-support. Present simple after no longer needs does/do before the subject and a base verb after it. Rewrite as No longer does the tram line serve the old factory estate.

Reject this; rewrite as "No longer does the tram line serve the old factory estate."
**E) Only after did the museum reopen were tickets put on sale.**

Only after did the museum reopen wrongly inverts inside the time clause. Keep Only after the museum reopened in normal order, then invert the main clause alone. The sale-of-tickets clause should lead with were: Only after the museum reopened were tickets put on sale.

Trap: same misfire as not until did… — auxiliary glued to the time clause instead of the main clause.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Only after the museum reopened were tickets put on sale."
tasks.solution_overview:
Advanced traps put the auxiliary in the wrong clause (not until / only after). Remember: the time or condition clause stays normal; the following main clause inverts. Also watch missing do-support after no longer.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not until / only after: never put did inside the time clause - invert the main clause only. In no circumstances = under no circumstances for modal inversion. Seldom + present perfect. No longer + present simple → does/do.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see Not until did… or Only after did… glued to the time clause, mark FALSE. Re-attach the auxiliary to the main clause. For no longer without does, invent do-support.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not only did the soup burn, but the bread went stale as well.
Scarcely had the rehearsal ended than the costume call began.
Never again will the club host fireworks without a fire marshal.
Little does the neighbourhood appreciate how quiet the park becomes at dusk.
Under no circumstances the lifeguard may leave the pool unattended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Not only did the soup burn, but the bread went stale as well.**

Not only did the soup burn correctly invents did after fronted not only. But the bread went stale as well finishes the contrast acceptably. But also and but… as well both work once the first half inverts.

That pairing is sound — not only did… but… as well is inverted and balanced.
**B) Scarcely had the rehearsal ended than the costume call began.**

Scarcely had the rehearsal ended already places had correctly. The fail is than: scarcely/hardly/barely take when, while than belongs with no sooner. Swap the linker even though the inversion looks exam-ready.

Trap: right had-order plus a no-sooner correlative is a polished-looking false.

That correlative fails — rewrite as "Scarcely had the rehearsal ended when the costume call began."
**C) Never again will the club host fireworks without a fire marshal.**

Never again will the club host places will before the subject. Never again / never before behave like never for inversion after the front. The fireworks rule already shows that modal swap.

Keep this: never again will + subject already shows modal inversion.
**D) Little does the neighbourhood appreciate how quiet the park becomes at dusk.**

Little does the neighbourhood appreciate invents do-support for present simple. Little meaning "not at all" fronts like a negative and takes does/do + subject + base verb. The dusk-park line matches the usual template.

Accept the line: little does + subject + base verb is the present restrictive pattern.
**E) Under no circumstances the lifeguard may leave the pool unattended.**

Under no circumstances fronts the pool rule, so a modal should follow immediately. The lifeguard may still keeps subject before may. Move the modal: Under no circumstances may the lifeguard leave the pool unattended.

Trap: may already feels careful and formal, which hides the missing modal-before-subject swap.

Reject this; prefer "Under no circumstances may the lifeguard leave the pool unattended."
tasks.solution_overview:
Inversion looks right on the scarcely line, but the correlative is wrong. Pair that check with the modal-order miss on under no circumstances - soup, rehearsals, fireworks, a quiet park, and pool safety.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not only + did + but… as well. Scarcely takes when, not than. Never again + will. Little + does. Under no circumstances needs the modal before the subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Audit correlatives on scarcely/hardly/barely even when had is correct. Audit modal placement after under no circumstances even when the rest of the sentence looks polished. Either failure is enough for FALSE.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only when the Wi-Fi returned did the online class continue.
No sooner the suitcase was packed than the taxi horn sounded.
At no stage were residents told about the water shut-off.
Rarely do we publish the newsletter without a photo gallery.
Not only the soundtrack disappointed; the plot disappointed too.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only when the Wi-Fi returned did the online class continue.**

Only when the Wi-Fi returned keeps normal order inside the time clause. Did the online class continue inverts the main clause once that clause ends. Main-clause inversion only is the whole only-when check.

Keep this: only when… did… rightly inverts the main clause alone.
**B) No sooner the suitcase was packed than the taxi horn sounded.**

No sooner is followed by the suitcase was packed — subject right after the opener. After no sooner the next word should be was/were/had, not the subject. Invert: No sooner was the suitcase packed than the taxi horn sounded.

Trap: than is already correct, so the correlative can distract from the missing inversion.

Mark it wrong and prefer "No sooner was the suitcase packed than the taxi horn sounded."
**C) At no stage were residents told about the water shut-off.**

At no stage were residents told inverts be in the passive after a negative time phrase. At no stage / at no point / at no time are equivalent triggers. Were before the subject is exactly what the frame needs.

Accept the line: at no stage + were + subject is already be-inverted.
**D) Rarely do we publish the newsletter without a photo gallery.**

Rarely do we publish invents do for present simple after a frequency negative. There is no other auxiliary to move, so do before we is the required invention. The newsletter line already shows that shape.

That works: rarely do + subject + base verb is present-simple inversion done right.
**E) Not only the soundtrack disappointed; the plot disappointed too.**

Not only leads the sentence, but the soundtrack disappointed stays subject-first. Fronted not only still needs did/does/do before the subject even if a second half echoes the idea. Repair: Not only did the soundtrack disappoint; the plot disappointed too.

Trap: a parallel second clause ("the plot… too") can feel complete while the opener still lacks inversion.

That fails — rewrite as "Not only did the soundtrack disappoint; the plot disappointed too."
tasks.solution_overview:
Two failures omit inversion after no sooner and not only. The survivors show only when, at no stage, and rarely done properly - Wi-Fi classes, packing, shut-offs, newsletters, and soundtracks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only when + clause → did in the main clause. No sooner requires inversion of be/had immediately after it. At no stage + were. Rarely + do. Fronted not only needs did/does before the subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If no sooner or not only is glued to a bare subject, mark FALSE and invent or move the auxiliary. Mirror the three correct lines for the working templates.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not until the fridge was emptied the movers wheeled it downstairs.
Under no circumstances may allergy medication be shared between guests.
Seldom has a community garden produced such a crop of tomatoes.
Only by rearranging the furniture can the sofa fit through the door.
Hardly had the babysitter arrived than the toddler woke up crying.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Not until the fridge was emptied the movers wheeled it downstairs.**

Not until the fridge was emptied is fine as a time clause. The movers wheeled still keeps subject-verb order in the main clause. Invert with did: Not until the fridge was emptied did the movers wheel it downstairs.

Trap: a clean not-until opener can mask a main clause that never inverted.

Reject this near-miss; prefer "Not until the fridge was emptied did the movers wheel it downstairs."
**B) Under no circumstances may allergy medication be shared between guests.**

Under no circumstances may allergy medication be shared parks may before the subject. After this phrase, expect may/will/should next — and may is correctly placed. Policy English still follows ordinary modal inversion.

Keep this: under no circumstances + may + subject already parks the modal first.
**C) Seldom has a community garden produced such a crop of tomatoes.**

Seldom has a community garden produced inverts present perfect after the frequency negative. Has precedes the subject; produced is the past participle that follows. That is the standard seldom + perfect shape.

Accept the line: seldom has + subject + past participle is correctly inverted.
**D) Only by rearranging the furniture can the sofa fit through the door.**

Only by rearranging the furniture leaves the -ing phrase as written. Can the sofa fit then inverts the main clause with the modal before the subject. Only by / only with / only through all trigger that following-clause swap.

That works: only by… can + subject correctly inverts the main clause.
**E) Hardly had the babysitter arrived than the toddler woke up crying.**

Hardly had the babysitter arrived already inverts past perfect correctly. Than is wrong after hardly — the correlative must be when. A polished had-swap still fails if the linker is borrowed from no sooner.

Trap: top-band items often pass the order scan and fail only on when vs than.

Mark it wrong and rewrite as "Hardly had the babysitter arrived when the toddler woke up crying."
tasks.solution_overview:
Top-band items stay inside negative/restrictive inversion: not until, under no circumstances, seldom, only by, hardly. Judge each line by whether the auxiliary moved - and whether than/when is the right partner.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Not until → invert the main clause. Under no circumstances + may. Seldom + present perfect. Only by + -ing → modal inversion in the main clause. Hardly + had still fails if than replaces when.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Run two passes: (1) auxiliary before subject after every fronted trigger; (2) correlative audit on hardly/no sooner. A line can pass pass one and still fail pass two.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Under no circumstances is smoking permitted near the playground.
No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore.
Not only were tickets refunded, but free drinks were offered as well.
Seldom does a weekday market feel this crowded before noon.
Little did neighbours expect the street party to last past midnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Under no circumstances is smoking permitted near the playground.**

Under no circumstances is smoking permitted inverts be after the policy opener. Is precedes smoking; no extra do is needed when be carries the sentence. Use this as a clean be-inversion model.

This is sound: under no circumstances + is + subject is clean be-inversion.
**B) No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore.**

No sooner had the ferry docked than foot passengers streamed ashore is exact. Had before the subject and than afterward remain the gold standard. Both pieces are present.

Keep this: no sooner + had + subject + than is already complete.
**C) Not only were tickets refunded, but free drinks were offered as well.**

Not only were tickets refunded inverts were after fronted not only. The but… as well half completes the contrast with parallel passive ideas. With were/was, invert be and skip do-support.

Accept the line: not only were… but… as well is correctly inverted and paired.
**D) Seldom does a weekday market feel this crowded before noon.**

Seldom does a weekday market feel invents does for present simple. Frequency negative + does/do + subject + base verb is the everyday template. The crowded-market line matches it.

That works: seldom does + subject + base verb is present-simple inversion in place.
**E) Little did neighbours expect the street party to last past midnight.**

Little did neighbours expect is classic restrictive inversion. Little meaning "not at all" fronts like a negative and takes did + subject + base verb. Store the shape as a production model.

Keep this: little did + subject + base verb already shows the restrictive swap.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are model answers across the core triggers - playground rules, ferries, ticket refunds, weekday markets, and street parties. Treat this task as a checklist of shapes you should be able to produce under exam pressure.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Under no circumstances + is (be). No sooner + had + than. Not only + were + but. Seldom + does. Little + did. Every line should already show the auxiliary immediately after the front.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each opener, confirm the swap, confirm any correlative. With no misses in this set, every statement is TRUE - store them as production models.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Only after the gym closed members were allowed to collect belongings.
Not until the vet confirmed the results did the owners relax.
Barely had the campsite been booked when a storm warning arrived.
On no account should unfinished cakes leave the kitchen counter.
Never the caretaker had unlocked every classroom before dawn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Only after the gym closed members were allowed to collect belongings.**

Only after the gym closed is a normal time clause. Members were allowed still keeps subject-first order in the main clause. Invert be: Only after the gym closed were members allowed to collect belongings.

Trap: only after can look finished at the comma while the main clause never flips.

That order fails — prefer "Only after the gym closed were members allowed to collect belongings."
**B) Not until the vet confirmed the results did the owners relax.**

Not until the vet confirmed the results keeps normal order in the time clause. Did the owners relax supplies the required main-clause inversion. Time clause normal, main clause inverted — both halves are right.

Accept the line: not until… did… inverts only the main clause, as required.
**C) Barely had the campsite been booked when a storm warning arrived.**

Barely had the campsite been booked when… inverts had even in passive past perfect. When matches barely/hardly as the correlative. Been booked stays after the subject once had has moved left.

Keep this: barely had… when… is correctly formed even in the passive.
**D) On no account should unfinished cakes leave the kitchen counter.**

On no account should unfinished cakes leave parks should before the subject. On no account and under no circumstances share that modal-before-subject rule. The kitchen prohibition already follows it.

This is sound — on no account + should + subject already shows the modal swap.
**E) Never the caretaker had unlocked every classroom before dawn.**

Never fronts the caretaker line, but the caretaker still precedes had. Never + past perfect needs Never had + subject + past participle. Move had left: Never had the caretaker unlocked every classroom before dawn.

Trap: past perfect content is present, so the line can feel "advanced" while subject-before-had remains wrong.

Reject this; rewrite as "Never had the caretaker unlocked every classroom before dawn."
tasks.solution_overview:
Two lines forget to invert after only after and never. The others show not until, barely, and on no account in full working order - gym closing, vet results, campsite booking, kitchen rules, and dawn unlocks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Only after + clause → invert the main clause. Not until… did…. Barely had… when… (including passive past perfect). On no account + should. Never + past perfect → Never had + subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Jump to the main clause after only after / not until and demand the auxiliary first. After never + past perfect, demand had before the subject. Match the three correct templates to the two repairs.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention the Monday trail closure.
Not only did the hostel refill the kettle, but it also left fresh towels.
Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on.
Under no circumstances the landlord will enter without written notice.
No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention the Monday trail closure.**

Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does it mention correctly inverts after a negative place adverbial. Does follows the nowhere phrase and precedes the subject. Nowhere / no place at the front always demand that auxiliary swap.

Accept the line: nowhere… does + subject is already in question-style order.
**B) Not only did the hostel refill the kettle, but it also left fresh towels.**

Not only did the hostel refill the kettle already invents did after the front. But it also left fresh towels keeps the second half parallel. Match verb forms across both halves of not only / but also — and both halves do.

Keep this: not only did… but also… is inverted and parallel.
**C) Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on.**

Hardly had the blackout ended when the street lights flickered back on is standard. Had before the subject and when afterward are both required and both present. Do not borrow than from the no-sooner pair.

That pairing is sound — hardly had… when… is correctly linked.
**D) Under no circumstances the landlord will enter without written notice.**

Under no circumstances opens the landlord notice, so will should come next. The landlord will still keeps subject before the modal. Final checklist on this opener: modal, then subject — Under no circumstances will the landlord enter without written notice.

Trap: legal-sounding under no circumstances… will enter can still fail if the subject sits before will.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Under no circumstances will the landlord enter without written notice."
**E) No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up.**

No sooner had the suitcases been labelled than the taxi pulled up closes the set cleanly. Passive past perfect still inverts had before the subject. Than after no sooner seals the correlative.

This is sound: no sooner had… than… is complete, including passive past perfect.
highlights: Nowhere in the hiking leaflet does
tasks.solution_overview:
Four model inversions and one classic miss: under no circumstances without modal-subject swap. Hiking leaflets, hostel service, blackouts, landlord notice, and labelled suitcases wrap the final checklist.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Nowhere… does…. Not only did… but also…. Hardly had… when…. Under no circumstances → will before the subject. No sooner had… than….

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you catch the under-no-circumstances pattern every time - modal before subject - this topic is exam-ready. Use the four true lines as production models and fix the one order miss the same way.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Walking through the market, the spices smelled amazing.
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena carried the fragile vase home.
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers set out before dawn.
Burned on one side, the toast still tasted fine with jam.
Running late for practice, the gym bag was left by the door.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Walking through the market, the spices smelled amazing.**

As written, the -ing opener attaches to "the spices," so the sentence claims the spices were walking through the market. A participial opener must modify the grammatical subject that follows the comma, and that subject has to be who really did the walking. Name the walker first: "Walking through the market, we noticed that the spices smelled amazing."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Walking through the market, we noticed that the spices smelled amazing."

**B) Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena carried the fragile vase home.**

"Packed carefully in tissue paper" currently modifies "Lena," as if Lena herself had been wrapped. The fragile vase is what was packed; Lena is merely the carrier. Put the object that was packed next: "Packed carefully in tissue paper, the vase travelled home with Lena."

That packing opener fails on Lena — rewrite as "Packed carefully in tissue paper, the vase travelled home with Lena."

**C) Hoping for clear skies, the hikers set out before dawn.**

The hikers hoped for clear skies, and "the hikers" is exactly the subject that follows the comma. The same people who hope are the ones setting out, so the -ing opener attaches cleanly. No dangling modifier here — agent and subject match.

Keep this: the hikers both hope for clear skies and set out, so the -ing phrase attaches cleanly.

**D) Burned on one side, the toast still tasted fine with jam.**

The toast was burned on one side, and "the toast" is the subject that follows. Past participles often describe a state of whatever comes next, which is the natural reading here. The jam detail is narrative colour; the grammar already works.

Accept the line: "Burned on one side" names the toast’s state before it tastes fine with jam.

**E) Running late for practice, the gym bag was left by the door.**

An -ing opener about being late wants a person (or other agent) as subject, not an inanimate bag. As written, the gym bag appears to be running late while somehow also being left by the door. Rewrite with the athlete first: "Running late for practice, she left the gym bag by the door."

Reject the gym-bag subject; the clean version is "Running late for practice, she left the gym bag by the door."
highlights: Walking through the market, the spices
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers
Burned on one side, the toast
Running late for practice, the gym bag
tasks.solution_overview:
Participial openers can make everyday scenes (markets, toast, gym bags) feel vivid — and they also create classic dangling-modifier traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

A participial phrase at the start of the sentence (-ing or -ed) is meant to describe the grammatical subject that comes right after the comma. If spices walk through a market or a gym bag runs late, the opener has attached to the wrong noun. Past participles (burned, packed) often describe a state; present participles (walking, hoping, running) usually describe an action someone is doing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask: who or what is really doing or undergoing the participle? That answer must be the subject of the main clause. When the subject fails the test, the sentence is false — rewrite by naming the logical doer first.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tired after the long flight, Maya collapsed onto the sofa.
Covered in mud after the match, the boots needed a thorough scrub.
Having lost the map, the trail suddenly seemed endless.
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma filled the kitchen.
Excited about the museum trip, the children packed their sketchbooks.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tired after the long flight, Maya collapsed onto the sofa.**

Maya was tired after the long flight, and she is the subject right after the comma. Adjective-like past participles still need that matching subject — here the match is exact. Collapsing onto the sofa is a natural next action for that tired traveller.

That works — tired Maya is exactly who collapses onto the sofa.

**B) Covered in mud after the match, the boots needed a thorough scrub.**

The boots were covered in mud, and "the boots" is the subject — a clean condition-of-a-thing attachment. Nothing wrongly claims a person is muddy, because no person sits in the subject slot. When the participle names a thing’s condition, that thing should follow the comma.

This is sound: the muddy covering belongs to the boots that need scrubbing.

**C) Having lost the map, the trail suddenly seemed endless.**

"Having + past participle" still requires the logical agent as the subject of the main clause. The trail did not lose the map; the hikers did. Repair: "Having lost the map, the hikers found that the trail suddenly seemed endless."

**Trap:** "Having lost…" looks polished, but trails and paths cannot be the lost-map agents.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Having lost the map, the hikers found that the trail suddenly seemed endless."

**D) Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma filled the kitchen.**

An aroma cannot stir soup; the cook who is stirring is missing from the subject slot. Active -ing openers need a person (or agent) who performs that action. Rewrite: "Stirring the soup slowly, the cook noticed a rich aroma filling the kitchen."

That aroma cannot stir soup — rewrite as "Stirring the soup slowly, the cook noticed a rich aroma filling the kitchen."

**E) Excited about the museum trip, the children packed their sketchbooks.**

The children were excited about the museum trip, and they are the subject packing the sketchbooks. Emotion adjectives built from participles belong with people, not with sketchbooks or museums. Here the attachment is clean: the excited children do the packing.

Accept the line: the excited children are the ones packing the sketchbooks.
highlights: Tired after the long flight, Maya
Covered in mud after the match, the boots
Having lost the map, the trail
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma
Excited about the museum trip, the children
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes tired/excited states, muddy boots, and "having + past participle" forms with a couple of active -ing traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Past participles and emotion adjectives (tired, covered, excited) still need a matching subject: the person who is tired, or the thing that is covered. "Having lost…" and "Stirring…" look polished, but they still demand the logical agent next — trails and aromas cannot lose maps or stir soup.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the agent of the opener, then check that it appears as the subject after the comma. Condition-of-a-thing participles belong with that thing; intentional actions belong with people (or other agents).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Looking out the train window, the countryside rushed past in a blur.
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar ducked under a café awning.
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card was hard to read.
Waiting for the ferry, seagulls circled above the pier.
Finished with homework, Priya started a new puzzle.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Looking out the train window, the countryside rushed past in a blur.**

Sight and perception -ing phrases almost always need a person as subject. The countryside was not looking out the window; the passenger was. Repair: "Looking out the train window, I watched the countryside rush past in a blur."

Reject countryside-as-looker; prefer "Looking out the train window, I watched the countryside rush past in a blur."

**B) Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar ducked under a café awning.**

Omar was soaked by the sudden shower, and "Omar" follows the comma — correct attachment. Past participles like soaked, drenched, or frozen naturally modify the person who got wet. Ducking under the awning is a sensible next move for that soaked subject.

Keep this: soaked Omar is the right subject under the café awning.

**C) Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card was hard to read.**

The recipe card was written in tiny handwriting, so the past participle describes the card itself. This is the passive sense of the participle pointing at the object that was written. Hard to read or not, the grammar is clean.

That pairing is sound — "Written in tiny handwriting" correctly describes the recipe card.

**D) Waiting for the ferry, seagulls circled above the pier.**

Seagulls were not waiting for the ferry; the travellers were. Location scenes tempt dangling openers because wildlife is already in the shot — still check who waited. Repair: "Waiting for the ferry, we watched seagulls circle above the pier."

**Trap:** Scenery subjects after a waiting -ing phrase look atmospheric but usually dangle.

That ferry-wait opener fails on seagulls — rewrite as "Waiting for the ferry, we watched seagulls circle above the pier."

**E) Finished with homework, Priya started a new puzzle.**

Priya finished her homework, and "Finished with homework" correctly modifies her. The pattern works when the subject is the person who finished, then moves on to the next activity. Starting a puzzle is a clean follow-on for that subject.

This is sound: Priya finished the homework and then starts the puzzle.
highlights: Looking out the train window, the countryside
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card
tasks.solution_overview:
Travel and home scenes still obey one attachment rule: the participle’s logical subject must be the sentence subject.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Sight and waiting openers (-ing) almost always need a person. Passive-feeling past participles (soaked, written, finished) often describe what happened to the subject — Omar, a recipe card, Priya. Landscape and wildlife after an -ing opener are frequent danglers.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the subject can literally look, wait, be soaked, be written, or finish homework. If the countryside is "looking" or seagulls are "waiting for the ferry," mark false and reattach the opener to the traveller.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having packed the tent, the campsite looked ready for the night.
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans urged the team forward.
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough rose beautifully.
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze turned the pages.
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed stood out among the trees.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having packed the tent, the campsite looked ready for the night.**

"Having packed…" always needs the packer as subject. The campsite did not pack the tent; the campers did. Repair: "Having packed the tent, we thought the campsite looked ready for the night."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Having packed the tent, we thought the campsite looked ready for the night."

**B) Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans urged the team forward.**

The fans were cheering loudly from the stands, and they are the subject who urge the team forward. Crowd actions belong with people subjects, not with the score or the pitch. Agent and subject match, so the attachment is clean.

Keep this: the cheering fans are also the ones urging the team forward.

**C) Left overnight in the fridge, the dough rose beautifully.**

The dough was left overnight in the fridge, so the past participle modifies "the dough" that then rose. Food-prep sentences often use past participles for what happened to the ingredient. Here the fridge overnight stay and the rising belong to the same subject.

Accept the line: the dough left overnight is what then rises beautifully.

**D) Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze turned the pages.**

A breeze does not read on the balcony; the reader is missing from the subject slot. If the opener is an intentional human action, the subject must be someone who can perform it. Repair: "Reading on the balcony, she felt a cool breeze turn the pages."

That breeze cannot read — rewrite as "Reading on the balcony, she felt a cool breeze turn the pages."

**E) Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed stood out among the trees.**

The garden shed was painted bright yellow last spring, and that shed is the subject. "Painted/repaired/built…" usually modifies the object that received the action. No dangling modifier — the shed both received the paint and stands out among the trees.

This is sound: the shed painted bright yellow is what stands out among the trees.
highlights: Having packed the tent, the campsite
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed
tasks.solution_overview:
Camping, sports, kitchen prep, and a garden shed: same participle test, everyday props.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having packed…" needs the packer. Crowd -ing openers need fans or people. Past participles on dough or a shed (left overnight, painted) correctly modify those objects. A breeze that "reads" is a classic intentional-action dangler.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate human actions from object states. If the opener is something a person does on purpose, the subject must be that person; if it describes what was done to an object, that object should follow the comma.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Jogging along the canal path, Sam spotted a heron in the reeds.
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film felt twice as cosy.
Having trained all week, the final whistle still came as a shock.
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions sweetened the sauce.
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light cast long shadows.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Jogging along the canal path, Sam spotted a heron in the reeds.**

Sam was jogging along the canal path and spotted a heron — the same person does both actions. When one agent performs the opener and the main verb, an -ing opener is usually safe. Here the match is exact, so the participial phrase attaches cleanly.

That works — Sam jogs the path and spots the heron in one clean attachment.

**B) Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film felt twice as cosy.**

The film was not wrapped in a thick blanket; the viewer was. Comfort and clothing participles modify people or bodies, not the entertainment on screen. Repair: "Wrapped in a thick blanket, we found the film twice as cosy."

**Trap:** Cosy film + blanket opener feels natural until you check who was wrapped.

Reject film-as-wrapped; prefer "Wrapped in a thick blanket, we found the film twice as cosy."

**C) Having trained all week, the final whistle still came as a shock.**

"Having trained…" must be followed by the athlete or team, not by a result or signal. The final whistle did not train all week. Repair: "Having trained all week, the players still found the final whistle a shock."

**Trap:** Sports results after "having trained" look related but cannot be the training agent.

That whistle did not train — rewrite as "Having trained all week, the players still found the final whistle a shock."

**D) Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions sweetened the sauce.**

The onions were chopped finely and fried gently, so stacked past participles modify the ingredient. Cooking sequences often use this pattern before the food noun that then does something in the main clause. Here the onions both receive the prep and sweeten the sauce.

Keep this: the chopped and fried onions are what sweeten the sauce.

**E) Standing in the doorway, the hallway light cast long shadows.**

Posture verbs (standing, sitting, leaning) need a person or object that can hold that pose. The hallway light was not standing in the doorway. Repair: "Standing in the doorway, she watched the hallway light cast long shadows."

Flag the dangling light; the clean version is "Standing in the doorway, she watched the hallway light cast long shadows."
highlights: Jogging along the canal path, Sam
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film
Having trained all week, the final whistle
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light
tasks.solution_overview:
Difficulty steps up: some wrong lines sound natural until you ask who wrapped, trained, or stood.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When the same person does both the opener and the main verb (jogging + spotting), -ing is usually safe. Comfort/clothing and "having trained" must stay with people, not films or whistles. Cooking past participles stack cleanly before the ingredient. Posture verbs need a body that can hold the pose.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check agent match first, then whether an abstract result (whistle, hallway light) has stolen the subject slot. Only Sam and the onions keep a clean logical pairing here.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks were easy to find.
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath needed warm water.
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina practised against the garage wall.
Filled with fresh berries, Tom carried the bowl to the picnic table.
Turning the page slowly, the mystery finally made sense.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks were easy to find.**

Time-of-arrival openers need a person as subject, not the place or the furniture. Quiet study desks did not arrive early; the student did. Repair: "Arriving early at the library, she found quiet study desks easy to claim."

Mark it wrong and prefer "Arriving early at the library, she found quiet study desks easy to claim."

**B) Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath needed warm water.**

The birdbath was frozen solid after the cold night, so the past participle describes that object. Weather effects on outdoor objects are natural past-participle modifiers. Needing warm water is a sensible consequence for that frozen subject.

Accept the line: frozen solid correctly names the birdbath that needs warm water.

**C) Hoping to improve her serve, Nina practised against the garage wall.**

Nina hoped to improve her serve, and she practised — purpose/hope -ing phrases want the person with that goal. The attachment here is exact: the same person hopes and practises. Garage-wall drills are colour; the grammar already works.

This is sound: Nina both hopes to improve her serve and practises against the wall.

**D) Filled with fresh berries, Tom carried the bowl to the picnic table.**

"Filled/loaded/packed with…" modifies the container, not the person carrying it. Tom was not filled with fresh berries; the bowl was. Repair: "Filled with fresh berries, the bowl went with Tom to the picnic table."

**Trap:** Carrier-versus-container is a classic mix-up when someone carries a filled bowl.

That filled-with opener lands on Tom, not the bowl — rewrite as "Filled with fresh berries, the bowl went with Tom to the picnic table."

**E) Turning the page slowly, the mystery finally made sense.**

Reading actions belong with the reader, not with "the mystery." The mystery did not turn the page. Repair: "Turning the page slowly, she finally made sense of the mystery."

Reject mystery-as-page-turner; prefer "Turning the page slowly, she finally made sense of the mystery."
highlights: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina
Turning the page slowly, the mystery
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch container versus carrier, and arrival versus furniture — two of the most common participial mix-ups.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Time-of-arrival openers need a person, not desks. Weather past participles on objects (frozen birdbath) are fine. Hope/purpose -ing belongs with the athlete who hopes. "Filled with…" modifies the bowl, not Tom carrying it. Page-turning needs a reader, not "the mystery."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each opener, decide: person acting, or object in a state? Then verify the noun after the comma matches that role. Shuffle roles and you get a dangler even if the scene still "makes sense" narratively.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having watered the plants, the windowsill looked bright again.
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we missed the opening kick-off.
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough became smooth and elastic.
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence settled over the group.
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map lasted the rest of the hike.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having watered the plants, the windowsill looked bright again.**

"Having watered…" requires the gardener as subject before you praise how bright the sill looked. The windowsill did not water the plants. Repair: "Having watered the plants, she noticed the windowsill looking bright again."

That windowsill did not water anything — rewrite as "Having watered the plants, she noticed the windowsill looking bright again."

**B) Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we missed the opening kick-off.**

We were stuck in traffic near the stadium, and "we" is the subject who then missed kick-off. "Stuck/caught/trapped…" with a human subject is a common correct pattern. The opener and the missed kick-off share the same people.

Keep this: the same we who were stuck in traffic also missed kick-off.

**C) Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough became smooth and elastic.**

The bread dough was kneaded for ten minutes, and that dough is the subject that became smooth. Baking steps as past participles usually modify the dough, batter, or loaf. Smooth and elastic is what that kneaded subject becomes.

That pairing is sound — kneaded dough is what becomes smooth and elastic.

**D) Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence settled over the group.**

Abstract subjects (silence, calm, tension) rarely perform -ing actions in openers. Silence was not watching the sunset; the hikers were. Repair: "Watching the sunset from the ridge, the group fell into silence."

**Trap:** Mood nouns after scenic -ing openers feel literary but almost always dangle.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Watching the sunset from the ridge, the group fell into silence."

**E) Repaired with strong tape, the torn map lasted the rest of the hike.**

The torn map was repaired with strong tape, so the past participle modifies the map. "Repaired/mended/patched…" modifies the damaged object that then survives the hike. Attachment and meaning line up cleanly.

Accept the line: the tape-repaired map is what lasted the rest of the hike.
highlights: Having watered the plants, the windowsill
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map
tasks.solution_overview:
Home gardening, traffic, baking, ridgelines, and trail maps recycle the same attachment test.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having watered…" needs the gardener. "Stuck in traffic…" with "we" is a clean human-state pattern. Kneaded dough and a repaired map take past participles naturally. Abstract nouns like "silence" almost never perform watching or similar -ing actions.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask who did the -ing/-ed action, then insist that noun is the subject. Furniture and mood nouns after active openers are nearly always false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration proved difficult.
Dried on the washing line, the sheets smelled of sunshine.
Having booked the earliest train, Lara reached the coast by noon.
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk needed clearing.
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium erupted in cheers.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration proved difficult.**

Result nouns (concentration, success, fatigue) cannot be the agent of the opener. Concentration did not skip breakfast; the student did. Repair: "Skipping breakfast before the exam, she found concentration difficult."

**Trap:** Abstract result subjects after a human -ing opener are a frequent near-miss.

Reject abstract concentration as breakfast-skipper; prefer "Skipping breakfast before the exam, she found concentration difficult."

**B) Dried on the washing line, the sheets smelled of sunshine.**

The sheets were dried on the washing line, and they are the subject smelling of sunshine. "Dried/hung/aired…" naturally modifies laundry or similar objects. The attachment is exact.

This is sound: the sheets dried on the line are what smell of sunshine.

**C) Having booked the earliest train, Lara reached the coast by noon.**

Lara booked the earliest train, so "Having booked…" correctly modifies her. Travel logistics with "having + past participle" need the traveller as subject. Reaching the coast by noon follows from that same traveller.

Keep this: Lara booked the earliest train and reached the coast by noon.

**D) Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk needed clearing.**

The desk was cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, so the past participle matches that surface. "Cluttered/covered/littered with…" modifies the space, not a person walking by. Needing clearing is the right consequence for that cluttered subject.

That works — the cluttered desk is exactly what needed clearing.

**E) Scoring the winning goal, the stadium erupted in cheers.**

Sports highlights often dangle when the venue follows a player’s action. The stadium did not score the winning goal; the player did. Repair: "Scoring the winning goal, the striker watched the stadium erupt in cheers."

**Trap:** Venue subjects after scoring openers look vivid but assign the goal to the ground.

That stadium did not score — rewrite as "Scoring the winning goal, the striker watched the stadium erupt in cheers."
highlights: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration
Dried on the washing line, the sheets
Having booked the earliest train, Lara
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium
tasks.solution_overview:
Study habits, laundry, travel booking, a cluttered desk, and a stadium goal — three attachments succeed, two fail loudly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Result nouns (concentration) cannot skip breakfast. Laundry past participles modify the sheets. "Having booked…" needs the traveller. "Cluttered with…" modifies the desk. Sports action openers need the player, not the venue that erupts afterward.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject subjects that are effects, places, or venues when the opener describes a human action. Accept object-state participles only when the subject truly carries that state.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea sounded irresistible.
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes were unusually sweet.
Having finished the crossword, Eli started a new novel.
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote finally turned up.
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps flickered on one by one.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea sounded irresistible.**

Sensory desires as subjects after bodily -ing phrases usually create danglers. Hot tea was not shivering in the queue. Repair: "Shivering in the queue for tickets, we found hot tea irresistible."

**Trap:** Desire-as-subject after a cold-person opener is a classic mid-level dangler.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Shivering in the queue for tickets, we found hot tea irresistible."

**B) Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes were unusually sweet.**

The tomatoes were grown in the neighbour’s garden, so the past participle modifies the produce. "Grown/picked/harvested…" attaches to the crop that then tastes sweet. Agent and subject match.

Accept the line: the garden-grown tomatoes are what taste unusually sweet.

**C) Having finished the crossword, Eli started a new novel.**

Eli finished the crossword, and "Having finished…" attaches clearly to him. "Having finished X" plus a person subject is a reliable non-dangling pattern. Starting a novel is the natural next action for that same person.

This is sound: Eli finished the crossword and then starts a new novel.

**D) Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote finally turned up.**

The remote was hidden behind the sofa cushions, so the past participle fits the lost-and-found item. Household finds often take "hidden/buried/tucked…" before the object recovered. "Finally turned up" completes that same subject cleanly.

Keep this: the remote hidden behind the cushions is what finally turned up.

**E) Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps flickered on one by one.**

Motion openers need the cyclist, walker, or runner as subject — not the scenery lighting up. Streetlamps were not cycling through the park. Repair: "Cycling through the park at dusk, she watched streetlamps flicker on one by one."

**Trap:** Dusk scenery after a cycling opener feels cinematic but leaves the rider out.

Streetlamps cannot cycle — rewrite as "Cycling through the park at dusk, she watched streetlamps flicker on one by one."
highlights: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps
tasks.solution_overview:
Mid-difficulty danglers look vivid: shivering queues and dusk cycling can hypnotise you into accepting the wrong subject.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Bodily -ing openers followed by sensory desires ("hot tea") usually dangle. Produce and lost-item past participles (grown, hidden) attach well to tomatoes and remotes. "Having finished…" + person is reliable. Motion openers need the cyclist, not the streetlamps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep asking whether this subject could literally shiver, grow, finish, hide, or cycle. Related scene props (tea, lamps) are not enough.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies disappeared fast.
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps became clear.
Having lost his gloves, Noah kept his hands in his pockets.
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots waited for the weekend.
Crossing the busy square, a street musician started a lively tune.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies disappeared fast.**

The cookies were burned at the edges but soft in the centre, and that food noun is the subject. Descriptive food states before the food noun are usually a clean past-participle attachment. Disappearing fast is what those cookies then do.

That food-state opener works: the edge-burned cookies are what disappeared fast.

**B) Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps became clear.**

"Listening/watching/reading…" needs a person (or animal) subject who can pay attention. Recipe steps do not listen to podcasts. Repair: "Listening carefully to the podcast, she found the recipe steps became clear."

**Trap:** Clarity-as-subject after a listening opener looks related but cannot be the listener.

Reject steps-as-listener; prefer "Listening carefully to the podcast, she found the recipe steps became clear."

**C) Having lost his gloves, Noah kept his hands in his pockets.**

Noah lost his gloves, so "Having lost…" correctly modifies him. Possession loss with "having lost" must be followed by the owner. Keeping hands in pockets is a natural follow-on for that same owner.

Accept the line: Noah lost the gloves and keeps his hands in his pockets.

**D) Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots waited for the weekend.**

The hiking boots were stacked neatly beside the door, so the arrangement participle modifies them. Stacked/lined/arranged patterns belong with the things in that arrangement. Waiting for the weekend is figurative colour on the same subject.

This is sound: the neatly stacked boots are what wait for the weekend.

**E) Crossing the busy square, a street musician started a lively tune.**

Grammatically, "a street musician" is said to be crossing while starting a tune — but the intended crosser is usually a passer-by, not the performer already in place. Reattach the opener to the walker, or drop it. Repair: "Crossing the busy square, we heard a street musician start a lively tune."

**Trap:** A plausible human subject after "Crossing…" can still be the wrong agent for what the writer meant.

That crossing opener and the musician do not match — rewrite as "Crossing the busy square, we heard a street musician start a lively tune."
highlights: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots
Crossing the busy square, a street musician
tasks.solution_overview:
Cookies and boots look solid; listening and crossing create the traps you need to catch at this level.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Food-state past participles before the food noun are usually correct. Perception verbs (listening) need a person. "Having lost…" needs the owner. Arrangement participles modify the arranged items. "Crossing…" must be followed by whoever crossed — not a musician who may already be performing in the square.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reattach any -ing opener that describes intentional human behaviour to a human subject. Keep past-participle state descriptions on the objects that underwent them.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic smelled of old cedar.
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves stayed crisp.
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket stayed packed indoors.
Sliding into third base, the umpire called him safe.
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer advertised the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic smelled of old cedar.**

"Having climbed…" needs the climber as subject before you mention how the attic smelled. The attic did not climb the staircase. Repair: "Having climbed the spiral staircase, we noticed the attic smelled of old cedar."

**Trap:** Place-as-subject after a climbing opener is a frequent travel/home dangler.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Having climbed the spiral staircase, we noticed the attic smelled of old cedar."

**B) Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves stayed crisp.**

The salad leaves were rinsed under cold water, so the past participle modifies the food. Prep verbs on ingredients (rinsed, peeled, sliced) attach to the food that then stays crisp. That is exactly the pairing here.

Keep this: rinsed salad leaves are what stayed crisp.

**C) Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket stayed packed indoors.**

Emotion participles (worried, delighted, annoyed) modify people, not objects. The picnic basket was not worried about the forecast; the hosts were. Repair: "Worried about the weather forecast, they left the picnic basket packed indoors."

**Trap:** Scene props after emotion openers feel connected but cannot hold mental states.

That picnic basket was not worried — rewrite as "Worried about the weather forecast, they left the picnic basket packed indoors."

**D) Sliding into third base, the umpire called him safe.**

Sports action openers must be followed by the player who performed the move. The umpire did not slide into third base; the runner did. Repair: "Sliding into third base, the runner heard the umpire call him safe."

**Trap:** Officials in the sentence tempt you to attach the slide to them instead of the runner.

Reject umpire-as-slider; prefer "Sliding into third base, the runner heard the umpire call him safe."

**E) Printed on recycled paper, the flyer advertised the school concert.**

The flyer was printed on recycled paper, so the past participle describes the notice. "Printed/published/posted…" usually modifies the document that then carries the message. Advertising the concert is what that printed flyer does.

Accept the line: the flyer printed on recycled paper is what advertises the concert.
highlights: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket
Sliding into third base, the umpire
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer
tasks.solution_overview:
Emotion and sports danglers are easy to miss when the scenery feels connected to the action.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Having climbed…" needs the climber, not the attic. Prep verbs on ingredients (rinsed) modify the food. Emotion participles (worried) modify people, never picnic baskets. Sliding belongs with the runner, not the umpire. "Printed on…" correctly modifies the flyer.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mental states and athletic moves stay with people. Object subjects are fine only for make/print/prep states that truly describe those objects.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Folded into neat squares, the napkins brightened the dinner table.
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions still felt unfamiliar.
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel filled quickly.
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook recommended three streets nearby.
Exhausted but pleased, the choir packed away the music stands.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Folded into neat squares, the napkins brightened the dinner table.**

The napkins were folded into neat squares, so the past participle matches the fabric items. Household "folded/ironed/pressed…" modifies the textile that then brightens the table. Attachment is clean.

That works — folded napkins are what brighten the dinner table.

**B) Having studied until midnight, the exam questions still felt unfamiliar.**

"Having studied…" must be followed by the student who still finds the questions unfamiliar. Exam questions did not study until midnight. Repair: "Having studied until midnight, she still found the exam questions unfamiliar."

**Trap:** Test material after a studying opener looks related but cannot be the studying agent.

Exam questions did not study till midnight — rewrite as "Having studied until midnight, she still found the exam questions unfamiliar."

**C) Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel filled quickly.**

The rain barrel was not dripping from the eaves; the water was. Make sure the participle’s subject is what drips, hangs, or falls — not only the container if the opener describes the runoff. Repair: "Dripping from the eaves after the storm, rain filled the barrel quickly."

**Trap:** Container subjects after a dripping opener are a subtle weather/home near-miss.

That barrel was not dripping from the eaves — prefer "Dripping from the eaves after the storm, rain filled the barrel quickly."

**D) Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook recommended three streets nearby.**

Search/look-for openers need a traveller as subject, not the book that lists streets. The guidebook was not searching for a café. Repair: "Searching for a quiet café, we checked the guidebook’s three recommended streets."

**Trap:** Guidebooks after travel -ing openers feel helpful but cannot be the searcher.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Searching for a quiet café, we checked the guidebook’s three recommended streets."

**E) Exhausted but pleased, the choir packed away the music stands.**

The choir was exhausted but pleased, and that animate group is the subject packing the stands. Paired emotion adjectives still require a human (or animate) subject. Here the choir fits both feelings and the packing action.

This is sound: the exhausted-but-pleased choir packs away the music stands.
highlights: Folded into neat squares, the napkins
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook
tasks.solution_overview:
Only napkins and a choir keep solid matches; study, weather, and travel lines shuffle agents onto questions, barrels, and guidebooks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Household "folded…" modifies fabric. "Having studied…" needs the student. "Dripping from the eaves…" describes water, not the barrel as the thing that drips. Search openers need a person. Paired emotion adjectives (exhausted but pleased) still require an animate subject — the choir works.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the opener is a human mental action or motion, reject furniture, guides, and result nouns as subjects. If it is a fabric or body state that the subject can hold, accept it.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken came out of the oven golden.
Having missed the last bus, the walk home took nearly an hour.
Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid tilted toward the light.
Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton felt heavier than usual.
Written by a local poet, the short story won the school prize.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken came out of the oven golden.**

The roast chicken was seasoned generously with herbs, so the past participle modifies the dish. Seasoned/marinated/basted attaches to the food that then comes out golden. That pairing is exact.

Keep this: the herb-seasoned roast is what comes out golden.

**B) Having missed the last bus, the walk home took nearly an hour.**

"Having missed…" needs a person subject, not the resulting journey. The walk home did not miss the last bus; the traveller did. Repair: "Having missed the last bus, she faced a walk home of nearly an hour."

**Trap:** Consequence phrases ("the walk") after "having missed" are a high-level dangler.

That walk home did not miss the bus — rewrite as "Having missed the last bus, she faced a walk home of nearly an hour."

**C) Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid tilted toward the light.**

The orchid was balanced carefully on the windowsill, so the position participle modifies the plant. Position participles can modify plants and objects that sit or rest. Tilting toward the light is what that balanced orchid then does.

Accept the line: the carefully balanced orchid tilts toward the light.

**D) Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton felt heavier than usual.**
