whether can the courier… is direct yes/no inversion after whether. Never put the modal before the subject in an embedded clause. Slide can back after courier.

**Trap:** Modal fronting after whether copies Can the courier…? almost exactly.

Flag it false and rewrite as "whether the courier can arrive by noon."
**E) Tell me how much the tickets will cost.**

how much the tickets will cost is statement order after Tell me. will stays after tickets, not before how much. Degree how much/how many phrases behave like other wh-embeds.

Hold onto this: how much the tickets will cost keeps will after tickets.
highlights: how much the tickets will cost
tasks.solution_overview:
Subject who stays simple; modal whether-clauses and how much-clauses keep the modal after the subject. Awkward passive inversions are a separate red flag.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

who as subject needs no flip and no stranded-by rewrite that drags the auxiliary forward. whether + subject + can… is fine; whether can the… is not. how much… will… similarly refuses will-fronting.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate who / whether / how much and check what immediately follows. If a modal or auxiliary has jumped ahead of its subject, reject the item. Prefer the clean subject who + past participle pattern when both active and awkward passive are offered.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell me how much will the tickets cost.
The note does not say how long the delay lasted.
The note does not say how long did the delay last.
Parents asked what the school intended to do next.
Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tell me how much will the tickets cost.**

how much will the tickets cost inverts will and the subject after Tell me. The same how much phrase is fine with statement order: how much the tickets will cost. That contrast is intentional across these tasks.

**Trap:** will-fronting after how much is a near-miss of the Direct How much will…? shape.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Tell me how much the tickets will cost."
**B) The note does not say how long the delay lasted.**

how long the delay lasted keeps statement order after say. lasted is a plain past verb after its subject; no auxiliary is waiting to front. Duration how long-clauses follow the same calm pattern as why-clauses.

Accept the line: how long the delay lasted is flat statement order after say.
**C) The note does not say how long did the delay last.**

how long did the delay last smuggles do-support into the embed. If the clause would be a perfect stand-alone question, it is too inverted for this frame. Delete did and keep the past verb after the subject.

**Trap:** did after how long feels natural from oral drills, but embeds ban it here.

That fails here — rewrite as "how long the delay lasted."
**D) Parents asked what the school intended to do next.**

what the school intended… is an object-wh clause with subject before verb. school sits before intended; what is the object of intended. After asked, keep what + subject + verb.

Keep this: what the school intended puts the subject before the past verb.
**E) Parents asked what did the school intend to do next.**

what did the school intend… is a direct question sitting inside asked. Drop did and keep intended after school. Object what often tempts learners into full question order — resist it in embeds.

**Trap:** Object what + did is a very plausible direct-question transfer.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "what the school intended to do next."
highlights: how much will the tickets cost
how long did the delay last
tasks.solution_overview:
how much, how long, and object what-clauses all crash when will or did jumps before the subject. Correct embeds keep the finite verb after the subject noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Tell me / say / asked open the frame; the damage lives inside the subordinate clause. will-fronting after how much and did-support after how long or what are the usual scars.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read from the wh-word to the verb and ask whether anything has skipped ahead of the subject. If will or did appears before the noun that should be the subject, mark false. If the subject sits in its ordinary slot, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I can't remember where I put my passport.
I can't remember where did I put my passport.
Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?
Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?
She wondered why everyone was whispering.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I can't remember where I put my passport.**

where I put my passport is statement order after remember. I is the subject; put is the past verb — nothing is inverted. Memory verbs still take embedded statement order.

Leave it as written: where I put my passport is memory-clause statement order.
**B) I can't remember where did I put my passport.**

where did I put… is direct-question do-support inside an embedded clause. can't remember does not license a second, inverted question. Use where I put….

**Trap:** did after where is the default oral memory-question shape learners paste into embeds.

That fails — drop did and prefer "where I put my passport."
**C) Have you found out whether the museum opens on Mondays?**

whether the museum opens… keeps opens after the subject. No does appears, and none is needed. Perfect for a yes/no fact-check after find out.

This is sound: whether the museum opens never invents does after whether.
**D) Have you found out whether does the museum open on Mondays?**

whether does the museum open… invents do-support after whether. does belongs in Does the museum open…? as a stand-alone question, not here. Use whether the museum opens….

**Trap:** does after whether looks like careful tense marking but recreates a direct question.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whether the museum opens on Mondays."
**E) She wondered why everyone was whispering.**

why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject. wonder why… wants a reason clause, not a flipped be-question. The progressive was whispering stays intact after everyone.

Trust the order: why everyone was whispering keeps was after the subject.
tasks.solution_overview:
Memory, discovery, and wonder verbs — remember, find out, wonder — all embed statement order. Stand-alone question shapes after where or whether do not belong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

did-fronting after where and does-fronting after whether are the scrapes. Correct why / where / whether clauses place the subject before was, opens, or the past verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the matrix verb and judge only the subordinate string. If it still sounds like a quiz (where did I…?, whether does the…?), reject it. If it sounds like a report (where I put…, whether the museum opens…), accept it.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She wondered why was everyone whispering.
Let me know which bus you are taking.
Let me know which bus are you taking.
We still don't know who broke the window.
We still don't know who did break the window.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She wondered why was everyone whispering.**

why was everyone… inverts was before the subject after wondered. The twin with why everyone was whispering is the correct shape. wonder why… never takes be-fronting inside the reason clause.

**Trap:** Be-inversion after why is a classic wonder-clause near-miss.

Reject this be-fronting; rewrite as "why everyone was whispering."
**B) Let me know which bus you are taking.**

which bus you are taking keeps you before are. which + noun + subject + verb is the embedded choice pattern. Let me know simply softens the request; it does not invert the clause.

Accept the line: which bus you are taking keeps you before are.
**C) Let me know which bus are you taking.**

which bus are you taking flips are before you inside the embed. If you can hear Are you taking…? after stripping the frame, the item is false. Use which bus you are taking.

**Trap:** are-fronting after which + noun copies the Direct Which bus are you…? drill.

Flag it false and go with "which bus you are taking."
**D) We still don't know who broke the window.**

who broke the window is a clean subject question with no do-support. who is the agent; broke is the past verb. Subject who + past verb needs no did.

Keep this: subject who broke the window needs no did.
**E) We still don't know who did break the window.**

who did break adds unnecessary emphatic or wrong do to a subject question. Emphatic did can appear in speech for contrast, but it is not the neutral embed pattern tested here. Use who broke, not who did break.

**Trap:** Emphatic did after subject who looks confident and still fails the exam pattern.

That fails — prefer the neutral "who broke the window."
tasks.solution_overview:
This set pairs be-inversion after why with are-fronting after which, then finishes on subject who without fake did.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

why was everyone… and which bus are you… both mark direct-question order. Subject who broke… stays simple: never who did break in this embed.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After wonder / let me know / don't know, check whether was/are/did has jumped ahead of its subject. For who, ask whether who is the subject of a plain past verb — if yes, reject any added did. Statement order wins every time.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm curious how often she practises the piano.
I'm curious how often does she practise the piano.
Can anyone say where the nearest pharmacy is?
Can anyone say where is the nearest pharmacy?
They asked if we had packed enough water.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'm curious how often she practises the piano.**

how often she practises… keeps subject–verb order after curious. Frequency phrases do not change the embedded rule. practises sits after she, as in ordinary prose.

**Tip:** Frequency wh-phrases still take statement order.

That works: how often she practises still takes statement order after curious.
**B) I'm curious how often does she practise the piano.**

how often does she practise… inserts do-support as in a direct question. I'm curious already softens the ask; does is leftover from classroom drills. Use how often she practises….

**Trap:** does after how often is a near-miss of How often does she…?

Mark it wrong and prefer "how often she practises the piano."
**C) Can anyone say where the nearest pharmacy is?**

where the nearest pharmacy is places is after the subject noun phrase. That is the classic location embed. Can anyone say… is the outer question; the where-clause stays flat.

Hold onto this: where the nearest pharmacy is parks is after the noun phrase.
**D) Can anyone say where is the nearest pharmacy?**

where is the nearest pharmacy flips is before the subject inside say. This is the same signature contrast you meet with wonder where… throughout the topic. Use where the nearest pharmacy is.

**Trap:** is-fronting after where remains the signature location trap at every difficulty.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "where the nearest pharmacy is."
**E) They asked if we had packed enough water.**

if we had packed… is a yes/no embed with statement order. had stays after we; the past perfect is intact. if/whether + subject + verb — never invert.

This is sound: if we had packed keeps had after we.
tasks.solution_overview:
Frequency how often, location where…is, and if-clauses all stay calm: subject then verb, no fronted auxiliary.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

how often fails when does jumps before she. where…is fails when is jumps before the nearest pharmacy. if-clauses fail when any auxiliary front-runs the subject.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat how often and where like any other wh-embed: cover curious / say / asked and judge the rest. Accept only the versions that could be rewritten as statements without moving words around. Reject any that still need quiz-show intonation.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They asked if had we packed enough water.
Nobody knows how many people will show up.
Nobody knows how many people will show up will.
Please check whether the oven has preheated.
Please check whether has the oven preheated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) They asked if had we packed enough water.**

if had we packed… inverts had before we after asked. The true twin if we had packed… shows the correct order. Auxiliaries do not front after if.

**Trap:** had-fronting after if is a close twin of Had we packed…?

That fails here — rewrite as "if we had packed enough water."
**B) Nobody knows how many people will show up.**

how many people will show up keeps will after the subject people. how many + noun + will + verb is the calm degree pattern. Nobody knows… frames it without turning it into a direct question.

Accept the line: how many people will show up leaves will after people.
**C) Nobody knows how many people will show up will.**

Extra will at the end is garbled; the clause is already complete after show up. Stop at how many people will show up. A trailing echo of will usually means someone rewrote the clause twice and forgot to delete.

Mark it wrong and stop at "how many people will show up" — drop the trailing will.
**D) Please check whether the oven has preheated.**

whether the oven has preheated keeps has after the subject. whether + subject + auxiliary + participle is the perfect yes/no embed. Please check softens the request without inverting the clause.

Keep this: whether the oven has preheated leaves has after oven.
**E) Please check whether has the oven preheated.**

whether has the oven… flips has before the subject. Same scar as if had we… — auxiliaries do not front after whether/if. Use whether the oven has….

**Trap:** has-fronting after whether is a textbook near-miss yes/no embed error.

Flag it false and prefer "whether the oven has preheated."
highlights: how many people will show up
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch for had-fronting after if, has-fronting after whether, and a garbled extra will at the end of an otherwise finished how many-clause.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The yes/no embeds invert when auxiliaries leapfrog the subject. how many people will show up is fine once; trailing will is noise, not grammar.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After if or whether, demand subject then auxiliary. For how many, accept a single will after the subject noun and stop when the clause is complete. Anything that restacks will or has before the subject fails.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide explained how the bridge had been built.
The guide explained how had the bridge been built.
I need to find out whose jacket this is.
I need to find out whose is this jacket.
Did anyone mention when the concert starts?
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guide explained how the bridge had been built.**

how the bridge had been built keeps passive statement order after explained. had stays after bridge; the passive stack been built follows. Passive embeds still place the first auxiliary after the subject.

**Tip:** Passive embeds still place had after the subject.

Leave it as written: how the bridge had been built keeps had after the subject.
**B) The guide explained how had the bridge been built.**

how had the bridge been… inverts had into direct-question order. Explained how… does not invite a quiz-show flip of the auxiliary. Use how the bridge had been built.

**Trap:** Passive stacks tempt had-fronting that looks especially 'complete' in exams.

Reject this flip; rewrite as "how the bridge had been built."
**C) I need to find out whose jacket this is.**

whose jacket this is keeps this before is. whose + noun + subject + be is the ownership embed. find out frames the question without fronting is.

**Tip:** whose + noun + subject + be.

That works — whose jacket this is keeps this before is.
**D) I need to find out whose is this jacket.**

whose is this jacket flips is before this inside find out. Moving whose alone and fronting be is the classroom direct-question habit. Use whose jacket this is.

**Trap:** whose is this… looks polished and still breaks embed order.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whose jacket this is."
**E) Did anyone mention when the concert starts?**

when the concert starts is statement order after mention; the outer Did anyone… is the only direct question. Outer inversion does not license inner inversion. starts sits after concert, as a fact report would.

**Tip:** Outer inversion does not license inner inversion.

Trust the outer question alone: when the concert starts stays flat inside.
highlights: how the bridge had been built
tasks.solution_overview:
Passive how-clauses and whose…is patterns both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. A direct outer question never licenses inversion inside the embed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

how had the bridge… and whose is this jacket move had/is ahead of their subjects. when the concert starts after mention stays statement-ordered even though Did anyone… opens the sentence.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate outer inversion from inner order. Only the outer frame may flip; the subordinate clause must still read as a statement. For whose, keep the noun with whose and put the subject before be.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did anyone mention when does the concert start?
We're trying to work out what the noise is coming from.
We're trying to work out what is the noise coming from.
He refused to say whether he would join us later.
He refused to say whether would he join us later.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Did anyone mention when does the concert start?**

when does the concert start inserts do-support inside the embedded clause. Did anyone mention… already asked; the embed should not ask again. Use when the concert starts.

**Trap:** does inside when after a direct Did anyone… is a double-ask near-miss.

That fails — strip does and prefer "when the concert starts."
**B) We're trying to work out what the noise is coming from.**

what the noise is coming from keeps is after the subject noise. Object what + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition) is the modern embed. work out only introduces the clause; it does not invert it.

**Tip:** Object what + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition).

Accept the line: what the noise is coming from keeps is after noise.
**C) We're trying to work out what is the noise coming from.**

what is the noise coming from flips is before the subject inside work out. The stranded from is fine; the fronted is is not. Use what the noise is coming from.

**Trap:** Stranded prepositions often co-travel with illegal is-fronting in learner English.

Reject this is-fronting; the clean version is "what the noise is coming from."
**D) He refused to say whether he would join us later.**

whether he would join… keeps would after the subject. whether + subject + modal + verb is the standard yes/no embed with a modal. refused to say frames it without flipping would.

Keep this: whether he would join parks would after he.
**E) He refused to say whether would he join us later.**

whether would he join… is modal inversion after whether. would before he is the direct Would he join…? shape wearing an embed costume. Use whether he would join….

**Trap:** would-fronting after whether is a high-yield exam scar.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whether he would join us later."
highlights: what the noise is coming from
what is the noise coming from
tasks.solution_overview:
Stranded-preposition embeds (coming from) and whether + modal clauses both require subject before the finite verb. Reject does-fronting and would-fronting inside the subordinate clause.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

when does the concert… is the false twin of the previous true when-clause. what is the noise… fronts is; whether would he… fronts the modal.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore polite or narrative frames and read the embed alone. If does, is, or would sits before its subject, mark false. A stranded preposition at the end (from) does not change that subject-first rule.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It remains unclear which neighbour complained first.
It remains unclear which neighbour did complain first.
Could you clarify how far the campsite is from here?
Could you clarify how far is the campsite from here?
The coach asked who would captain the side on Saturday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It remains unclear which neighbour complained first.**

which neighbour complained first is a subject which-clause with no do-support. which neighbour is the agent of complained. Subject which + noun + past verb needs no did.

**Tip:** Subject which + noun + past verb — no did.

This is sound: which neighbour complained first needs no fake did.
**B) It remains unclear which neighbour did complain first.**

which neighbour did complain adds fake do to a subject question. did here is not needed for tense and is not the neutral written pattern. Use which neighbour complained….

**Trap:** Fake did after subject which looks emphatic and almost grown-up.

Flag it false and rewrite as "which neighbour complained first."
**C) Could you clarify how far the campsite is from here?**

how far the campsite is… keeps is after the subject. Degree how far/how tall phrases behave like other wh-embeds. Could you clarify… softens without fronting be.

**Tip:** how far/how tall + subject + be.

Hold onto this: how far the campsite is keeps is after the subject.
**D) Could you clarify how far is the campsite from here?**

how far is the campsite… inverts is before the subject after clarify. The distance question tempts direct order; keep the campsite before is. Use how far the campsite is….

**Trap:** Degree how far often triggers Direct How far is…? order inside soft frames.

That fails here — prefer "how far the campsite is from here."
**E) The coach asked who would captain the side on Saturday.**

who would captain… keeps would after subject who. who is the subject; would captain is the modal verb phrase. Subject who + modal + verb — no inversion.

**Tip:** Subject who + modal + verb — no inversion.

Accept the line: who would captain keeps would after subject who.
tasks.solution_overview:
Subject which and subject who need no did or inversion. Degree phrases like how far keep be after the subject noun — not before it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Fake did after which neighbour…, is-fronting after how far, and any urge to flip who would… are the traps. Subject wh-words already fill the subject slot.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask who or what performs the verb. If the answer is the wh-phrase itself, ban did and inversion. For how far / how tall, keep is/are after the measured noun. Modal who would… stays who + would + verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach asked who would the side be captained by on Saturday.
I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether the Wi-Fi password has changed.
I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether has the Wi-Fi password changed.
No one could remember how the recipe went.
No one could remember how did the recipe go.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The coach asked who would the side be captained by on Saturday.**

who would the side be captained by… forces awkward inversion; prefer who would captain… or by whom the side would be captained. Avoid inverting inside a passive who-embed just to strand by. The previous true who would captain… is the better sibling.

**Trap:** Inverted passive who-embeds look formal while quietly failing word order.

Reject that inverted passive; prefer "who would captain the side on Saturday."
**B) I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether the Wi-Fi password has changed.**

whether the Wi-Fi password has changed keeps has after the subject inside a long polite frame. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me… is still just packaging. Long softeners take statement order in the embed.

**Tip:** Long softeners still take statement order in the embed.

That works — even a long softener leaves has after password.
**C) I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether has the Wi-Fi password changed.**

whether has the Wi-Fi password… flips has before the subject. Password length and tech topic do not change the word-order rule. Use whether the Wi-Fi password has….

**Trap:** has-fronting after whether survives even inside long polite packaging.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whether the Wi-Fi password has changed."
**D) No one could remember how the recipe went.**

how the recipe went is statement order after remember. recipe is the subject; went is the past verb. how + subject + past — no did.

Keep this: how the recipe went is calm subject-then-past order.
**E) No one could remember how did the recipe go.**

how did the recipe go inserts do-support into the embed. If you can ask How did the recipe go? alone, you have reinvented a direct question. Use how the recipe went.

**Trap:** how did… is the usual manner/story scar after remember/ask.

That fails — rewrite as "how the recipe went."
tasks.solution_overview:
Awkward passive who-inversion and has-fronting after whether are both wrong. Everyday how-clauses after remember stay subject–verb: how the recipe went, not how did….

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

who would the side be captained by… forces the auxiliary past the subject to save a passive. Long polite frames still take statement order in the whether-clause. how did… is the usual duration/manner scar.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer active who would captain… over inverted passives. After whether, keep has after the subject noun phrase. After how, ban did unless you truly need an object question in direct speech — which this embed is not.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The review depends on whether the supplier can meet the deadline.
The review depends on whether can the supplier meet the deadline.
She couldn't decide whom she should invite first.
She couldn't decide whom should she invite first.
Tell us what made the engine stall.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The review depends on whether the supplier can meet the deadline.**

whether the supplier can meet… keeps can after the subject even after depends on. Preposition + whether still takes statement order. The economic topic does not change the grammar.

**Tip:** Preposition + whether still takes statement order.

Leave it as written: depends on whether still wants can after supplier.
**B) The review depends on whether can the supplier meet the deadline.**

whether can the supplier… is modal inversion after whether. can before supplier is Direct Can the supplier…? with a formal hat on. Use whether the supplier can….

**Trap:** Modal fronting after whether under a formal noun subject looks especially exam-like.

Reject this modal flip; rewrite as "whether the supplier can meet the deadline."
**C) She couldn't decide whom she should invite first.**

whom she should invite keeps she before should. Object whom + subject + modal + verb is the formal object pattern. decide whom… embeds that pattern without flipping should.

**Tip:** Object whom + subject + modal + verb.

This is sound: whom she should invite keeps she before should.
**D) She couldn't decide whom should she invite first.**

whom should she invite flips should before she inside decide. Formal whom does not revive direct-question order. Use whom she should invite.

**Trap:** Formal whom often smuggles Should she…? order into the embed.

Flag it false and prefer "whom she should invite first."
**E) Tell us what made the engine stall.**

what made the engine stall is a subject what-clause with no do-support. what is the cause; made is the past verb. what + past verb when what is the subject.

**Tip:** what + past verb when what is the subject.

Accept the line: subject what made the engine stall needs no did.
tasks.solution_overview:
depends on whether… and object whom… should… both keep the subject before the modal. Subject what made… needs no did — do not invent one.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preposition + whether still takes statement order. Object whom flips wrongly when should jumps before she. Subject what made… is complete without do-support.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

After whether or whom, demand subject then modal. For what, ask whether what is the subject of made; if yes, leave the past verb alone. Reject any can/should that has moved left of its subject.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tell us what did make the engine stall.
I'm still unsure of how the app works offline.
I'm still unsure of how does the app work offline.
They wanted to know to whom the parcel should be delivered.
They wanted to know to whom should the parcel be delivered.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tell us what did make the engine stall.**

what did make… adds unnecessary do to a subject question. The prior true Tell us what made… is your template. Use what made, not what did make.

**Trap:** did after subject what feels like careful tense but is the wrong twin.

Mark it wrong and prefer "what made the engine stall."
**B) I'm still unsure of how the app works offline.**

how the app works offline keeps works after the subject after unsure of. Preposition + how still takes statement order. offline is just an adjunct; it does not move words.

**Tip:** Preposition + how still takes statement order.

That works — unsure of how the app works keeps statement order after of.
**C) I'm still unsure of how does the app work offline.**

how does the app work… inserts do-support inside the embed. unsure of how… is not the same as asking How does…? aloud. Use how the app works….

**Trap:** does after how under unsure of is a polished near-miss.

That fails here — rewrite as "how the app works offline."
**D) They wanted to know to whom the parcel should be delivered.**

to whom the parcel should be delivered keeps should after the subject in a formal prepositional wh-clause. to whom + subject + modal + verb is the careful written pattern. Passive be delivered does not change the subject-first rule.

**Tip:** to whom + subject + modal + verb.

Keep this: to whom the parcel should be delivered leaves should after parcel.
**E) They wanted to know to whom should the parcel be delivered.**

to whom should the parcel… inverts should before the subject. Formal register is not a license for modal fronting. Use to whom the parcel should be….

**Trap:** Formal to whom often unlocks illegal should-fronting in learner writing.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "to whom the parcel should be delivered."
tasks.solution_overview:
Subject what never takes did in embeds. After of how and to whom, keep the subject before the finite verb or modal — never front does or should.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

what did make… is the false twin of subject what made…. how does the app… and to whom should the parcel… front the auxiliary/modal.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If what is the subject, ban did. After a preposition (of, to), treat the remaining wh-clause like any other embed: subject first. Formal to whom does not license should-fronting.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions the yeast activates.
The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions does the yeast activate.
We never learned why the lights flickered every evening.
We never learned why did the lights flicker every evening.
Ask her which shelf the spices belong on.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions the yeast activates.**

under what conditions the yeast activates keeps the subject before the verb after a prepositional wh-opener. yeast is the subject; activates follows. Preposition + wh + subject + verb is the long-opener rule.

**Tip:** Preposition + wh + subject + verb.

Hold onto this: under what conditions the yeast activates stays subject-first.
**B) The puzzle is figuring out under what conditions does the yeast activate.**

under what conditions does the yeast… adds do-support as in a direct question. Long scientific openers tempt classroom question order — resist it. Use under what conditions the yeast activates.

**Trap:** does after a long under what conditions opener is a high-difficulty near-miss.

Mark it wrong and prefer "under what conditions the yeast activates."
**C) We never learned why the lights flickered every evening.**

why the lights flickered… is statement order after learned. lights before flickered; no auxiliary is waiting to front. why + subject + past — no did.

Accept the line: why the lights flickered needs no did after learned.
**D) We never learned why did the lights flicker every evening.**

why did the lights flicker… smuggles do-support into the embed. We never learned why… already contains the questioning; did is leftover drill. Use why the lights flickered….

**Trap:** why did… reappears even in narrative past embeds.

Flag it false and go with "why the lights flickered every evening."
**E) Ask her which shelf the spices belong on.**

which shelf the spices belong on keeps the spices before belong. which + noun + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition) is modern and correct. Ask her frames it without flipping do.

**Tip:** which + noun + subject + verb (+ stranded preposition).

This is sound: which shelf the spices belong on keeps spices before belong.
highlights: under what conditions the yeast activates
under what conditions does the yeast
which shelf the spices belong on
tasks.solution_overview:
Complex openers (under what conditions) and stranded which…on still demand statement order. Any does/did inside the subordinate clause is a direct-question scar.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preposition + wh openers keep subject before verb. why did… reintroduces the classic do-support trap. which shelf…belong on is fine with subject then verb plus stranded on.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the wh-word even if a preposition comes first, then insist on subject–verb order after it. Ban does/did unless the clause is a stand-alone direct question — which none of these embeds are. Stranded prepositions at the end are style, not inversion licenses.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Ask her which shelf do the spices belong on.
It is hard to say whether or not the weather will clear by noon.
It is hard to say whether or not will the weather clear by noon.
The children kept asking where Father Christmas lived.
The children kept asking where did Father Christmas live.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Ask her which shelf do the spices belong on.**

which shelf do the spices… inserts do before the subject inside Ask her. The stranded on is fine; the fronted do is the error. Use which shelf the spices belong on.

**Trap:** do after which + noun is the false twin of the prior stranded-preposition item.

That fails — drop do and prefer "which shelf the spices belong on."
**B) It is hard to say whether or not the weather will clear by noon.**

whether or not the weather will clear… keeps will after the subject; or not does not change order. whether (or not) + subject + verb is the full pattern. hard to say merely frames the uncertainty.

**Tip:** whether (or not) + subject + verb.

Leave it as written: whether or not still parks will after weather.
**C) It is hard to say whether or not will the weather clear by noon.**

whether or not will the weather… inverts will before the subject. Adding or not does not unlock Direct Will the weather…? order. Use whether or not the weather will….

**Trap:** or not often fools writers into thinking modal fronting is now allowed.

Reject this will-fronting; rewrite as "whether or not the weather will clear by noon."
**D) The children kept asking where Father Christmas lived.**

where Father Christmas lived is classic storybook statement order after asking. Father Christmas before lived — no auxiliary flip. where + subject + past.

Keep this: where Father Christmas lived is flat storybook order.
**E) The children kept asking where did Father Christmas live.**

where did Father Christmas live is direct-question order inside kept asking. Children's narratives still obey the embed rule in careful writing. Use where Father Christmas lived.

**Trap:** Storybook where did… is adult do-support scarring of a calm past embed.

Mark it wrong and prefer "where Father Christmas lived."
highlights: whether or not the weather will
whether or not will the weather
tasks.solution_overview:
or not after whether never licenses modal fronting. Storybook where-clauses and which…belong on both stay subject–verb; drop do/did from the embed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

which shelf do the spices… is the false twin of the prior true item. whether or not will the weather… fronts will. where did Father Christmas… is children's-story material with adult do-support scarring.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat or not as invisible for word order — it does not buy you a flip. After which / whether / where, keep subject before any do/will/past verb. If the embed would work as a bedtime-story statement, it is probably true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes do not record on what basis the exemption had been granted.
The minutes do not record on what basis had the exemption been granted.
Partners remain divided over which vendor we should engage.
Partners remain divided over which vendor should we engage.
I wonder who seconded the motion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The minutes do not record on what basis the exemption had been granted.**

on what basis the exemption had been granted keeps had after the subject. Prepositional wh-openers still take statement order. The minutes frame is formal packaging, not a license to invert.

**Tip:** Prepositional wh-openers still take statement order.

That works — on what basis the exemption had been granted keeps had after exemption.
**B) The minutes do not record on what basis had the exemption been granted.**

on what basis had the exemption… inverts had before the subject. Passive had been granted follows the subject; it does not jump ahead of it. Use on what basis the exemption had….

**Trap:** had-fronting after on what basis looks boardroom-formal and still fails.

That fails here — rewrite as "on what basis the exemption had been granted."
**C) Partners remain divided over which vendor we should engage.**

which vendor we should engage keeps we before should. which + noun + subject + modal + verb is the object-choice embed. divided over… is only the matrix scenery.

**Tip:** which + noun + subject + modal + verb.

Accept the line: which vendor we should engage leaves we before should.
**D) Partners remain divided over which vendor should we engage.**

which vendor should we engage flips should before we. should we is the Direct Should we…? shape. Use which vendor we should engage.

**Trap:** should-fronting after which vendor is a polished boardroom near-miss.

Flag it false and prefer "which vendor we should engage."
**E) I wonder who seconded the motion.**

who seconded the motion is a clean subject who-clause. who is the agent; seconded is the past verb. Subject who + past — never invert or add did.

**Tip:** Subject who + past — never invert or add did.

This is sound: subject who seconded the motion needs no did.
highlights: on what basis the exemption had
on what basis had the exemption
tasks.solution_overview:
Prepositional wh-openers (on what basis) and object which-clauses (which vendor we should…) both fail when the auxiliary precedes the subject. Subject who remains the simplest correct pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

had-fronting after on what basis and should-fronting after which vendor are the formal scars. who seconded… needs neither inversion nor did.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Longer openers still unpack the same way: after the wh-chunk, demand subject then auxiliary/modal. For who as subject of a past verb, leave the past alone. Boardroom vocabulary does not rewrite the grammar.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes do not record who did second the motion.
Friends remain divided over whether the trip itself makes sense.
Friends remain divided over whether does the trip itself make sense.
I wonder where the caretaker is during the blackout.
I wonder where is the caretaker during the blackout.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The minutes do not record who did second the motion.**

who did second… adds emphatic or wrong do to a subject question. The prior true who seconded the motion is your answer key in miniature. Use who seconded — never who did second in this embed.

**Trap:** Emphatic did after subject who closes the topic on a familiar scar.

Reject the fake did; rewrite as "who seconded the motion."
**B) Friends remain divided over whether the trip itself makes sense.**

whether the trip itself makes… keeps makes after the subject; itself is just a focusing pronoun. Extra focus words do not change embedded order. divided over whether… still wants subject then verb.

**Tip:** Extra focus words do not change embedded order.

Hold onto this: whether the trip itself makes sense still puts makes after trip.
**C) Friends remain divided over whether does the trip itself make sense.**

whether does the trip… invents do-support after whether. does before the trip is Direct Does the trip…? wearing a whether hat. Use whether the trip makes….

**Trap:** does after whether with a focusing itself is still illegal do-support.

Mark it wrong and prefer "whether the trip itself makes sense."
**D) I wonder where the caretaker is during the blackout.**

where the caretaker is… is the classic wonder pattern with statement order. caretaker before is; the blackout phrase is only a time adjunct. I wonder where + subject + is.

**Tip:** I wonder where + subject + is.

Keep this: where the caretaker is after wonder is the topic's signature calm pattern.
**E) I wonder where is the caretaker during the blackout.**

where is the caretaker… reverts to direct-question inversion after wonder. Use where the caretaker is — the core contrast of this topic. If you remember only one repair from G.19, make it this one.

**Trap:** where is… after wonder is the opening scar of the whole chapter.

That fails — rewrite as "where the caretaker is during the blackout."
tasks.solution_overview:
Close on the signature contrast: wonder where the caretaker is (statement order) versus where is the caretaker (direct inversion). Along the way, reject fake do after who or whether — embeds do not need it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

who did second… invents do on a subject question. whether does the trip… invents do after whether. where is the caretaker… reverts to the topic's opening mistake.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for did/does that do not belong, then finish with the where + subject + is checklist. Focus pronouns like itself do not change order. If the clause after wonder could stand alone as a quiz question, mark it false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Pass the remote to whoever finds it under the sofa.
The neighbour, who's garden we borrowed tools from, waved hello.
Late nights affect my concentration in morning classes.
Between you and I, the reunion dinner felt awkward.
Fewer guests arrived than we had expected.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Pass the remote to whoever finds it under the sofa.**

Whoever is the subject of finds inside the relative clause, so the nominative form is required. The preposition to governs the whole clause, not a lone object pronoun right after it. Read the clause on its own: whoever finds it — that is clearly a subject slot.

**Tip:** Ignore the preposition; judge case inside the clause.

Keep this: whoever correctly fills the subject slot inside the clause after to.
**B) The neighbour, who's garden we borrowed tools from, waved hello.**

Who's expands only to who is or who has, and neither fits before garden. Possession before a noun is marked with whose: whose garden. If the expansion test fails, the form cannot be a contraction.

**Trap:** Who's looks like a neat possessive but collapses under expansion — examiners count on that.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The neighbour, whose garden we borrowed tools from, waved hello."
**C) Late nights affect my concentration in morning classes.**

Affect is the verb meaning influence, and that is exactly what late nights do to concentration. Effect as a noun would need a different frame such as have an effect on…. Here the finite verb slot wants affect.

That works — affect correctly names the influence on concentration.
**D) Between you and I, the reunion dinner felt awkward.**

After the preposition between, both pronouns must be object case. Between you and I is a familiar hypercorrection; the careful form is Between you and me. Strip you and — nobody would say between I.

**Trap:** Polished between you and I still fails the object-case test.

That fails here — rewrite as "Between you and me, the reunion dinner felt awkward."
**E) Fewer guests arrived than we had expected.**

Guests are a countable plural, so fewer is the careful choice. Less typically pairs with mass nouns such as less sugar or less time. Headcount plurals take fewer in formal exam English.

Accept the line: fewer correctly pairs with countable guests.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five sentences are quick swaps among confusable pairs: case after to, possession vs contraction, affect vs effect, object pronouns after between, and fewer vs less.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Each line turns on one classic exam trap. Watch subject case inside a clause after a preposition, whose versus who's, the verb affect for influence, object me after between, and fewer with countable plurals.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For whoever/whomever, find the verb of the relative clause and ask who does the action. For who's/whose, try expanding who's. For affect/effect, ask influence or bring about. For pronouns after between, keep object case. For fewer/less, ask whether the noun is countable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Give the spare ticket to whomever arrives at the gate first.
The coach, whose whistle broke mid-match, borrowed another.
Too much sugar will effect your energy after lunch.
Between you and me, the playlist needs more variety.
The selection criteria is printed on the club noticeboard.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Give the spare ticket to whomever arrives at the gate first.**

Whomever looks formal after to, but the relative is the subject of arrives. Subjects need whoever: whoever arrives at the gate first. Find the verb in the clause; if the wh-word does the action, choose whoever.

**Trap:** Object-looking whomever after a preposition is a classic false formal cue.

Reject this near-miss; the clean version is "Give the spare ticket to whoever arrives at the gate first."
**B) The coach, whose whistle broke mid-match, borrowed another.**

Whose correctly marks possession before whistle: the coach's whistle. Who's would mean who is or who has and would not fit before a noun of possession. Whose works for people and things in formal English.

This is sound — whose correctly marks the coach's possession of the whistle.
**C) Too much sugar will effect your energy after lunch.**

The meaning is influence on energy after lunch, so you need the verb affect. Will effect would mean bring about, which does not fit your energy as the direct object here. Reserve verb effect for bring about or cause to happen.

**Trap:** Effect after will looks lofty but mismatches influence meaning.

Flag this and rewrite as "Too much sugar will affect your energy after lunch."
**D) Between you and me, the playlist needs more variety.**

Object pronouns after between are correct: you and me. Between you and I is the hypercorrection this line carefully avoids. Formal speech still uses me here.

Keep this: between you and me keeps both pronouns in object case.
**E) The selection criteria is printed on the club noticeboard.**

Criteria is a plural Latin form, so it needs a plural verb. The selection criteria is must become are printed. The singular form is criterion.

**Trap:** Singular is with plural criteria is a frequent Latin-loan slip.

That choice falls; prefer "The selection criteria are printed on the club noticeboard."
tasks.solution_overview:
This set recycles the same confusable pairs with swapped outcomes, so do not answer by habit from Task 1.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Ask whether the wh-word is a subject, whether the 's is a contraction or a possessive, whether the sentence means influence or bring about, whether the pronoun sits after a preposition, and whether criteria is treated as plural.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Test case inside the clause after to, expand who's when you see it, swap effect to affect for influence, keep me after between, and pair criteria with are/were/have.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Whoever finishes the puzzle should claim the prize.
Who's responsible for locking the studio tonight?
The committee hopes the new rule will effect a change in attendance.
Less messages were left on the noticeboard this week.
The entry criteria are clear and posted online.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Whoever finishes the puzzle should claim the prize.**

Whoever correctly acts as the subject of finishes at the head of the sentence. No outer preposition tempts you toward whomever here. Start-of-sentence subject slots almost always need whoever.

Accept the line: whoever rightly heads the subject clause.
**B) Who's responsible for locking the studio tonight?**

Who's expands cleanly to who is before responsible. That is exactly when the contraction is allowed. Always run the expansion test before you accept who's.

That works — who's expands cleanly to who is in this question.
**C) The committee hopes the new rule will effect a change in attendance.**

Verb effect meaning bring about is correct with a change. Effect a change, reform, or improvement is the rare but valid formal pattern. This is not the everyday influence use of affect.

**Tip:** Effect a change/reform is the one frame where verb effect is intentional.

This is sound — effect correctly means bring about a change.
**D) Less messages were left on the noticeboard this week.**

Messages are countable items, so Less messages is wrong. Repair to Fewer messages were left…. If you can count the noun one by one, prefer fewer.

**Trap:** Less before a plural count noun is a mass/count mix-up exams love.

Call it wrong — the fix is "Fewer messages were left on the noticeboard this week."
**E) The entry criteria are clear and posted online.**

Plural criteria correctly takes are. The line models the agreement pattern examiners expect. Formal exam English keeps criteria plural.

Keep this: plural criteria agrees with are.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four of these are carefully correct models; one countable/mass slip remains.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm each pair quickly: whoever as subject, who's = who is, effect = bring about, fewer with countables, and criteria with a plural verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand contractions, check whether effect means bring about, and ask whether the noun after less/fewer can be counted one by one.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Invite whomever the class nominates as quiz master.
Please name the classmate who's notes we borrowed.
Cold weather can affect joint pain overnight.
Keep this secret between you and me.
We need less luggage before we board the train.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Invite whomever the class nominates as quiz master.**

Whomever is the object of nominates: the class nominates someone. When another subject does the verb, the wh-word is traditionally an object. Invite whomever the class nominates is the careful traditional form.

**Tip:** If another subject does the verb, the wh-word is often the object.

Hold this form: whomever correctly fills the object slot of nominates.
**B) Please name the classmate who's notes we borrowed.**

Possession is needed before notes, so write whose notes. Who's notes never expands to a sensible who is notes. A noun right after the wh-form almost always signals whose.

**Trap:** Who's before a noun looks possessive but fails the expansion test.

Strike this; prefer "Please name the classmate whose notes we borrowed."
**C) Cold weather can affect joint pain overnight.**

Cold weather influences joint pain, and the verb for that is affect. Ask whether something influences something else — if yes, choose affect. No bring-about result noun is in play here.

Accept the line: affect correctly names the influence on joint pain.
**D) Keep this secret between you and me.**

Object pronouns after between are required: you and me. Everyday English still marks between you and I wrong. Keep both coordinated pronouns in object case.

That pairing is sound — between you and me uses correct object case.
**E) We need less luggage before we board the train.**

Luggage is uncountable in this everyday sense, so less is appropriate. Mass nouns such as time, luggage, and advice take less. Fewer luggage would be the trap flip of this item.

Leave it as written: less correctly pairs with mass luggage.
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch the genuine object-case whomever and the mass-noun less; the rest hinge on possession, influence, and prepositional object pronouns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

One line is a true object whomever after nominates; another correctly uses less with luggage. Only mark false where the wrong member of a confusable pair appears.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate the clause verb to choose whoever/whomever, expand who's, confirm affect for influence, keep me after between, and treat luggage as mass.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Forward the parcel to whomever is at the front desk.
The café whose windows fog up in winter serves great soup.
Loud music will effect the baby's nap downstairs.
This argument stays between my sister and I.
One key criterion is still missing from the checklist.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Forward the parcel to whomever is at the front desk.**

Is needs a subject form: whoever is at the front desk. Whomever after to is a false formal signal when the next verb is finite be. To + whomever + is is almost always wrong.

**Trap:** Formal-looking whomever after to collapses when is follows immediately.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Forward the parcel to whoever is at the front desk."
**B) The café whose windows fog up in winter serves great soup.**

Possessive whose correctly links the café to windows. Whose is fine with inanimate subjects in formal prose. Who's would fail the expansion test before windows.

This is sound — whose correctly marks possession for the café's windows.
**C) Loud music will effect the baby's nap downstairs.**

The meaning is influence on the baby's nap, so write will affect. There is no a change or result object to license verb effect. If nothing is being brought about, prefer affect.

**Trap:** Will effect sounds deliberate but only fits bring-about objects.

That fails here — rewrite as "Loud music will affect the baby's nap downstairs."
**D) This argument stays between my sister and I.**

The object of between must be me: between my sister and me. Sister and I is subject-case hypercorrection after a preposition. The same rule applies as between you and me.

**Trap:** Coordinated I after between looks elegant but is still wrong.

Reject this; rewrite as "This argument stays between my sister and me."
**E) One key criterion is still missing from the checklist.**

Singular criterion correctly pairs with is. One key item forces the singular Latin form. One item → criterion; several → criteria.

Keep this: singular criterion agrees with is.
tasks.solution_overview:
Difficulty steps up: clause subjects after to, possessive whose with places, affect vs effect, object pronouns after between, and criterion vs criteria.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Several lines look polish-formal yet hide subject-case or influence errors. Check be after the wh-word, whose with café, affect for influence, me after between, and singular criterion.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If a finite verb follows the wh-word, suspect subject case. Expand who's. Ask influence vs bring about. Strip the coordination after between. Match number: one criterion / several criteria.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We will ask whoever the tutor recommends.
Who's been watering the plants while we were away?
The announcement had little effect on the waiting queue.
Fewer than twelve seats were still free.
These criteria was written after the rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We will ask whoever the tutor recommends.**

Whoever is widely accepted as the object of recommends and is the safer exam default when case is contested. Markers rarely accept whomever as a subject; they often accept whoever as an object. Ask whoever the tutor recommends reads cleanly in modern exam English.

**Tip:** Prefer whoever in contested object slots unless traditional object case is unmistakable.

Trust this wording: whoever is the safe object form after recommends.
**B) Who's been watering the plants while we were away?**

Who's equals who has before the past participle been. Who's been watering… is a standard perfect contraction. Expansion: who has been.

That works — who's correctly contracts who has before been.
**C) The announcement had little effect on the waiting queue.**

Noun effect meaning result or impact is correct after little. Article or quantifier + effect usually signals the noun, not the verb. Had little effect on… is the classic frame.

Accept the line: effect as a noun correctly names the result.
**D) Fewer than twelve seats were still free.**

Countable seats take fewer than: Fewer than twelve seats. Fewer than + number + plural noun is the careful form. Less than twelve seats is the common informal trap.

Keep this: fewer than correctly counts the free seats.
**E) These criteria was written after the rehearsal.**

Plural criteria needs were, not was. These criteria was written flips number against the plural head. Never pair criteria with a singular verb in formal answers.

**Trap:** Was with these criteria is a textbook Latin-plural agreement miss.

Discard this and write "These criteria were written after the rehearsal."
tasks.solution_overview:
Four statements are solid; one plural-agreement error with criteria closes the set.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm contractions (who's been), the noun effect after little, fewer with numbered countable items, and plural verb agreement with criteria.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept whoever in contested object slots when unsure, expand who's, treat little effect as a noun phrase, prefer fewer than with plurals, and force were/are/have with criteria.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Assign the chore to whoever the rota lists as free.
The runner who's shoes came untied lost several seconds.
Spicy food can affect sleep if you eat late.
Less volunteers signed up for the clean-up.
The judging criteria remain unchanged this year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Assign the chore to whoever the rota lists as free.**

Whoever functions acceptably as the object of lists in modern exam English. Prefer whoever unless the object case is unmistakable and required. Assign… to whoever the rota lists as free is the safe mark-winning form.

Keep this: whoever is the safer object form after lists.
**B) The runner who's shoes came untied lost several seconds.**

Possession is needed — whose shoes, not who's. Who's expands to who is or who has and fails before shoes. Expand every who's before you accept it.

**Trap:** Who's shoes looks neat but cannot mean who is shoes.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The runner whose shoes came untied lost several seconds."
**C) Spicy food can affect sleep if you eat late.**

Verb affect correctly means influence sleep after late spicy food. Subject influences object → affect. No bring-about result frame appears here.

This is sound — affect correctly names the influence on sleep.
**D) Less volunteers signed up for the clean-up.**

Volunteers are countable people, so use Fewer volunteers. Less volunteers is the headcount error examiners love. Headcount plurals take fewer.

**Trap:** Less before a countable people plural is a classic fewer/less flip.

That fails here — rewrite as "Fewer volunteers signed up for the clean-up."
**E) The judging criteria remain unchanged this year.**

Plural criteria correctly takes plural remain. Watch subject–verb number with Latin plurals. Remain is a clean plural partner for criteria.

Accept the line: remain correctly agrees with plural criteria.
tasks.solution_overview:
Scan for the possessive/contraction slip and the fewer/less headcount error; keep affect and criteria agreement clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Two false lines misuse who's for whose and less for fewer. The affect and criteria lines should read true if you keep influence and plural agreement in mind.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand who's, ask whether volunteers can be counted, confirm affect for influence, and match criteria to a plural verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Congratulate whomever you choose for the lead role.
A bakery whose ovens failed closed early on Friday.
Management intends to effect several schedule changes.
Please discuss the surprise only between you and me.
We noticed less delays on the morning bus route.
tactical_explanations:
